sections.body:
Endocarditis is a diagnostic and therapeutic emergency with a 15–30% in-hospital mortality. The Duke criteria diagnose it, the echocardiogram characterises it, and the indications for emergency surgery are some of the most carefully defined in all of cardiology.

## Pathogenesis

IE begins with bacteraemia seeding a susceptible site — typically damaged, abnormal, or prosthetic valve endothelium. The sequence:

1. Valve endothelial damage (from turbulent flow, pre-existing valve disease, prosthetic material) → fibrin and platelet deposition → non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE)
2. Transient bacteraemia (dental procedures, GI/GU procedures, IV access, skin infection) → bacteria adhere to NBTE
3. Bacterial colonisation → vegetations (fibrin, platelets, bacteria) → progressive leaflet destruction, abscess formation, perforation

## Microbiology — organism and valve type

| Organism | Source / context | Key features | Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Staph. aureus | Healthcare-associated, IV drug use, skin/soft tissue infection, IV lines, prosthetic valves | Most aggressive — rapid valve destruction, high embolic risk, frequent brain abscess. Both native and prosthetic. Right-sided in IVDU. | ~30% of IE (most common overall) |
| Viridans streptococci (S. sanguinis, S. mutans, S. mitis) | Oral cavity, dental procedures | Sub-acute course, classic "bacterial endocarditis" pattern. Native valves with pre-existing disease. Highly penicillin-sensitive. | ~20–25% |
| Streptococcus gallolyticus (S. bovis group) | Gastrointestinal tract (bacteraemia from colon) | Associated with colorectal carcinoma — always colonoscopy when this organism is identified | ~10% |
| Enterococci (E. faecalis, E. faecium) | GI/GU tract, elderly, nosocomial | Often aminoglycoside-resistant. Difficult to treat — prolonged dual therapy. | ~10% |
| HACEK organisms | Oral flora (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) | Slow-growing, sub-acute, large vegetations, high embolic risk. Require prolonged culture. | ~5% |
| Coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis) | Prosthetic valve endocarditis (early, within 1 year of surgery); line-associated | Biofilm-forming, methicillin-resistant often. Difficult to eradicate — usually requires surgery. | ~10–15% (prosthetic) |
| Fungi (Candida, Aspergillus) | Immunocompromised, prolonged antibiotics, IV drug use, TPN | Very large vegetations, high embolic risk, poor prognosis, surgery almost always required | Rare (~2%) |

## Duke criteria — the diagnostic framework

### Major criteria

1. Positive blood cultures: ≥2 separate cultures with a typical IE organism (Viridans strep, S. bovis, HACEK, S. aureus, or community-acquired Enterococcus) OR persistently positive cultures (>12h apart) with any organism OR single positive culture for Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) or anti-phase 1 IgG titre >1:800
2. Imaging evidence of endocardial involvement: vegetation, abscess, pseudoaneurysm, or new intracardiac fistula on echo or CT; new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve; new valvular regurgitation (new murmur alone is not sufficient)

### Minor criteria

Predisposing cardiac condition or IV drug use; fever ≥38°C; vascular phenomena (arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, Janeway lesions, intracranial haemorrhage, conjunctival haemorrhages); immunological phenomena (glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, positive rheumatoid factor); microbiological evidence not meeting major criteria (single positive blood culture or serology for an organism consistent with IE).

### Classification

- Definite IE: 2 major criteria, OR 1 major + 3 minor, OR 5 minor criteria
- Possible IE: 1 major + 1 minor, OR 3 minor criteria
- Rejected: firm alternate diagnosis, resolution with ≤4 days antibiotics, or criteria not met

Key concept: Three blood cultures before antibiotics — this is the single most important investigation in suspected IE
Blood cultures are the most diagnostically important test in IE. The bacteraemia of IE is continuous (bacteria are constantly being shed from the vegetation), so all three cultures should be positive if IE is present. Crucially: DO NOT give antibiotics before drawing blood cultures unless the patient is in septic shock. Once antibiotics are given, blood cultures are negative within hours — you lose your best chance at identifying the organism and guiding targeted therapy. The delay of 30–60 minutes to draw three sets of cultures before antibiotics in a non-shocked patient is worth the delay. Draw three sets from three different sites, 30 minutes apart (or simultaneously if the patient is unstable). Two out of three cultures positive with the same organism = a major Duke criterion.

## Echocardiography in IE

- Transthoracic echo (TTE): first investigation. Sensitivity 60–75% for native valve vegetation; lower for prosthetic. If positive and diagnostic → acceptable. If negative but clinical suspicion high → proceed to TOE.
- Transoesophageal echo (TOE): gold standard. Sensitivity >95% for native valve vegetation; 85–90% for prosthetic. Far superior for: perivalvular abscesses (aortic root abscess in ~30% of aortic IE), fistulae, prosthetic valve dehiscence, leaflet perforation. TOE should be performed in all suspected IE, especially if prosthetic valve, intracardiac device, or if TTE is non-diagnostic.
- CT/PET-CT: useful for detecting peripheral emboli, mycotic aneurysms, and in prosthetic valve IE where TOE may have limited views.

## Indications for emergency surgery in IE (ESC 2023)

| Indication | Urgency | Class |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Severe acute AR or MR causing refractory pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock | Emergency (within 24h) | Class I |
| Perivalvular abscess or fistula | Urgent (within days) | Class I |
| Fungal endocarditis or organism resistant to antibiotics | Urgent | Class I |
| Mobile vegetation >10 mm with severe valve dysfunction (high embolic risk) | Urgent | Class IIa |
| Persistent bacteraemia or fever >7–10 days despite appropriate antibiotics | Elective (within weeks) | Class I |
| Prosthetic valve endocarditis with severe dysfunction or dehiscence | Urgent | Class I |
| Second embolic episode despite adequate antibiotic therapy | Urgent | Class IIa |

## Antibiotic therapy — principles and key regimens

- Empirical therapy (before cultures): IV amoxicillin-sulbactam + gentamicin (native valve, community-acquired); vancomycin + gentamicin (prosthetic valve or healthcare-associated)
- Staph. aureus native valve: IV oxacillin (MSSA) or vancomycin (MRSA) for 4–6 weeks
- Viridans streptococci: IV penicillin G or amoxicillin ± gentamicin for 4 weeks (or 2-week accelerated regimen in selected uncomplicated cases)
- Enterococcus: IV amoxicillin + ceftriaxone (preferred for E. faecalis) for 6 weeks — the double beta-lactam combination avoids aminoglycoside toxicity

Exam tip: Anticoagulation in IE — the clinical dilemma: Patients with IE on mechanical valves need anticoagulation to prevent valve thrombosis. But IE carries high embolic risk (vegetation fragments). Anticoagulation does not prevent embolic events from vegetations (it prevents thrombus, not vegetation). The risk: anticoagulation + intracranial embolic event = haemorrhagic transformation → intracranial haemorrhage → death. Guidelines: if a patient on anticoagulation for mechanical valve develops IE and then has a neurological complication → stop warfarin for 2–4 weeks. Resume only after imaging shows no haemorrhage and neurological status is stable. For native valve IE: anticoagulation is NOT indicated unless there is another indication (AF, VTE, etc.) — routine anticoagulation does not reduce embolic events and increases bleeding risk.

Checkpoint: A 45-year-old dentist presents with 3 weeks of fever, fatigue, and new onset dyspnoea. He had dental extraction 4 weeks ago without antibiotic prophylaxis. Blood cultures: 3/3 positive for Streptococcus sanguinis. TOE: 12 mm mobile vegetation on the anterior mitral leaflet with perforation and severe MR. He is haemodynamically stable, NYHA II. What are the two key management decisions?
1. Antibiotic therapy immediately: Streptococcus sanguinis (viridans group) is highly penicillin-sensitive. Start IV benzylpenicillin (penicillin G) 12–18 MU/day in divided doses (or IV amoxicillin 200 mg/kg/day) for 4–6 weeks. Add gentamicin synergy for the first 2 weeks (if renal function permits). Blood cultures should be repeated 48–72h after starting antibiotics to confirm clearance. Do not stop antibiotics early even if fevers settle rapidly. 2. Plan for urgent cardiac surgery within days: the surgical indications are met: (a) vegetation >10 mm with severe valve dysfunction (Class IIa → urgent surgery); (b) leaflet perforation causing severe MR — this will not heal with antibiotics alone; the structural damage requires repair. The goal: surgical intervention after a short course of antibiotics (5–10 days if haemodynamically stable) to reduce bacteraemia risk during surgery and reduce vegetation burden, but before progressive LV dilation or further embolic events. Mitral valve repair (if feasible — the anterior leaflet perforation may be repaired with pericardial patch) is preferred over replacement to preserve LV function. Given his age (45) and the lesion, an experienced mitral repair surgeon should be involved from the outset. Antibiotic prophylaxis: this case illustrates exactly why antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures was historically recommended for patients with valvular disease — however, current ESC guidelines restrict prophylaxis to only highest-risk patients (prosthetic valves, prior IE, congenital heart disease with unrepaired or residual defects at high-risk sites).

sections.body:
Rheumatic heart disease is the most common cause of cardiovascular morbidity in young adults across the developing world. In Indonesia, it is responsible for the majority of valvular surgery performed outside tertiary Java centres. The story from streptococcal sore throat to valve replacement is entirely preventable — and understanding why prevention fails is as important as knowing how to treat the disease.

## From strep throat to rheumatic fever to valve disease

The pathogenic sequence begins with Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus (GAS, S. pyogenes) pharyngeal infection. In a susceptible host (genetic predisposition — HLA alleles), the immune response generates antibodies that cross-react with cardiac myosin, laminin, and valve endothelium — a molecular mimicry mechanism. This autoimmune attack causes pancarditis (myocarditis, pericarditis, and most importantly — valvulitis) during acute rheumatic fever (ARF). The valvulitis leaves scarring on the leaflets and chordae that progressively worsens with recurrent episodes.

The Jones Criteria for ARF diagnosis (2015 revised):

- Major criteria: carditis (clinical or subclinical on echo), arthritis (migratory polyarthritis in low-prevalence; monoarthritis acceptable in high-prevalence populations), chorea (Sydenham's chorea), erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules
- Minor criteria: fever, elevated ESR/CRP, prolonged PR interval
- Diagnosis: 2 major OR 1 major + 2 minor criteria, PLUS evidence of preceding GAS infection (positive throat culture, elevated ASO titre, anti-DNase B)
- High-prevalence populations (Indonesia): monoarthritis alone (not just polyarthritis) qualifies as a major criterion; subclinical carditis (echo without auscultatory signs) counts as major

## Pattern of valve involvement in rheumatic disease

Rheumatic fever causes valvulitis in a characteristic distribution. The mitral valve is nearly always affected first and most severely:

- Mitral valve alone: ~65% of rheumatic HD — most commonly as MR initially, progressing to combined MS+MR, then eventually pure MS as commissural fusion advances
- Mitral + aortic valve: ~25% — combined lesions are common in advanced rheumatic disease
- Aortic valve alone: ~5%
- Tricuspid and pulmonary valves: rarely affected directly by rheumatism; TV involvement is usually secondary to elevated right heart pressures from MS-driven pulmonary hypertension

Key concept: The mitral valve is the dominant rheumatic target — rheumatic aortic disease almost never occurs without concurrent mitral involvement
This is clinically useful: if you find isolated aortic valve disease in a young Indonesian patient without mitral involvement, rheumatic aetiology is less likely — think bicuspid AV, connective tissue disease, or other causes. Conversely, if both mitral and aortic valves are diseased in a 30–40 year-old, rheumatic heart disease is the most likely cause in Indonesia. Always examine the mitral valve carefully in patients with rheumatic aortic disease — concurrent MS may be missed because the aortic murmur dominates the physical examination, and the mitral diastolic rumble of MS is quiet and easily overlooked.

## Secondary prophylaxis — the most important intervention in RHD

Once ARF has occurred, recurrent GAS infections trigger further attacks of carditis, causing progressive valve damage. Secondary prophylaxis (regular penicillin injections to prevent GAS re-infection) is the most effective intervention to prevent RHD progression:

- Benzathine penicillin G (BPG) 1.2 MU IM every 28 days — the global standard. Every-3-week dosing (every 21 days) provides more consistent trough levels and is used in very high-risk patients.
- Oral alternatives: phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) 250 mg BD or amoxicillin 250 mg OD — inferior to injection (compliance is unreliable)
- Penicillin allergy: erythromycin 250 mg BD (alternative; sulphonamides are used in some countries)

Duration:

- ARF without carditis: prophylaxis for 5 years or until age 21 (whichever is longer)
- ARF with mild-moderate carditis: until age 25 (or 10 years post-episode, whichever longer)
- ARF with severe carditis, significant valve disease, or post-valve surgery: until age 40 or lifelong — because recurrent strep infection on a diseased/prosthetic valve carries high risk of endocarditis and accelerated valve deterioration

## Indonesian context — barriers and challenges

Several factors in Indonesia amplify the RHD burden and complicate secondary prophylaxis:

- Healthcare access: monthly BPG injection requires regular health facility visits — challenging in rural NTB, Papua, and remote Eastern Indonesia regions. Distance, cost of transport, and patient education gaps reduce adherence.
- BPJS Kesehatan coverage: BPG injections are covered under BPJS Kesehatan but may not always be available at all Faskes Tingkat I (primary care facilities). Supply chain gaps mean injections are sometimes missed.
- Diagnosis gap: many children with subclinical carditis from ARF are never diagnosed. Echo-based screening programmes (WHO-endorsed) are needed to identify pre-symptomatic RHD.
- Late presentation: patients in Indonesia commonly present with advanced RHD (severe MS with AF, pulmonary hypertension, NYHA III–IV) having lived with the condition for years without diagnosis. Balloon valvuloplasty under BPJS coverage provides definitive treatment but waiting lists at major centres (RSUP Sanglah, RSUP Kariadi, RSUP Dr Wahidin) can be long.

## Echocardiographic screening for subclinical RHD (World Heart Federation criteria)

Echocardiographic screening in school-age children identifies subclinical RHD (valve changes without audible murmur) at a pre-symptomatic stage when secondary prophylaxis can prevent progression:

- Definite RHD: pathological MR by Doppler (≥2 cm long, velocity >2.5 m/s, pansystolic) with morphological valve changes (anterior MV leaflet thickening, restricted posterior MV leaflet motion, elongated anterior MV leaflet, chordal thickening)
- Borderline RHD: isolated pathological MR without morphological changes, or morphological changes without MR

Checkpoint: A 24-year-old woman from Sumbawa is referred to your cardiology clinic in Mataram. She presents with dyspnoea NYHA III and palpitations for 3 months. She recalls no childhood joint pains or hospitalisation. Echo: MVA 1.1 cm² (Wilkins score 7), severe MR (EROA 0.45 cm², prolapse — no rheumatic morphology), EF 65%, PASP 52 mmHg, LA 5.8 cm, AF on ECG. What is the valve assessment, what complicates the decision for BMV, and what is the single contraindication you must exclude before proceeding?
Valve assessment: moderate-severe mitral stenosis (MVA 1.1 cm², borderline for severe by MVA <1.0 cm² but functionally significantly stenotic given her symptoms and PASP) WITH concurrent severe mitral regurgitation (EROA 0.45 cm²). The presence of both lesions — MS and severe MR on the same valve — is typical of rheumatic combined MV disease. The "no rheumatic morphology" comment on prolapse may reflect incomplete assessment; rheumatic valves with mixed MS+MR can have anterior leaflet prolapse as part of the pathology. What complicates BMV: significant concurrent MR (EROA 0.45 cm² = severe) is a relative contraindication to BMV. BMV tears the fused commissures open — if the valve is already severely regurgitant, further commissurotomy may worsen the MR dramatically → acute severe MR → emergency surgery. With severe MR + moderate MS → surgical mitral valve repair or replacement is the more appropriate intervention rather than BMV. Absolute contraindication to exclude before any decision: left atrial appendage thrombus. She has AF + severely dilated LA (5.8 cm) + significant MS — a classic thrombus setup. TOE must be performed before any intervention (BMV, cardioversion, or even surgery with cardioplegia). If LAA thrombus is present: anticoagulate for ≥3 months with warfarin and confirm resolution on repeat TOE before intervention. This step cannot be skipped — missing an LAA thrombus and proceeding to intervention risks catastrophic systemic embolism.

sections.body:
Risk is not a fixed property of a person — it is a probability estimate that changes with every intervention, every year of age, and every lifestyle modification. Understanding what risk means, how it behaves, and how to communicate it is the foundation of all preventive practice.

## The cardiovascular risk continuum

Cardiovascular risk is not binary (high-risk vs not-at-risk). It exists on a continuum from the very first LDL particle that enters an artery wall in adolescence to the fatal MI decades later. Every stage of atherosclerosis — from endothelial dysfunction to fatty streak to fibrous plaque to rupture — represents an opportunity to slow or reverse progression. This is why prevention works at any age: even treating a 70-year-old with statin after their first event (secondary prevention) reduces subsequent events substantially.

## Primary vs secondary vs primordial prevention

Primordial prevention: Preventing the development of risk factors in the first place. Population-level interventions: tobacco advertising bans, school nutrition programmes, urban design for physical activity, sodium reduction in processed foods. No risk factors have yet developed — the intervention keeps the trajectory flat.

Primary prevention: Preventing a first cardiovascular event in someone with risk factors but no established ASCVD. Identifying high-risk individuals and treating their risk factors (statin, antihypertensive) before the first MI or stroke occurs.

Secondary prevention: Preventing recurrent events in patients with established ASCVD (prior MI, stroke, PCI, CABG, PAD). These patients are at much higher absolute risk — the benefit of intervention is proportionally larger. All secondary prevention patients receive dual antiplatelet, statin, ACEi/ARB, and beta-blocker (where appropriate) as a default bundle.

Tertiary prevention / rehabilitation: Minimising the consequences of established disease — cardiac rehabilitation, chronic HF management, palliative care. Beyond pure prevention but part of the continuum of care.

## Absolute risk vs relative risk — the most important distinction in preventive medicine

Key concept: Absolute risk reduction (ARR), not relative risk reduction (RRR), is the number that determines whether to treat an individual patient
Example: a statin reduces 10-year ASCVD risk by 30% relative risk reduction. What does this mean for two different patients?
Patient A: 10-year absolute risk = 20% → with statin: 20% × 0.70 = 14% → ARR = 6%. NNT = 1/0.06 ≈ 17 (treat 17 people to prevent 1 event over 10 years).
Patient B: 10-year absolute risk = 2% → with statin: 2% × 0.70 = 1.4% → ARR = 0.6%. NNT = 1/0.006 ≈ 167.
The relative benefit of the statin is identical (30%) in both patients. The absolute benefit is 10× larger in Patient A. Treatment of Patient A is clearly worthwhile; treatment of Patient B from a pure population perspective is inefficient. Pharmaceutical trials report RRR (it sounds more impressive); clinicians need ARR and NNT to make treatment decisions.

## The concept of residual risk

Even when all currently treatable risk factors are optimally managed, substantial cardiovascular risk remains. This "residual risk" is driven by factors that current standard-of-care does not fully address:

- Residual lipid risk: even with LDL-C at target, triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (TG, remnant cholesterol), low HDL-C, and Lp(a) contribute independently
- Residual inflammatory risk: atherosclerosis is an inflammatory disease. Persistent systemic inflammation (measured by hs-CRP) predicts events even with optimal LDL-C (the CANTOS trial showed anti-inflammatory therapy with canakinumab reduced CV events beyond LDL-C reduction)
- Residual thrombotic risk: platelet activation, coagulation cascade, and fibrinolysis impairment — addressed by antiplatelet therapy but not eliminated

Residual risk explains why even perfectly-treated patients continue to have events, and drives the search for additional therapies targeting inflammation, Lp(a), and thrombosis.

## The burden of risk factors in Indonesia — Riskesdas 2018

Indonesian context: Indonesia's preventive cardiology landscape is shaped by an epidemiological transition — the classic infectious disease burden is declining while non-communicable diseases are rising steeply:
Hypertension: 34.1% prevalence (adults ≥18y). Only 11.8% controlled. Majority unaware they have hypertension ("silent killer" problem). Higher in urban areas, older age groups, women > men ≥45 years.
Dyslipidaemia: 28.0% with total cholesterol >200 mg/dL. Only a minority on treatment. Access to statins through BPJS at Faskes Tingkat I: simvastatin 10–40 mg (generic, widely available); atorvastatin 10–40 mg (FORNAS). High-potency statins (rosuvastatin) and non-statin agents (ezetimibe, PCSK9i) are rarely available at primary care level.
Diabetes: 10.9% prevalence (2018), rising from 5.7% in 2007 — a near-doubling in 11 years. Indonesia is in the top 10 countries globally for diabetes burden. 70% of diabetics are undiagnosed.
Smoking: 76% of adult men smoke (among the highest in the world). Youth initiation age is decreasing. Kretek (clove cigarettes) constitute ~90% of the market — they deliver higher tar and nicotine than regular cigarettes.
Physical inactivity: 33.5% of adults do not meet minimum physical activity recommendations. Urban sedentary behaviour is increasing with smartphone and motorised transport penetration.
Obesity: 13.6% obesity (BMI >27 kg/m² — WHO Asia-Pacific threshold); 21.8% overweight. Abdominal obesity (waist circumference >90 cm in men, >80 cm in women) is highly prevalent and underdiagnosed.

Mental model: Think of cardiovascular risk as a river system. Each risk factor is a tributary feeding into the river. The size of the main river (absolute risk) depends on which tributaries are flowing and how full they are. Intervening on one tributary (treating LDL alone) reduces flow but doesn't stop all tributaries. The most effective prevention strategy addresses the largest tributaries simultaneously. In Indonesia, tobacco is Kali Code — its contribution dwarfs most other tributaries, which is why smoking cessation has the largest single-risk-factor benefit of any preventive intervention. Every consultation with a smoker is an opportunity to intervene on the largest tributary in that patient's risk river.

Checkpoint: A pharmaceutical company presents data that their new drug reduces CV events by 25% relative risk reduction. A cardiologist says: "That's very impressive — we should prescribe it to everyone." What is wrong with this analysis, and what additional information do you need before recommending it?
The 25% RRR statistic alone is insufficient to make a prescribing decision. Needed: (1) Absolute risk of the study population: if the trial enrolled high-risk patients (15–20% 10-year risk) → ARR ≈ 4–5%, NNT ≈ 20–25 → meaningful benefit. If trial enrolled low-risk patients (3–4% 10-year risk) → ARR ≈ 0.75–1%, NNT ≈ 100–133 → very modest absolute benefit. The 25% RRR is the same in both cases. (2) Side effects and harm: what is the absolute risk increase of serious adverse events? A drug that reduces CV events by ARR 1% but increases serious bleeding by ARR 0.8% has a much less favourable risk-benefit ratio. (3) Cost: NNT 100 with a drug costing USD 5,000/year means USD 500,000 per event prevented — a relevant consideration in BPJS-covered settings. (4) Applicability to Indonesian patients: was the trial conducted in Asian populations? Indonesian patients may have different baseline risk profiles, pharmacokinetics (CYP polymorphisms), and comorbidity patterns. The lesson: always convert RRR to ARR and NNT before making population-level prescribing recommendations.

sections.body:
Standard risk scores miss a substantial proportion of patients who will develop cardiovascular events. Novel biomarkers and coronary imaging fill the gap — refining risk estimates in borderline patients, identifying hidden high-risk individuals, and guiding the decision to initiate preventive therapy in the uncertain middle ground.

## hs-CRP and the JUPITER trial

High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) is a marker of systemic inflammation produced by the liver in response to IL-6. It is an independent predictor of CV events beyond traditional risk factors. JUPITER trial (2008): 17,802 men and women with LDL-C <3.4 mmol/L but hs-CRP ≥2 mg/L → randomised to rosuvastatin 20 mg vs placebo. Rosuvastatin reduced LDL-C 50%, hs-CRP 37%, and the primary CV endpoint by 44% (ARR 1.8%). Trial stopped early. This established that: (1) statins benefit patients with low LDL-C but elevated hs-CRP, and (2) hs-CRP is a clinically useful biomarker to identify statin candidates beyond LDL-C.

Current guideline use of hs-CRP: a risk-enhancing factor (ACC/AHA 2018) — hs-CRP ≥2.0 mg/L supports initiating statin therapy in borderline-risk (PCE 7.5–20%) patients who are otherwise uncertain candidates. Not recommended as a universal screening test — use selectively in borderline-risk patients where the result will change management.

## Lipoprotein(a) — Lp(a)

Lp(a) is an LDL-like particle covalently bound to apolipoprotein(a). Its levels are 80–90% genetically determined (largely independent of lifestyle or diet), and elevated Lp(a) is a causal, independent risk factor for atherosclerotic CVD and aortic stenosis, confirmed by Mendelian randomisation studies.

- Elevated Lp(a) threshold: ≥50 mg/dL (≥125 nmol/L) is the commonly used cut-off for increased risk (ESC/EAS consensus 2022)
- Prevalence: ~20% of the general population; higher in South Asians and Black populations
- Current treatment limitation: Lp(a) is not reduced by statins, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors (only modest 20–25% reduction with PCSK9i — still reduces Lp(a) somewhat). PCSK9 inhibitors are currently the only approved drug that reduces Lp(a), though only modestly. Niacin reduces Lp(a) 20–30% but had no CV benefit in HPS2-THRIVE.
- Emerging therapies: antisense oligonucleotides (pelacarsen — LICA study) and siRNA therapies (olpasiran — OCEAN(a)-DOSE) reduce Lp(a) by 80–95%. Phase 3 CV outcomes trials ongoing (HORIZON trial). These agents could become the first Lp(a)-specific treatment.
- Current clinical use: measure Lp(a) once in every patient's lifetime — high Lp(a) (≥50 mg/dL) reclassifies borderline-risk patients to higher risk, supports earlier/more intensive statin therapy, and cascade screens first-degree relatives.

## Coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring

Non-contrast CT scan of the coronary arteries quantifies calcium in the coronary walls. Calcium = irreversible atherosclerosis marker. Reported as Agatston score.

| CAC Score | Interpretation | Clinical action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | No calcified plaque — "warranty period" of ~10 years | May defer statin in borderline-risk patients. Reassure but advise lifestyle. Repeat CAC in 5–10 years. |
| 1–99 | Mild atherosclerosis | Supports statin initiation in borderline-risk patients. Lifestyle intensification. |
| 100–399 | Moderate atherosclerosis | Statin initiation appropriate in most patients. |
| ≥400 | Severe atherosclerosis — risk equivalent to established ASCVD | High-intensity statin, consider aspirin discussion, aggressive risk factor management. |
| ≥75th percentile for age/sex/race | Above-average calcification for demographic | Supports upward risk reclassification. |

MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis): CAC score outperforms traditional risk scores in predicting 10-year CV events. CAC = 0 confers an annual event rate of ~0.1–0.2% — remarkably low, supporting a "statin holiday" discussion in borderline-risk patients who prefer to defer drug therapy.

## Ankle-brachial index (ABI) — peripheral arterial disease as a risk marker

ABI = ankle systolic BP / brachial systolic BP. Normal: 1.0–1.4. ABI <0.9 = peripheral arterial disease (PAD). ABI >1.4 = non-compressible calcified vessels (common in DM, CKD — falsely elevated ABI). ABI <0.9 is a risk-enhancing factor that reclassifies borderline-risk patients upward. PAD is a manifestation of systemic atherosclerosis — patients with PAD have the same (or higher) CV event rates as those with CAD or prior stroke. Low ABI is associated with 2–4× higher CV mortality.

## Coronary CT angiography (CCTA)

CCTA provides anatomical information about coronary plaque burden and stenosis severity without invasive catheterisation. Beyond stenosis detection, CCTA characterises plaque vulnerability (low-attenuation non-calcified plaque = vulnerable/unstable plaque; pericoronary fat attenuation = local inflammation). SCOT-HEART trial (2018): CCTA-guided management vs standard care in chest pain patients → improved diagnosis of stable CAD, reduction in fatal MI at 5 years (2.3% vs 3.9%). CCTA is increasingly being studied as a primary prevention tool — high plaque burden on CCTA predicts events beyond risk scores.

Exam tip: The risk-enhancing factor clinical decision tree — when to order additional testing: Patient is borderline or intermediate risk (PCE 5–20%) AND the treatment decision is uncertain (patient ambivalent, or risk factors at threshold)
Step 1: check for risk-enhancing factors (family history, Lp(a), hs-CRP, ABI, metabolic syndrome)
Step 2: if still uncertain after reviewing risk-enhancing factors → order CAC score
CAC = 0 in a borderline-risk patient with no other risk enhancers → statin deferral reasonable
CAC ≥100 in same patient → statin initiation appropriate
Do NOT order CAC in very-high-risk patients (established ASCVD, FH, DM with organ damage) — they already qualify for high-intensity statin; CAC score will not change management.

Checkpoint: A 54-year-old male teacher, PCE 10-year risk 9% (intermediate), LDL-C 3.2 mmol/L, no DM, non-smoker. He is unwilling to take statins ("I don't want to take drugs for the rest of my life"). He asks if there is a test that can show him whether he personally is at risk. How do you use CAC scoring in this consultation?
This is the ideal use case for CAC scoring — a motivated, informed patient in the intermediate-risk range who is willing to act on objective test results. Frame it: "We can take a special CT scan that counts calcium deposits in your heart arteries. No injections, no radiation equivalent to more than 10 chest X-rays. It directly shows whether atherosclerosis has already started in your arteries." Explain the two possible outcomes and what each means: If CAC = 0: your arteries have no detectable calcium — your risk is likely lower than the score suggests. We would recommend lifestyle intensification (Mediterranean diet, exercise, no smoking) and revisit the statin question in 5–10 years or if risk factors worsen. If CAC ≥100: atherosclerosis has already started in your arteries. This level of calcium confirms that your risk is real and statin therapy is appropriate. The question is no longer "should I take a statin?" — it is "which statin and at what dose?" Most patients who see their own calcium score find it highly motivating — a concrete, visual representation of their own arterial health is often more persuasive than any population statistics. This is one of the few areas in medicine where a diagnostic test has been shown to improve patient adherence to preventive therapy. The CAC scan converts an abstract probability into a personal finding.

sections.body:
Few preventive cardiology topics have shifted as dramatically in recent years as aspirin in primary prevention. Three landmark trials in 2018 — ASPREE, ARRIVE, and ASCEND — collectively changed the guideline recommendation from "consider aspirin in intermediate-risk patients" to "aspirin is not routinely recommended for primary prevention." Understanding why requires a careful analysis of absolute risks and benefits.

## Aspirin's mechanism and secondary prevention evidence

Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2) → reduces thromboxane A2 synthesis → reduces platelet aggregation → antithrombotic effect. This mechanism reduces atherothrombotic events (plaque rupture → platelet thrombus → MI/stroke) — which is why aspirin has robust secondary prevention evidence. The Antithrombotic Trialists Collaboration: aspirin in secondary prevention reduces serious vascular events by 19% (ARR ~1.5–2%/year in high-risk patients).

## The 2018 trials and the paradigm shift

### ASPREE (2018) — healthy elderly

19,114 healthy adults ≥70 years in Australia/USA, no prior CVD, randomised to aspirin 100 mg vs placebo. Primary endpoint: disability-free survival. Result: aspirin did not improve disability-free survival; increased major bleeding by 38% (GI haemorrhage, intracranial bleeding). Alarming: all-cause mortality was actually numerically higher in the aspirin group (primarily from cancer-related mortality — uncertain mechanism). Conclusion: aspirin in elderly patients without established CVD causes net harm.

### ARRIVE (2018) — intermediate-risk primary prevention

12,546 patients, estimated 10-year CV risk ~17.3% (intermediate), randomised to aspirin 100 mg vs placebo. Result: no significant reduction in the primary endpoint (MACE). Gastrointestinal bleeding doubled in the aspirin group. Lower-than-expected event rates (actual observed risk was only ~9% over 5 years — may have been primary-secondary prevention crossover by the trial's end). No net benefit.

### ASCEND (2018) — diabetics without established CVD

15,480 diabetics without established CVD, randomised to aspirin 100 mg vs placebo. Result: aspirin reduced serious vascular events by 12% (ARR 0.5%/year) but increased major bleeding by 29% (ARR 0.33%/year). The benefits and harms were nearly exactly offsetting — no net clinical benefit. The bleeding reduction from intensive statin therapy further narrows the aspirin benefit window in diabetics.

Key concept: Aspirin is no longer recommended for primary prevention in most patients — the bleeding risk from modern medicine's longer life expectancy and antiplatelet-naive populations has erased the marginal CV benefit
Why did aspirin lose its primary prevention role? The population risk has changed. In the 1980s–90s when the early aspirin trials were conducted, background CV risk was higher and antiplatelet therapy had a larger absolute benefit. Today: statins, antihypertensives, and smoking cessation have dramatically reduced event rates in primary prevention populations. Lower background event rates → smaller absolute benefit from aspirin. But aspirin's bleeding risk has NOT decreased. Result: the benefit:harm ratio has shifted unfavourably. Current recommendations (ACC/AHA 2022, ESC 2021): Aspirin for primary prevention — do not routinely recommend. Only consider in very-high-risk primary prevention patients (10-year risk ≥20%) without increased bleeding risk, and only after a shared decision-making discussion acknowledging the uncertain risk-benefit balance.

## Secondary prevention — aspirin remains standard of care

The paradigm shift applies only to primary prevention. In secondary prevention (established ASCVD: prior MI, stroke, PCI, CABG, PAD), aspirin's absolute benefit is large and well-established:

- Post-MI: aspirin 75–100 mg OD indefinitely — reduces recurrent MI, stroke, and vascular death
- Post-PCI: dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT: aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor) for the duration specified by the clinical context (12 months post-ACS-PCI; 1–6 months post-stable-angina-PCI depending on bleeding risk)
- Post-CABG: aspirin indefinitely
- Post-ischaemic stroke/TIA: aspirin + clopidogrel for 21 days (POINT/CHANCE trials), then aspirin alone or clopidogrel alone

## P2Y12 inhibitors — ticagrelor and prasugrel

P2Y12 inhibitors block the ADP receptor on platelets, preventing ADP-induced platelet aggregation. Used in combination with aspirin (DAPT) and in some high-risk patients as monotherapy (aspirin + P2Y12 drop, keep P2Y12 only — DE-ESCALATION strategy). Three agents compared in ACS:

- Clopidogrel: prodrug requiring CYP2C19 activation → variable effect (CYP2C19 loss-of-function variants in 25–30% of Asians — including Indonesians — reduce activation → subtherapeutic effect). Widely used, cheap, BPJS-covered.
- Ticagrelor: direct-acting (no CYP activation needed) → more reliable platelet inhibition. PLATO trial: ticagrelor superior to clopidogrel in ACS (mortality reduction). Side effect: dyspnoea (adenosine-mediated, usually mild, does not affect outcome). Not affected by CYP2C19 polymorphism.
- Prasugrel: prodrug but more efficient CYP activation than clopidogrel → more potent. TRITON-TIMI 38: superior to clopidogrel in PCI-treated ACS. Contraindicated: prior stroke/TIA (excess intracranial haemorrhage), age ≥75 years, weight <60 kg.

Exam tip: CYP2C19 polymorphism and clopidogrel in Southeast Asian patients: Clopidogrel is a prodrug requiring CYP2C19 for activation. The loss-of-function alleles CYP2C19*2 and CYP2C19*3 are present in approximately 25–30% of Southeast Asian and East Asian populations (vs ~15–20% in Europeans). These patients are "poor metabolisers" — clopidogrel does not work adequately, and their platelet aggregation is not reliably inhibited. In Indonesian patients with ACS or post-PCI: preferring ticagrelor over clopidogrel is supported by the pharmacogenomics and the PLATO trial outcome data. When ticagrelor is unavailable under BPJS (it is on the FORNAS at secondary/tertiary level), clopidogrel with awareness of the poor metaboliser risk is the pragmatic alternative. Point-of-care pharmacogenomic testing (CYP2C19 genotyping) is not routinely available in Indonesia but is available at some tertiary centres.

Checkpoint: A 64-year-old man, no prior CVD, T2DM on metformin, BP 128/78 on amlodipine, LDL-C 2.1 mmol/L on statin, non-smoker. He read online that "aspirin prevents heart attacks" and asks you to prescribe it. His 10-year PCE is 11%. How do you respond?
He has done exactly what a health-conscious patient should — reading, asking. The answer requires respectful, honest communication of the nuanced current evidence. Start with: "That was the recommendation a few years ago, but three large trials in 2018 showed that for people who haven't had a heart attack or stroke yet, aspirin causes about as much bleeding harm as cardiovascular benefit." For this patient specifically: PCE 11% = intermediate-high risk. His risk factors are well-controlled (BP, LDL, no smoking). ARRIVE-equivalent risk — no net benefit shown for aspirin at this risk level. The ASCEND trial (diabetic cohort like him) showed near-exact cancellation of benefit and bleeding harm. Current recommendation: do NOT prescribe aspirin for primary prevention. Explain: the drugs he is already taking (statin + antihypertensive) are proven to reduce events with a more favourable risk-benefit ratio than aspirin. His bleeding risk from aspirin (GI haemorrhage — especially relevant at age 64, more common in Indonesians due to high H. pylori prevalence and dietary factors) likely exceeds his CV benefit. Aspirin does NOT protect against: cancer, Alzheimer's disease, or general ageing — common misperceptions. Document the shared decision-making discussion. If he strongly prefers to take aspirin after understanding the evidence: 75–100 mg OD with a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) to reduce GI bleeding risk — but this is his informed preference, not a guideline recommendation.

sections.body:
Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in women globally — yet it is systematically under-recognised, under-investigated, and undertreated in women compared to men. Women have sex-specific risk factors that are entirely absent from standard risk scores, and the biology of atherosclerosis in women differs from men in ways that change clinical presentation, diagnosis, and treatment.

## Sex differences in CV risk — why standard scores miss women

Standard risk scores (FRS, PCE, SCORE2) were derived predominantly from male cohorts and apply the same risk calculation logic to women. The problem:

- Women present with ASCVD 7–10 years later than men — premenopausal oestrogen is cardioprotective (promotes vasodilation, reduces LDL oxidation, maintains HDL levels). After menopause, this protection is lost.
- Same risk factors are more dangerous in women: diabetes confers 2× higher relative CV risk in women vs men (diabetic women lose the oestrogen-conferred protection almost entirely); smoking carries a higher relative risk in women vs men; hypertension in women is more frequently associated with HFpEF and stroke than CHD.
- Atypical presentation: women with ACS more often present with atypical symptoms (fatigue, dyspnoea, nausea, back or jaw pain) rather than classic crushing chest pain → delayed diagnosis → worse outcomes. Women are more likely to be dismissed with non-cardiac diagnoses at initial presentation.
- MINOCA and spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD): more common in women. SCAD (non-atherosclerotic coronary dissection) is responsible for up to 40% of MI in women <50 years — and requires different management (avoid PCI, anticoagulation preferred, beta-blockers to reduce aortic shear stress).

## Female-specific risk factors — the "missing" risk factors in standard scores

| Risk factor | CV risk conferred | Clinical action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, gestational HTN) | 2× lifetime CHD risk; 4× stroke risk; early HF. Pre-eclampsia is not just a pregnancy complication — it is a marker of underlying vascular disease that persists. | Annual CV risk factor check post-delivery; early initiation of preventive therapy if additional risk factors develop. |
| Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) | 7× lifetime T2DM risk; increased ASCVD risk. GDM represents a "stress test" that reveals underlying β-cell insufficiency and insulin resistance. | Fasting glucose or OGTT at 6–12 weeks post-delivery; annual fasting glucose thereafter; lifestyle intervention. |
| Premature menopause (<40 years, surgical or natural) | Doubles CHD risk vs natural menopause ≥50 years. Loss of oestrogen protection accelerates atherosclerosis. | Consider hormone therapy (HRT) for symptom management + cardioprotection discussion. Low HRT risk in <10 years post-menopause and <60 years age. |
| Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) | Insulin resistance, obesity, DM, dyslipidaemia, HTN — metabolic syndrome cluster. Increased ASCVD risk over lifetime. | Cardiovascular risk factor screening and metabolic syndrome assessment in all PCOS patients. Lifestyle intervention; metformin for DM prevention. |
| Autoimmune conditions (SLE, RA) | 1.5–2× increased CVD risk. Chronic inflammation + corticosteroid use + immunosuppression effects. | Risk multiplier (1.5×) applied to risk score in RA. Hydroxychloroquine in SLE has cardioprotective properties. Minimise corticosteroid use. |
| Breast cancer treatment (radiation, chemotherapy) | Anthracyclines → cardiomyopathy; left thoracic radiation → coronary disease (10–20 year latency); trastuzumab → HF. | Cardio-oncology surveillance: echo before, during, and after treatment. CV risk factor optimisation before cancer treatment. |

## Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and CV risk — the nuanced evidence

The WHI (Women's Health Initiative, 2002) reported that combined oestrogen + progestogen HRT increased CHD, stroke, VTE, and breast cancer — causing a massive global withdrawal of HRT prescribing. However, re-analysis revealed that the WHI enrolled older women (mean age 63 — average 13 years post-menopause) who already had established subclinical atherosclerosis. In these women, oestrogen may have destabilised existing plaques rather than preventing new atherosclerosis.

The "timing hypothesis": oestrogen is cardioprotective when initiated in the "window of opportunity" — within 10 years of menopause and before age 60 — when arteries are still relatively disease-free. In these women, HRT reduces new ASCVD events (KEEPS trial, Danish Osteoporosis Prevention Study). HRT initiated >10 years post-menopause in older women with established disease → potential harm.

Current position (ESC 2021, NICE UK): HRT is not routinely recommended for CV prevention as a primary indication. However, for women <60 years within 10 years of menopause with vasomotor symptoms, HRT is reasonable — it improves quality of life and is not associated with increased CV risk in this group. Transdermal oestrogen (patch/gel) has lower VTE risk than oral oestrogen. Micronised progesterone preferred over synthetic progestins.

## Oral contraceptives and cardiovascular risk

Combined oral contraceptives (COC — oestrogen + progestin): increase VTE risk 3–4× (absolute risk remains low in young women without other risk factors — from ~1 to ~3–4 per 10,000 women-years). Small increased ischaemic stroke risk (mainly in women with migraine with aura — COC contraindicated in this group). Progestin-only pills: no significant VTE risk increase. Absolute CV risk from COC in healthy young non-smoking women is very low — but in women who smoke + COC: synergistic risk (40× increased MI risk in heavy smokers on COC aged >35 years — combined OCP contraindicated in smokers ≥35 years).

Key concept: A history of pre-eclampsia is a lifelong cardiovascular risk marker that every physician should document — not just a past obstetric complication
When a 45-year-old woman mentions "I had high blood pressure in my second pregnancy" — that is pre-eclampsia until proven otherwise, and it means her lifetime cardiovascular risk is doubled. Women who had pre-eclampsia develop hypertension 5–10 years earlier, have 2× CHD risk, and 4× stroke risk compared to women with normotensive pregnancies. At every cardiovascular consultation with a woman of reproductive age or older: ask specifically about hypertension in pregnancy, gestational diabetes, and premature birth (also a pregnancy complication associated with maternal CV risk). Record this in the CV risk assessment. Consider it a positive "stress test" that revealed underlying vascular vulnerability.

Checkpoint: A 42-year-old Indonesian woman, overweight (BMI 27.5 kg/m²), has had two pregnancies — one complicated by pre-eclampsia at 32 weeks (premature delivery) and one by gestational diabetes at term. She is otherwise well, non-smoker, BP today 132/84 mmHg, fasting glucose 6.2 mmol/L, LDL-C 3.4 mmol/L. No family history of early ASCVD. Her SCORE2 is 3.1% (low-moderate risk). How does the full clinical picture change your risk assessment and management?
Her SCORE2 of 3.1% significantly underestimates her true risk because it omits the female-specific risk factors. Adjusting the clinical picture: (1) Pre-eclampsia history: confers 2× lifetime CHD risk and early hypertension tendency. Her current BP 132/84 mmHg is above optimal — possibly the beginning of the hypertensive trajectory predicted by her pre-eclampsia history. (2) GDM history: 7× lifetime T2DM risk. Her current fasting glucose 6.2 mmol/L = impaired fasting glucose (pre-diabetes) — this is exactly the trajectory GDM leads to. She is one step from overt T2DM. (3) LDL-C 3.4 mmol/L: at intermediate risk with these risk enhancers, this is above the appropriate threshold. After reclassification: she is functionally high risk (at least), equivalent to a moderate-SCORE2 woman with risk-enhancing factors that double her underlying estimate. Management: (a) Lifestyle: Mediterranean/DASH diet pattern, weight loss to BMI <25 (waist circumference reduction), 150 min/week moderate exercise — all of which address all her risk factors simultaneously; (b) Annual fasting glucose (OGTT to accurately stage pre-diabetes → DM transition); (c) OGTT within 3 months — accurately determine glycaemic status; (d) Blood pressure monitoring: if BP consistently ≥130/80 mmHg on repeat measurement → start antihypertensive (perindopril/enalapril — also renoprotective if she progresses to DM); (e) Statin discussion: LDL-C 3.4 mmol/L in a reclassified high-risk patient → statin initiation appropriate. Target LDL-C <1.8 mmol/L (high-risk category); (f) Document pre-eclampsia and GDM in her lifelong CV risk record.

The kidneys and the heart are the two organs most tightly linked in cardiovascular disease. CKD is both a consequence of hypertension and diabetes, and an independent cause of cardiovascular events. The cardiorenal syndrome — where dysfunction of one organ propagates dysfunction of the other — requires simultaneous management of both.

## CKD as a cardiovascular risk multiplier

CKD (GFR <60 mL/min/1.73m² or albuminuria >30 mg/g for ≥3 months) confers markedly elevated CV risk — patients with CKD are more likely to die of a cardiovascular event than to progress to dialysis. Risk scales with severity:

- eGFR 45–59 (CKD G3a): CV risk 2× the general population
- eGFR 30–44 (CKD G3b): CV risk 4×
- eGFR 15–29 (CKD G4): CV risk 6–8×
- End-stage kidney disease (dialysis): CV mortality 10–30× age-matched general population

Mechanisms of accelerated atherosclerosis in CKD: uraemic toxins (indoxyl sulphate, p-cresyl sulphate) directly damage endothelium; anaemia increases cardiac work; secondary hyperparathyroidism drives vascular calcification; chronic inflammation; volume overload and hypertension accelerate cardiac remodelling; dyslipidaemia (hypertriglyceridaemia, reduced HDL, accumulation of atherogenic remnant particles).

## RAAS blockade in CKD — renoprotection and CV protection

ACE inhibitors and ARBs reduce intraglomerular pressure (by dilating the efferent arteriole) → reduce proteinuria → slow progression of diabetic nephropathy and proteinuric CKD. Key trials: RENAAL (losartan in DM nephropathy), IDNT (irbesartan), HOPE (ramipril in high-risk CKD subgroup). The combination of ACEi + ARB should NOT be used (ONTARGET: worse renal outcomes and hyperkalaemia). Monitoring: check K⁺ and creatinine 2 weeks after starting/up-titrating RAAS inhibitors in CKD — up to 30% creatinine rise is acceptable (indicates the haemodynamic effect is working); >30% rise or K⁺ >5.5 mmol/L → dose reduction or discontinuation.

## SGLT2 inhibitors in CKD — CREDENCE and DAPA-CKD

SGLT2 inhibitors have proven renoprotective benefits independent of their glucose-lowering effect:

- CREDENCE trial (canagliflozin, 2019): 4,401 patients with T2DM + CKD (eGFR 30–90, UACR ≥300 mg/g) → 30% reduction in renal failure, doubling of creatinine, or renal/CV death. Trial stopped early for overwhelming efficacy. The benefit was seen across eGFR range including eGFR 30–45.
- DAPA-CKD trial (dapagliflozin, 2020): 4,304 patients with CKD (eGFR 25–75, UACR ≥200 mg/g) — 33% of patients did NOT have diabetes (type 1 or no DM). Dapagliflozin reduced the primary renal endpoint 39% regardless of diabetes status. First time a drug showed renoprotection in non-diabetic CKD.

Mechanism of renal protection: SGLT2 inhibition reduces proximal tubule sodium reabsorption → tubuloglomerular feedback activation → afferent arteriole constriction → reduced intraglomerular hyperfiltration → less podocyte stress → reduced proteinuria and fibrosis. Additionally: reduced tubular oxygen demand → less tubular hypoxia (CKD kidneys are chronically hypoxic). SGLT2 inhibitors are now recommended in CKD with proteinuria (UACR ≥200 mg/g) regardless of diabetes status — a major paradigm shift.

## Statins in CKD — SHARP trial

SHARP (Study of Heart and Renal Protection, 2011): 9,270 patients with CKD (including 3,023 on dialysis), randomised to simvastatin 20 mg + ezetimibe 10 mg vs placebo. Major atherosclerotic events reduced 17% (ARR 3.5% over 5 years). Conclusion: statin + ezetimibe reduces ASCVD in CKD including pre-dialysis patients. Important caveat: statins do NOT reduce CV events in patients already on haemodialysis (4D and AURORA trials negative) — benefit is limited to pre-dialysis CKD. This is thought to be because HD patients' CV deaths are predominantly from sudden cardiac death and arrhythmia (not atherosclerotic plaque rupture) — a different mechanism that statins don't address.

## Blood pressure targets in CKD

More aggressive BP control is justified in CKD with proteinuria (antiproteinuric and renoprotective at lower BP): target SBP <120 mmHg in high-risk CKD (SPRINT CKD subgroup — improved both CV and renal outcomes). Standard CKD without proteinuria: <130/80 mmHg. Avoid excessive BP lowering (SBP <110 mmHg) in advanced CKD — renal perfusion may be compromised.

Exam tip: Drug dosing in CKD — the most commonly failed exam question in pharmacology: Metformin: reduce dose at eGFR 30–45; contraindicated at <30. BPJS most-used antidiabetic — check eGFR before prescribing.
ACEi/ARB: can be used in CKD (renoprotective) — monitor K⁺ and creatinine. Acceptable creatinine rise up to 30% on initiation.
SGLT2 inhibitors: eGFR threshold for glycaemic effect is 45 (below this, less glucose-lowering); for renal/CV protection benefit: canagliflozin down to eGFR 30; dapagliflozin down to eGFR 25 in heart failure indication.
NSAIDs: reduce renal blood flow (block prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriole dilation) → acute kidney injury on chronic CKD. Avoid or use with extreme caution.
Clopidogrel: no dose adjustment needed in CKD; accumulation of the active metabolite in severe CKD is not clinically problematic.
Digoxin: renally cleared; dose reduction required in CKD; toxic at normal doses with reduced eGFR.
Warfarin: enhanced anticoagulant effect in CKD (altered vitamin K metabolism, reduced protein binding). Requires more frequent INR monitoring and often lower doses.

Checkpoint: A 58-year-old man with T2DM, hypertension, and CKD G3b (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m², UACR 420 mg/g = macroalbuminuria) is currently on: metformin 1g BD, glibenclamide 5 mg BD, amlodipine 10 mg, ramipril 10 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg. His BP is 138/86 mmHg, LDL-C 2.2 mmol/L. Identify three specific drug-related problems and optimise his regimen.
Problem 1 — Metformin dose at eGFR 38: At eGFR 30–45, metformin should be dose-reduced (maximum 500–1000 mg BD). His dose of 1g BD is likely above the safe threshold at eGFR 38. Reduce to 500 mg BD and monitor eGFR quarterly. If eGFR falls to <30: stop metformin. Problem 2 — Glibenclamide in CKD: Glibenclamide is a long-acting sulphonylurea whose active metabolites accumulate in renal impairment → prolonged hypoglycaemia risk. Contraindicated at eGFR <60 by most guidelines. Replace with: (a) dapagliflozin 10 mg OD — DAPA-CKD supports use at eGFR ≥25 with macroalbuminuria (UACR 420 mg/g meets DAPA-CKD criteria); both renal protective AND cardioprotective. (b) Gliclazide MR is a safer sulphonylurea alternative in CKD if needed (shorter-acting metabolites, lower hypoglycaemia risk). Problem 3 — BP and LDL-C targets not at goal: BP 138/86 with UACR 420 mg/g (macroalbuminuria) → target SBP <130 mmHg (renoprotective and CV-protective). Add a thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide 1.5–2.5 mg — still effective at eGFR ≥30 and the preferred diuretic for hypertension in CKD) as a third antihypertensive. LDL-C 2.2 mmol/L: this patient is very-high-risk (CKD G3b + DM + macroalbuminuria) → target LDL-C <1.4 mmol/L. Escalate atorvastatin to 40–80 mg; add ezetimibe if still above target.

sections.body:
Secondary prevention is the highest-yield, evidence-densest area of preventive cardiology. A patient who has had one MI has a 15–20% chance of another within 10 years — but each element of the post-ACS bundle reduces that risk substantially. Adherence to the complete bundle is the most important predictor of long-term outcome.

## The post-ACS evidence bundle — the "ABCDE" framework

Every post-ACS patient should leave hospital on an optimised combination of these medication classes and lifestyle interventions. Remember: the clinical benefit of each drug is independent and additive.

Alert: The post-ACS ABCDE Bundle:
A — Antiplatelet therapy (DAPT: aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor; then lifelong aspirin)
A — Anticoagulation (if AF present: DOAC; not routinely for all post-ACS)
B — Beta-blocker (post-MI, EF ≤40%, or ongoing ischaemia; duration debated in preserved-EF post-PCI)
C — Cholesterol (high-intensity statin; add ezetimibe if LDL >1.4 mmol/L on statin; PCSK9i if still above target)
C — Cessation (smoking — varenicline/NRT; all other tobacco)
D — Diet and diabetes management (Mediterranean diet; SGLT2i if DM + established ASCVD)
D — BP control (target <130/80; ACEi/ARB first-line)
E — Exercise and cardiac rehabilitation (Phase II CR within 2 weeks of discharge)

## Antiplatelet therapy post-ACS — duration and selection

### DAPT duration

Standard recommendation: DAPT (aspirin 75–100 mg + ticagrelor 90 mg BD or prasugrel 10 mg OD) for 12 months post-ACS, then aspirin alone indefinitely. The 12-month duration balances ischaemic protection vs bleeding risk.

- Shortened DAPT (<12 months): for high bleeding risk patients (HBR criteria: age ≥75, anticoagulation needed, prior bleeding, severe anaemia, liver disease, CKD). TWILIGHT trial (ticagrelor monotherapy after 3 months of DAPT post-PCI): reduced bleeding without more ischaemic events. MASTER-DAPT: 1 month DAPT then antiplatelet monotherapy in HBR — non-inferior for MACE. Shorter DAPT acceptable in HBR patients.
- Extended DAPT (>12 months): for high ischaemic risk (DAPT score ≥2 — complex PCI, DM, prior MI, stent thrombosis history). PEGASUS (ticagrelor 60 mg BD beyond 12 months post-MI): reduced MACE but increased bleeding. DAPT trial (clopidogrel/prasugrel extension): reduced stent thrombosis and MI. Balance: extend DAPT in high ischaemic / low bleeding risk; shorten in high bleeding / lower ischaemic risk.

## Statin intensity and LDL targets in secondary prevention

Every patient with established ASCVD (post-ACS, post-PCI, post-CABG, stroke, PAD) should be on high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg). Target: LDL-C <1.4 mmol/L AND ≥50% reduction from baseline (ESC 2019 Class I). If target not achieved on maximal statin: add ezetimibe 10 mg OD. If still above target: PCSK9 inhibitor. The evidence: each 1 mmol/L LDL-C reduction reduces CV events by ~22% (CTT meta-analysis); this is additive for each additional reduction. There is no evidence of a "lower limit" of safe LDL-C reduction.

## ACE inhibitors/ARBs post-ACS

ACEi are indicated in all post-ACS patients with EF <40%, diabetes, hypertension, or CKD (Class I). In all other post-ACS patients: ACEi is Class IIa. The HOPE trial (ramipril) showed CV benefit even in patients without HF or LV dysfunction — suggesting a benefit beyond BP lowering (anti-ischaemic and anti-atherosclerotic pleiotropic effects of RAAS blockade). ARBs are equivalent substitutes for ACEi-intolerant patients (VALIANT, OPTIMAAL trials — valsartan equivalent to captopril post-MI). Sacubitril/valsartan (ARNi): for post-MI patients with EF <40% who are stable on ACEi — PARADISE-MI trial showed trend toward benefit; sacubitril/valsartan is an option in this setting.

## Secondary prevention adherence — the greatest challenge in preventive cardiology

Drug adherence after ACS declines rapidly: by 1 year post-ACS, 50% of patients have stopped at least one prescribed medication. By 5 years: 25% have stopped all secondary prevention medications. The consequences are severe — patients who stop statins after ACS have 50% higher 2-year mortality. Factors associated with non-adherence: polypharmacy, cost, side effects (real or perceived), lack of symptom feedback (medications prevent future events but don't relieve current symptoms), complex regimens, poor health literacy.

Indonesian context: Secondary prevention challenges in Indonesia: Polypill concept: WHO has championed the polypill (aspirin + statin + ACEi ± beta-blocker in a single tablet) as a strategy to improve adherence in low-resource settings. TIPS-3, PolyIran, and SECURE trials show polypill reduces MACE and improves adherence vs individual tablets. Indonesia is an ideal candidate for polypill rollout — BPJS coverage of a polypill containing generic components would dramatically reduce the daily pill burden and cost for patients. BPJS formulary for secondary prevention: aspirin (100 mg), clopidogrel, simvastatin, atorvastatin, captopril, enalapril, bisoprolol, metoprolol, and furosemide are all FORNAS-covered. Ticagrelor is available at secondary/tertiary level. PCSK9 inhibitors, sacubitril/valsartan: restricted to tertiary centres with specialist prescription. Medication cost: even with BPJS, co-pays and non-FORNAS drugs create barriers. Patients in rural areas may travel long distances for monthly prescriptions. Task-shifting to community health workers (kader) for follow-up phone calls and adherence support has been trialled in Indonesian settings with positive results. "Sudah sembuh, tidak perlu obat lagi" (already cured, no more medicine needed): a pervasive belief in Indonesia that once symptoms resolve (after PCI or CABG), medications are no longer necessary. Explicit, repeated counselling that secondary prevention medications prevent the next event — not the current one — is essential at every follow-up visit.

Checkpoint: A 56-year-old man was discharged after NSTEMI and PCI to the mid-RCA 8 months ago. His discharge medications were: ticagrelor 90 mg BD, aspirin 100 mg OD, atorvastatin 40 mg OD, ramipril 5 mg OD, bisoprolol 2.5 mg OD. At follow-up today: he stopped ticagrelor 3 months ago ("too expensive, and my chest pain is gone"). BP 138/84, LDL-C 2.4 mmol/L, EF 62% on recent echo. He feels well. How do you assess and manage this consultation?
This is a critically important consultation — premature ticagrelor discontinuation at 3 months post-ACS PCI is a major risk factor for stent thrombosis and recurrent ACS. Key issues: 1. Ticagrelor premature discontinuation: 8 months post-NSTEMI, he should be on DAPT for 12 months (standard duration for ACS). He stopped at 3 months — 9 months early. Stent thrombosis risk is highest in the first 6 months post-PCI; at 8 months post-procedure (and 5 months after ticagrelor cessation), the acute stent thrombosis window may have partially passed. However, recurrent ACS risk from premature DAPT cessation is substantial. If the stent has fully re-endothelialised (assumed by now), restarting ticagrelor will provide ongoing benefit for the remaining 4 months of the 12-month DAPT course. Restart ticagrelor 90 mg BD + aspirin. Address the cost barrier: BPJS should cover ticagrelor at secondary/tertiary level; help him navigate the prescription pathway. If BPJS-covered access is genuinely impossible: switch to clopidogrel 75 mg OD (BPJS-covered, cheaper, less potent — but acceptable given partial re-endothelialisation) + aspirin for the remaining 4 months. 2. LDL-C 2.4 mmol/L — target not met: Secondary prevention target is <1.4 mmol/L AND ≥50% reduction from baseline. LDL-C 2.4 mmol/L is far above target. Escalate: atorvastatin 40→80 mg OD. If LDL-C remains >1.4 mmol/L on 80 mg → add ezetimibe 10 mg OD. 3. BP 138/84: target <130/80 mmHg. Titrate ramipril upward (5 mg → 10 mg) and assess adherence. 4. Address cost and health literacy at the core of this consultation — these are the root causes of his non-adherence. A patient who understands that his stent can still block and cause another heart attack is a different adherence partner than one who thinks he was "cured" by the procedure.

sections.body:
The heart and the mind are not separate systems. Depression, anxiety, chronic psychosocial stress, and burnout are independent cardiovascular risk factors with effect sizes comparable to traditional risk factors — and they are the most undertreated risk factors in all of preventive cardiology.

## Depression and cardiovascular disease — a bidirectional relationship

Depression is both a consequence and a cause of cardiovascular disease. The relationship operates in both directions:

- Depression → CVD: major depression doubles the risk of incident MI. Post-MI depression is present in 20–30% of patients and independently predicts recurrent MI, HF hospitalisation, and mortality (hazard ratio ~2.0 for cardiac mortality). Depression impairs adherence to medications, reduces physical activity, and drives smoking and poor diet.
- CVD → Depression: MI, HF diagnosis, implantation of ICD, diagnosis of severe valvular disease — all trigger depression and anxiety. The physical limitation of heart failure (fatigue, dyspnoea) creates a powerful psychological burden.
- Shared mechanisms: inflammation (elevated CRP, IL-6, TNF-α in depression — the same inflammatory mediators drive atherosclerosis); HPA axis dysregulation → excess cortisol → hypertension, visceral obesity, insulin resistance; autonomic dysfunction (↑ sympathetic, ↓ vagal tone) → ventricular arrhythmia susceptibility and impaired HR variability; platelet hyperreactivity in depression → prothrombotic state.

## Psychosocial risk factors — the evidence

| Factor | Relative risk for CVD | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Major depression | 1.8–2.0× incident CHD; 2.0× post-MI mortality | Sympathoadrenal activation, inflammation, platelet hyperactivity, poor self-care |
| Anxiety disorders | 1.3–1.5× incident CVD; higher in panic disorder | Sympathetic activation, episodic tachycardia and BP spikes, hyperventilation-induced coronary spasm |
| Chronic work stress / job strain | 1.3–1.5× CVD (INTERHEART study) | Sustained HPA activation, poor sleep, reduced recovery time |
| Social isolation / loneliness | 1.3× CVD mortality (meta-analysis, 300,000 patients) | Reduced social buffering of stress; lower adherence; inflammatory activation |
| Type D personality (negative affect + social inhibition) | 2–4× adverse cardiac outcomes in patients with CHD | Suppressed emotional expression → chronic sympathetic activation; avoided healthcare |
| PTSD | 1.5–2× incident CVD; especially in women and veterans | Hypervigilance → chronic sympathetic activation; sleep disruption; substance use |

## Screening tools

- PHQ-2 (Patient Health Questionnaire-2): two questions ("Over the past 2 weeks, have you felt down, depressed, or hopeless?" and "Have you had little interest or pleasure in doing things?") — score ≥3 → full PHQ-9. Validated screening tool recommended at every post-ACS follow-up visit.
- PHQ-9: 9-item depression scale; score ≥10 = moderate depression → treatment consideration; score ≥20 = severe.
- GAD-7: generalised anxiety disorder scale. Score ≥8 = moderate anxiety.
- DASS-21: depression, anxiety, and stress scale — validated in Indonesian population; widely used in research and clinical settings in Indonesia.

## Treatment of depression in cardiac patients — what is safe?

- Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT): first-line; no cardiac side effects. ENRICHD trial: CBT improved depression post-MI but did not significantly reduce mortality (underpowered for this endpoint). Cardiac rehabilitation that incorporates psychological support improves both depression scores and exercise capacity.
- SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram): first-line pharmacological treatment in cardiac patients. SADHART trial: sertraline safe and effective post-ACS depression. SSRI-mediated serotonin reuptake inhibition also reduces platelet activation (an antiplatelet effect — generally beneficial in CHD patients). QTc effect: most SSRIs have minimal QTc prolongation; citalopram and escitalopram at high doses (citalopram >40 mg; escitalopram >20 mg) can prolong QTc — use caution in patients at risk for TdP.
- Avoid in cardiac patients: Tricyclic antidepressants (TCA — amitriptyline, imipramine): prolong QTc, sodium channel blockade (Ic-like effects), orthostatic hypotension — multiple cardiac adverse effects. Only use if no alternative available. SNRIs (venlafaxine): raises BP and HR — caution in poorly-controlled HTN and tachyarrhythmias.

## Burnout and chronic occupational stress — the physician's own risk

Clinical link: A chapter on mental health and CV risk would be incomplete without acknowledging that physicians — particularly those in demanding specialties like cardiology and critical care — are at significantly elevated risk of burnout, depression, and premature cardiovascular events from occupational stress. Indonesian medical residents and junior physicians face specific structural stressors: long working hours, inadequate sleep, high patient-to-physician ratios, financial pressure, and a culture that historically valorises stoicism over help-seeking. The research on physician CV risk is unequivocal: night shifts → increased MI and stroke risk; sleep deprivation → hypertension, insulin resistance, and systemic inflammation; chronic unprocessed work-related grief → depression and social isolation. Recognising and addressing these risk factors in oneself is not weakness — it is preventive cardiology at the most immediate scale available.

Checkpoint: A 52-year-old bank manager, 3 months post-MI and PCI, comes to your clinic. He is on all correct secondary prevention medications, LDL-C 1.5 mmol/L, BP 124/78 mmHg. His wife says he has been "different since the heart attack — withdrawn, not interested in anything, not sleeping." He dismisses concerns: "I'm fine, just tired from recovery." His PHQ-2 score is 4 out of 6. How do you proceed?
PHQ-2 score 4 = positive screen for depression → administer full PHQ-9. Post-MI depression is present in 20–30% of post-MI patients, doubles his risk of recurrent MI and cardiac mortality, impairs medication adherence, and worsens his quality of life. His dismissal ("just tired") is classic male under-reporting of emotional distress in Indonesian culture — the physician must gently but firmly persist. Frame it clinically: "The heart attack affects the mind as well as the heart — this is a very common medical response to what you've been through, and it needs treatment just like your other risk factors." If PHQ-9 ≥10 (moderate depression): (1) Start sertraline 50 mg OD (SADHART-proven safe post-ACS, titrate to 100–200 mg). No significant QTc concern at standard doses. Explain it takes 4–6 weeks to see full effect. (2) Refer for CBT or psychologist input — ideally integrated into his cardiac rehabilitation programme. (3) Set return appointment in 2–4 weeks to assess response. (4) Screen for suicidality (PHQ-9 item 9). (5) Involve the wife as a support — she has already identified the problem. Also reassess his cardiac rehabilitation engagement: "Have you been coming to the rehabilitation sessions?" Post-MI CR attendance in depressed patients is lower — active facilitation is needed. His secondary prevention medications are at target, which is excellent — now address the mental health component that will determine long-term adherence and quality of life.
