sections.body:
Every structural heart defect is a failure at a specific step of cardiac development. Understanding when the heart forms, how it folds, and where septation occurs gives you a mechanistic explanation for every lesion — and makes the anatomy of complex defects far more intuitive.

## Timeline of cardiac development

The heart is the first functional organ to develop. Cardiac development occurs almost entirely in the first 8 weeks of gestation — before most women know they are pregnant:

- Day 18–19: Mesodermal progenitor cells migrate to form two lateral heart-forming fields
- Day 20–21: Two endocardial tubes fuse into a single heart tube — the first functional, contracting structure. Starts beating around day 21–22.
- Day 23–28: Cardiac looping — the straight heart tube bends rightward (dextral looping, D-loop) placing the future right ventricle anterior and to the right. L-loop (leftward looping) → L-transposition/congenitally corrected TGA
- Week 4–8: Cardiac septation — the atria, ventricles, AV valves, outflow tracts, and great arteries are partitioned. This is the critical window for most CHD.

## Key septation events and where they can fail

### Atrial septation

The atria are separated by two overlapping septa. First, the septum primum grows downward from the atrial roof toward the endocardial cushions — the gap it leaves before fusing is the ostium primum. Before the ostium primum closes, programmed cell death creates perforations in the superior septum primum that coalesce into the ostium secundum. Then the septum secundum grows down to the right of the septum primum, creating an overlapping flap (the foramen ovale). After birth, when left atrial pressure exceeds right, the flap is pressed closed. Failure of this process:

- Incomplete fusion of septum primum with endocardial cushions → ostium primum ASD
- Excessive resorption of septum primum → large ostium secundum ASD
- Foramen ovale never sealing after birth → patent foramen ovale (PFO) (present in 25% of adults)

### Ventricular septation

The muscular ventricular septum grows upward from the ventricular apex. The membranous septum forms from fusion of the endocardial cushions with the muscular septum and the conal septum (which also spirals to separate the aorta and pulmonary artery). Failure:

- Incomplete muscular septum growth → muscular VSD
- Failed fusion of endocardial cushions + membranous septum → perimembranous (paramembranous) VSD — the most common type
- Malalignment of the conal/outlet septum → outlet VSD; when associated with aortic override and RVOTO → Tetralogy of Fallot

### AV canal and endocardial cushion development

The endocardial cushions form the inlet ventricular septum, the primum atrial septum, and contribute to both the mitral and tricuspid valves (forming the septal leaflets). Complete failure of endocardial cushion fusion → complete AVSD (AV canal defect) — a single large AV valve, primum ASD, and inlet VSD acting together.

### Outflow tract and great artery development

The truncus arteriosus (single outlet from the primitive heart) is divided by the spiral truncal ridges into the aorta and pulmonary artery. The spiral rotation means the aorta wraps around the pulmonary artery — explaining why the great arteries normally cross at their bases. Failure of spiralling:

- No spiralling → parallel great arteries → D-transposition of the great arteries (D-TGA)
- Insufficient rotation → truncus communis → persistent truncus arteriosus
- Rightward deviation of the conal septum → RVOTO + overriding aorta → Tetralogy of Fallot

## Classification of CHD

Acyanotic CHD: No shunting of deoxygenated blood to the systemic circulation. Either left-to-right shunts (pulmonary overcirculation) or obstructive lesions without shunting. Patient is pink. Examples: ASD, VSD, PDA, AVSD, PS, valvular AS, coarctation of the aorta.

Cyanotic CHD: Deoxygenated blood bypasses the pulmonary circulation and enters the systemic circulation ("right-to-left shunt"). Patient is blue. Subdivided into: (1) reduced pulmonary blood flow (pulmonary oligaemia) — e.g. TOF; and (2) increased or normal pulmonary blood flow — e.g. D-TGA (parallel circuits). SpO₂ <95% at rest in a newborn demands investigation.

## Shunt physiology — the Qp:Qs ratio

In any left-to-right shunt, the ratio of pulmonary blood flow (Qp) to systemic blood flow (Qs) describes the magnitude of the shunt:

Equation: Qp:Qs = (Systemic arterial O₂ saturation − Mixed venous O₂ saturation) / (Pulmonary vein O₂ saturation − Pulmonary artery O₂ saturation)

- Qp:Qs = 1:1 — No shunt. All pulmonary blood flow equals systemic.
- Qp:Qs = 1.5:1 — Small to moderate shunt. May be haemodynamically significant depending on the anatomy.
- Qp:Qs ≥ 2:1 — Large shunt. Significant pulmonary overcirculation. Intervention usually indicated.

A large left-to-right shunt means the right heart and pulmonary vasculature are receiving 2× the normal blood flow → pulmonary vascular congestion → reactive pulmonary arterial hypertension → eventually Eisenmenger syndrome (right-to-left shunt reversal) if unrepaired.

Key concept: The five determinants of shunt direction and magnitude: pressure difference, orifice size, pulmonary vascular resistance, systemic vascular resistance, and ventricular compliance
In a left-to-right shunt: blood flows from the high-pressure left side to the lower-pressure right side. The shunt magnitude depends on: how large the defect is (larger orifice → larger shunt), the ratio of pulmonary to systemic vascular resistance (PVR:SVR — normally PVR ≪ SVR → left-to-right predominates), and downstream compliance (the right ventricle is more compliant than the left → in an ASD, the right ventricle's compliance drives the shunt more than the pressure difference). Key: pulmonary vascular resistance rises progressively with a large left-to-right shunt → eventually PVR approaches SVR → shunt diminishes → then when PVR exceeds SVR → shunt reverses to right-to-left → Eisenmenger syndrome. At this point the defect cannot be closed — closure would remove the "pop-off" valve for the elevated RV pressure and cause acute RV failure and death.

## Genetic associations with CHD

| Syndrome / gene | Cardiac defect(s) | Key non-cardiac features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) | AVSD (40–50%), VSD, ASD, PDA, TOF | Intellectual disability, hypotonia, characteristic facies, hypothyroidism |
| Turner syndrome (45,X) | Bicuspid aortic valve (50%), coarctation of the aorta (30%), hypoplastic left heart (rare) | Short stature, webbed neck, gonadal dysgenesis, lymphoedema |
| DiGeorge/22q11.2 deletion | Conotruncal defects: ToF, truncus arteriosus, interrupted aortic arch, VSD | Thymus/parathyroid hypoplasia, palatal abnormalities, facial dysmorphia, learning disability |
| Noonan syndrome (PTPN11) | Pulmonary stenosis (50–70%), HCM, ASD | Short stature, webbed neck, pectus, ptosis — "male Turner phenotype" |
| Williams syndrome (7q11.23) | Supravalvular aortic stenosis, peripheral pulmonary stenosis | Elfin facies, intellectual disability, hypercalcaemia, friendly personality |
| Marfan syndrome (FBN1) | Aortic root dilation/dissection, mitral valve prolapse | Tall stature, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation, scoliosis |
| Holt-Oram syndrome (TBX5) | Secundum ASD (85%), VSD, conduction disease | Upper limb abnormalities (radial ray defects), thumb hypoplasia |

Checkpoint: A 3-month-old baby with Down syndrome is referred for cardiac evaluation. Why must echo be performed in all Down syndrome babies, and which CHD must you specifically look for?
Echo is mandatory in all Down syndrome newborns because CHD occurs in 40–50% — higher than any other chromosomal syndrome. The defect to specifically look for: complete AVSD (atrioventricular septal defect), which is the hallmark cardiac lesion of Down syndrome (present in ~40% of DS with CHD). Complete AVSD involves: a single large common AV valve straddling both ventricles, a primum ASD (below the fossa ovalis), and an inlet VSD — creating left-to-right shunting at both atrial and ventricular levels. Without repair, AVSD in Down syndrome progresses rapidly to irreversible pulmonary vascular disease (Eisenmenger physiology) faster than in non-Down syndrome children (by age 1–2 years). The window for surgical repair (complete AVSD repair) is the first 3–6 months of life. If the diagnosis is delayed past 12 months, pulmonary vascular resistance may already be significantly elevated, complicating or precluding repair. Other common CHD in Down syndrome to look for: VSD, ASD, PDA. The absence of a murmur does NOT exclude significant CHD in a newborn — particularly in the first days of life when pulmonary vascular resistance is still high and shunts are small. Echo is the only reliable diagnostic tool.

sections.body:
In TGA the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle — creating two parallel, non-mixing circulations. Without intervention, this is incompatible with sustained life. Understanding the distinction between D-TGA (a neonatal emergency requiring arterial switch) and L-TGA (congenitally corrected — a "self-correcting" anatomy with its own long-term problems) is critical for every cardiologist.

## D-TGA — ventriculo-arterial discordance, AV concordance

In D-TGA (dextro-transposition):

- AV connections are normal (concordant): RA → RV; LA → LV
- Ventriculo-arterial connections are reversed (discordant): RV → Aorta; LV → Pulmonary artery

The result: two parallel circuits. Deoxygenated blood from the body → RA → RV → aorta → body (never passes through the lungs). Oxygenated blood from the lungs → LA → LV → pulmonary artery → lungs (cycles within the pulmonary circuit without reaching the body). Survival is only possible through mixing at the atrial (foramen ovale/ASD), ventricular (VSD), or ductal (PDA) level — without mixing, the baby dies. D-TGA typically presents as profound cyanosis within hours of birth as the ductus closes.

## Neonatal management of D-TGA

### Step 1 — Prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) immediately

PGE1 IV infusion (0.01–0.1 mcg/kg/min) keeps the ductus arteriosus open → allows some mixing between the parallel circuits → improves SpO₂ from <50% to 60–70%. This is the first critical intervention — started as soon as D-TGA is suspected, before echo confirmation if necessary. PGE1 side effects: apnoea (common, particularly in premature infants — be prepared to intubate), fever, hypotension, flush, cortical hyperostosis with prolonged use.

### Step 2 — Balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure)

If ASD is small or absent and mixing is inadequate despite PGE1: a balloon catheter is advanced from the femoral vein to the LA via the foramen ovale. The balloon is inflated and forcefully withdrawn across the atrial septum → tears the septum → creates a larger ASD → improved atrial-level mixing. Performed at the bedside under echo guidance in a critically cyanotic neonate. Immediately improves SpO₂ to 70–80%. This is a temporising bridge to surgery — not definitive treatment.

### Step 3 — Arterial switch operation (ASO, Jatene operation)

The definitive surgical repair. Performed in the first 2 weeks of life (before the LV "de-trains" from pulmonary pressure). The operation:

1. Divide the aorta and pulmonary artery above their respective valves
2. Reimplant the coronary arteries from the native aortic root (now going to be the neo-PA) to the native PA root (now going to be the neo-aorta) — technically the most demanding step
3. Reconstruct the aorta from the native PA root ("neo-aorta") and the pulmonary artery from the native aortic root ("neo-PA") using the LeCompte manoeuvre (PA is brought anterior to the aorta)

After ASO: the LV pumps to the aorta and the RV pumps to the pulmonary artery — normal physiology restored. The neo-aortic valve (formerly the pulmonary valve) may develop regurgitation or stenosis over time. Long-term: surveillance for neo-aortic root dilation and regurgitation, coronary artery stenosis at reimplantation sites, branch PA stenosis (LeCompte manoeuvre stretches the PA branches).

## L-TGA (congenitally corrected TGA, ccTGA)

L-TGA (levo-transposition) is the most confusing anatomy in congenital heart disease — because it is "twice-wrong but right overall":

- AV discordance: RA → morphological LV; LA → morphological RV
- VA discordance: morphological LV → pulmonary artery; morphological RV → aorta

The double discordance means: venous blood (RA) → LV → PA → lungs → LA → RV → Aorta → body. The circulation is physiologically corrected — oxygenated blood still reaches the body via the aorta, deoxygenated blood still goes to the lungs. Hence "congenitally corrected." The patient may be entirely asymptomatic until middle age if there are no associated defects. However, two fundamental problems arise over time:

- The systemic ventricle is the morphological RV — a ventricle designed for low-pressure pulmonary work is now sustaining systemic pressures for decades → progressive RV (systemic ventricle) failure, typically by the 5th–6th decade
- Complete heart block: the AV node and bundle of His in ccTGA have an abnormal course (the AV node is anteriorly displaced, the bundle courses in the anterior wall of the RV rather than the septum) → high spontaneous complete heart block rate (1–2% per year, ~20% lifetime risk)

Additional associated defects in ccTGA: VSD (~70%), PS (~40%), Ebstein-like malformation of the left-sided tricuspid valve (~40%), WPW (from accessory pathways across the abnormally placed fibrous rings).

Key concept: In D-TGA the great arteries are in parallel — life depends on mixing. In ccTGA they are in series — blood circulates normally but the "wrong" ventricle supports the systemic circulation for life
The haemodynamic consequences are completely different: D-TGA is a neonatal emergency from cyanosis (parallel circuits must be urgently switched). ccTGA is a slowly failing system — the patient may live decades without diagnosis, then present with progressive right ventricular failure, complete heart block, or Ebstein-like tricuspid regurgitation in middle age. A key clinical pearl: ccTGA should be suspected in any adult presenting with unexplained complete heart block, particularly when there is an associated Ebstein-like valve or VSD. The 12-lead ECG in ccTGA often shows Q waves in the right precordial leads (V1-V2) instead of the left — because the morphological LV is on the right, its depolarisation creates right-sided Q waves.

Checkpoint: A 35-year-old man with known ccTGA (diagnosed incidentally at age 22) presents with increasing dyspnoea over 6 months. Echo: systemic RV (right-sided morphological RV) with EF 38%, moderate-severe systemic AV valve regurgitation (left-sided tricuspid valve with Ebstein-like morphology). No VSD. He is not on any medications. What are the two key management considerations?
1. GDMT for systemic RV failure: his systemic ventricle (the morphological RV, EF 38%) is failing. Evidence for standard HF GDMT in systemic RV is limited (no dedicated large RCTs). Extrapolating from HFrEF physiology: start ACEi/ARB (reduces RV wall stress and aldosterone activation), beta-blocker (carvedilol — evidence from small studies in systemic RV failure), and MRA (eplerenone/spironolactone). SGLT2 inhibitors: growing evidence in non-morphological LV heart failure (EMPEROR-Reduced enrolled patients regardless of HF aetiology) — reasonable to consider. The systemic RV in ccTGA behaves haemodynamically like HFrEF with the same neurohormonal activation — the GDMT logic is sound even without dedicated RCT evidence. 2. Systemic AV valve regurgitation (moderate-severe Ebstein-like tricuspid regurgitation in the systemic position): this is regurgitation of the systemic AV valve, which directly impairs forward systemic output. Unlike secondary MR in conventional HFrEF (where COAPT criteria guide repair), valve surgery for the systemic AV valve in ccTGA carries higher risk from the anatomical complexity but may be required as the regurgitation is contributing to systemic RV volume overload. Indication: symptomatic moderate-severe systemic AV valve regurgitation with declining systemic RV function → surgical valve repair or replacement. This requires a high-volume ACHD surgical centre. Additionally: monitor for complete heart block (baseline ECG + Holter; pacemaker prophylaxis when EF falls or if PR prolongs significantly — some centres advocate prophylactic PPM before planned surgery to avoid emergency pacing perioperatively).

sections.body:
When a child is born with a heart that has only one functional pumping chamber — whether from hypoplastic left heart syndrome, tricuspid atresia, or other complex anatomy — surgical palliation rather than cure is the goal. The Fontan circulation connects systemic venous blood directly to the pulmonary arteries, bypassing the missing ventricle. It is a triumph of surgical ingenuity — and a source of lifelong medical complexity.

## Single ventricle anatomy — the spectrum

Single ventricle (univentricular heart) describes any anatomy where one ventricle is so small, absent, or non-functional that a two-ventricle repair is not feasible. Common forms include:

- Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS): the most common form in Western countries. Severe underdevelopment of the left heart — hypoplastic LV, atretic or severely stenotic mitral and aortic valves, hypoplastic aortic arch. The single morphological RV must support the systemic circulation. Duct-dependent circulation at birth (PDA supplies the aorta retrogradely from the PA). Without intervention: fatal within 1–2 weeks of birth. Incidence: ~2 per 10,000 live births.
- Tricuspid atresia: absent tricuspid valve → no RA-RV communication. The morphological LV is the single ventricle. Often associated with VSD and relationship of the great arteries varies.
- Double-inlet left ventricle (DILV): both AV valves open into a single dominant LV. Various great artery relationships.
- Heterotaxy syndromes (asplenia — right isomerism; polysplenia — left isomerism): complex abnormalities of atrial, ventricular, and great artery anatomy associated with abnormal situs and AV connections.

## The staged Fontan pathway

The Fontan circulation is built in three surgical stages, each designed to progressively offload the single ventricle from both systemic and pulmonary work:

### Stage 1 — Norwood operation (neonatal, for HLHS)

Performed within the first week of life. Goals: (1) reconstruct the aortic arch using the native PA and homograft material (neo-aorta); (2) establish reliable pulmonary blood flow via a Modified Blalock-Taussig (mBTS) shunt (right subclavian-to-right PA) or Sano shunt (RV-to-PA conduit); (3) create an unobstructed atrial communication. After Norwood: the single RV supports systemic circulation; pulmonary blood flow is via the shunt. Saturations 70–85% (mixing physiology). This is the highest-risk stage (hospital mortality 10–20% even in experienced centres).

### Stage 2 — Bidirectional Glenn (BDG, cavopulmonary anastomosis) — 4–6 months

The superior vena cava (SVC) is anastomosed end-to-side to the right pulmonary artery — directing upper body venous return directly to the lungs, bypassing the heart. The mBTS shunt is taken down. Result: upper body venous blood (25–30% of systemic venous return) flows passively into the pulmonary circulation without a pumping chamber. The single ventricle now only has to pump oxygenated blood to the body — its workload is significantly reduced. SpO₂ typically 75–85% post-Glenn (lower body venous blood still mixes in the heart).

### Stage 3 — Fontan completion — 2–4 years of age

The inferior vena cava (IVC) is connected to the pulmonary artery via a lateral tunnel (within the RA) or extracardiac conduit. All systemic venous return now flows passively to the pulmonary arteries — bypassing the single ventricle entirely. Result: in theory, fully separated pulmonary and systemic circulations. SpO₂ typically 90–95%. The single ventricle now only has to pump blood through the systemic circulation — the pulmonary circulation is driven entirely by the systemic venous pressure (typically 10–15 mmHg) without a pulmonary ventricle.

## Fontan circulation physiology and chronic complications

The Fontan circulation is inherently non-physiological: systemic venous pressure must be high enough to drive passive flow through the pulmonary vasculature, creating chronic systemic venous hypertension. The long-term consequences accumulate with age:

| Complication | Mechanism | Management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fontan failure (single ventricle dysfunction) | Progressive systolic and/or diastolic dysfunction of the single ventricle. Volume overload years earlier + chronic systemic pressure support. | Optimise preload and afterload. GDMT (limited evidence). Fontan takedown or heart transplantation in end-stage failure. |
| Protein-losing enteropathy (PLE) | Elevated mesenteric venous pressure → intestinal lymphatic obstruction → protein loss into the bowel. Hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, diarrhoea, malabsorption. | High-protein diet, albumin infusions, sildenafil (reduces PVR), cardiac catheterisation to relieve obstructions. Poor prognosis — median survival after PLE diagnosis ~5 years without transplant. |
| Plastic bronchitis | Abnormal lymphatic flow → lymphatic channels empty into the airway → cast formation in the bronchi. Life-threatening airway obstruction from cast expectoration/obstruction. | Lymphatic interventions (thoracic duct embolisation, lymphatic drainage procedures). Very high mortality without treatment. |
| Hepatic disease (Fontan-associated liver disease, FALD) | Chronic hepatic venous hypertension → hepatic congestion → fibrosis → cirrhosis. Hepatocellular carcinoma risk increased. | Liver surveillance (ultrasound + AFP every 2 years). Liver biopsy for fibrosis staging. Combined heart-liver transplantation in cirrhosis + Fontan failure. |
| Thromboembolic disease | Sluggish flow in the Fontan circuit (particularly the lateral tunnel or conduit) → thrombus formation → pulmonary embolism, paradoxical embolism via residual communications, stroke. | Anticoagulation (warfarin) or antiplatelet therapy — debate continues regarding optimal strategy. Most centres anticoagulate with warfarin or DOAC in high-risk patients. |
| Arrhythmias | Atrial arrhythmias (intra-atrial reentrant tachycardia, IART = atrial flutter in repaired hearts) are extremely common. Sinus node dysfunction from surgical scarring. AF. | Antiarrhythmic drugs, catheter ablation (complex mapping in unusual anatomy), pacemaker for sinus node dysfunction. |

Checkpoint: A 22-year-old with HLHS who underwent Norwood → BDG → extracardiac Fontan presents with increasing abdominal swelling, severe peripheral oedema, and diarrhoea for 3 months. His serum albumin is 18 g/L (severely low). Echo: single RV function mildly reduced (EF ~45%), no mechanical obstruction in the Fontan circuit on echo. What is the diagnosis and the immediate management priorities?
Protein-losing enteropathy (PLE) in the context of Fontan circulation — confirmed by the triad: hypoalbuminaemia (18 g/L = severely low, normal 35–50), peripheral oedema, and diarrhoea. The mechanism: elevated mesenteric venous pressure from the Fontan circuit (systemic venous hypertension) obstructs intestinal lymphatic drainage → proteins leak into the bowel lumen → severe hypoproteinaemia. Immediate management priorities: (1) Confirm PLE: measure stool α1-antitrypsin (a marker of enteric protein loss — elevated in PLE), confirm low serum albumin, check CBC, coagulation factors (also lost in PLE). (2) IV albumin infusion to correct acute hypoalbuminaemia and reduce oedema — this is supportive, not curative. (3) Optimise Fontan haemodynamics: even if echo suggests no mechanical obstruction, cardiac catheterisation is essential — echo poorly visualises the extracardiac Fontan conduit, collateral vessels, and pulmonary artery pressures. Any obstruction or elevated PVR contributing to elevated Fontan pressure must be identified and treated (stent the Fontan conduit if obstructed, fenestrate the Fontan if pressures elevated). (4) Sildenafil: reduces PVR → reduces Fontan circuit pressure → may improve enteric lymphatic drainage. Evidence from case series. (5) High-protein diet and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation. (6) Heparin: IV unfractionated heparin has been reported to improve PLE acutely (mechanism: restores proteoglycans in the intestinal lymphatic endothelium) — a counterintuitive but supported intervention. (7) Long-term: assess for heart transplantation listing — PLE median survival ~5 years. Combined heart-liver transplant if FALD is also present.

sections.body:
Eisenmenger syndrome represents the end-stage of any uncorrected large left-to-right shunt. When pulmonary vascular resistance rises to equal or exceed systemic resistance, the shunt reverses — and closing the defect becomes not just futile but immediately fatal. Management shifts from surgery to targeted medical therapy and meticulous supportive care.

## Pathophysiology of PAH in CHD

Any large left-to-right shunt exposes the pulmonary vasculature to both increased flow (volume) and increased pressure. The pulmonary vascular response progresses through stages:

1. Reactive (reversible): pulmonary vasoconstriction in response to increased flow. PVR elevated but responds to vasodilators (O₂, NO, prostacyclin). Still left-to-right shunt. Repair at this stage resolves PAH completely.
2. Hyperplastic (partially reversible): medial hypertrophy and intimal proliferation of pulmonary arterioles. PVR elevated, partial vasodilator response. Repair may normalise PAH if performed early enough in this stage.
3. Obstructive (irreversible): plexiform lesions, fibrinoid necrosis, arteritis. PVR fixed at high levels — no vasodilator response. If repair attempted → acute RV failure and death (the VSD/ASD was acting as a "pop-off valve" for the RV — closing it removes this safety valve).

## Eisenmenger syndrome — definition and clinical features

Eisenmenger syndrome: PAH due to a large cardiac defect with reversal of the original left-to-right shunt to net right-to-left shunting → cyanosis. Named after Victor Eisenmenger who described a patient with VSD, cyanosis, and dyspnoea in 1897. Paul Wood formalised the concept of pulmonary vascular obstructive disease as the mechanism in 1958.

Clinical features:

- Central cyanosis (persistent or exercise-induced right-to-left shunting)
- Clubbing (chronic hypoxaemia)
- Polycythaemia: compensatory erythrocytosis from hypoxaemia → haematocrit 55–75% → hyperviscosity symptoms (headache, visual blurring, fatigue)
- Haemoptysis: rupture of dilated pulmonary vessels or pulmonary infarction (a dangerous complication)
- RV heave and loud P2 (pulmonary hypertension)
- The original shunt murmur may disappear (as pressure difference across the defect falls)

## The two most important rules in Eisenmenger management

Warning: Rule 1: NEVER close the defect in Eisenmenger syndrome. The defect is the only outlet for the overloaded RV. Removing it → acute RV pressure crisis → right heart failure → death within hours. Even small "residual" defects in patients with elevated PVR should not be closed without careful haemodynamic assessment. The decision to close requires demonstration that PVR is still reversible (catheterisation with O₂ and NO testing, "balloon occlusion test" — close the defect temporarily to assess RV pressure and cardiac output response).
Rule 2: NEVER perform phlebotomy for polycythaemia in Eisenmenger syndrome unless symptoms of hyperviscosity are present AND haematocrit is >65%. The polycythaemia is a compensatory response to maintain O₂ delivery to the tissues — reducing haematocrit reduces O₂-carrying capacity and worsens tissue hypoxia. Indiscriminate "therapeutic phlebotomy" (phlebotomy purely to lower haematocrit) causes iron deficiency and microcytosis → reduced O₂ delivery → worse outcomes. Iron deficiency itself increases stroke risk in Eisenmenger (iron-deficient red cells are less deformable → more thrombogenic). Only phlebotomy if haematocrit >65% AND symptomatic hyperviscosity AND iron stores adequate.

## Medical therapy for Eisenmenger syndrome — PAH-targeted therapy

PAH-targeted therapies were developed for idiopathic PAH but are used across all PAH subtypes including CHD-PAH (WHO Group 1). These drugs act on the three main pathways dysregulated in PAH:

- Endothelin receptor antagonists (ERA): Bosentan (dual ERA — blocks ET-A and ET-B), Ambrisentan (ET-A selective), Macitentan (next generation). Bosentan is the most extensively studied in Eisenmenger — BREATHE-5 trial (2006): bosentan in Eisenmenger with ASD/VSD/PDA → improved 6MWT, reduced PVR, improved WHO functional class, maintained or improved SpO₂. Hepatotoxicity monitoring required (LFTs monthly).
- Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (PDE5i): Sildenafil, Tadalafil. Inhibit PDE5 → ↑ cGMP → pulmonary vasodilation. Sildenafil also used in Fontan-PLE. Widely available and oral.
- Prostacyclin pathway agonists: Epoprostenol (IV, continuous infusion — most potent, for severe PAH), Treprostinil (SQ, inhaled, IV), Iloprost (inhaled). Reserved for severe functional class III–IV.

Combination therapy (ERA + PDE5i ± prostacyclin) is increasingly standard for functional class III–IV Eisenmenger. The GRIPHON trial (selexipag — prostacyclin IP receptor agonist) and other combination trials have extended the evidence base.

## Specific management issues in Eisenmenger

- Iron supplementation: monitor iron stores in all Eisenmenger patients — iron deficiency is common (from phlebotomy, haemoptysis, increased erythropoiesis demand) and worsens stroke risk and exercise intolerance. Supplement if ferritin low or transferrin saturation <20%.
- Avoid vasodilators (beyond PAH-targeted therapy): systemic vasodilators (nitrates, ACEi, ARBs at high doses) reduce SVR → increase right-to-left shunt → acutely worse cyanosis. Use with extreme caution.
- Pregnancy is contraindicated: maternal mortality in Eisenmenger pregnancy approaches 50%. The haemodynamic changes of pregnancy (↓ SVR, ↑ CO) dramatically worsen right-to-left shunting and cyanosis. Strongly counsel against pregnancy; if already pregnant → termination discussion mandatory with full counselling.
- Non-cardiac surgery: high perioperative risk from haemodynamic swings affecting R-L shunt, thrombosis vs bleeding risk, regional anaesthesia preferred, anaesthesiologist with CHD expertise required.

Indonesian context: Eisenmenger syndrome in Indonesia: Eisenmenger syndrome from uncorrected VSD, PDA, and AVSD is seen regularly in Indonesian tertiary cardiac centres — a direct consequence of late CHD diagnosis and delayed surgical access. A child who had a large VSD diagnosed at 3 months but could not access surgery in time (due to waiting lists, geographic barriers, or parental hesitation) may present at age 8–10 as an Eisenmenger patient. At that point, surgical closure is contraindicated. PAH-targeted therapy (bosentan, sildenafil) is available at some BPJS-covered tertiary centres but access is inconsistent. The burden of preventable Eisenmenger syndrome in Indonesia is a public health failure that reflects the systemic gap between CHD diagnosis and timely intervention. Every preventable Eisenmenger case represents a child who had a curable defect that was allowed to progress to an incurable one.

Checkpoint: A 25-year-old woman with Eisenmenger syndrome from a large, uncorrected PDA presents requesting advice about starting a relationship and potential future pregnancy. SpO₂ 88% at rest, haematocrit 62%, PASP estimated 110 mmHg. She is on bosentan. How do you counsel her about pregnancy?
This requires an honest, compassionate, but unambiguous consultation. Pregnancy in Eisenmenger syndrome carries a maternal mortality of approximately 30–50% — one of the highest risks in all of cardiology. The cause: the haemodynamic changes of pregnancy (↓ SVR by 20–30% due to progesterone-mediated vasodilation and the low-resistance placental circulation) dramatically worsen the right-to-left shunt in Eisenmenger. Her SpO₂ of 88% at rest will fall further in pregnancy — fetal hypoxia, intrauterine growth restriction, and preterm birth are near-universal. The peripartum period is particularly dangerous: sudden changes in SVR with delivery and autotransfusion can trigger acute haemodynamic collapse. Also: bosentan is teratogenic (Category X — causes major fetal malformations) and must be stopped before and during pregnancy, removing her primary PAH treatment. The counsel: (1) Pregnancy is strongly contraindicated in Eisenmenger syndrome — mWHO Class IV, absolute contraindication. This must be conveyed clearly, compassionately, and without ambiguity. (2) Effective contraception is mandatory: combined oral contraceptive pill is contraindicated (oestrogen increases VTE risk — already elevated in Eisenmenger from polycythaemia and sluggish flow). Use: progestin-only methods (depo-medroxyprogesterone acetate, levonorgestrel IUD), barrier methods, or surgical sterilisation for definitive solution. (3) Acknowledge her autonomy and emotional wellbeing — this is a young woman being told she cannot safely carry a pregnancy. This has profound psychosocial implications. Offer psychological support, discuss adoption, and ensure she understands the risks clearly without feeling judged. Offer ongoing monitoring and support. If she chooses to pursue pregnancy against this advice, she must be managed at a highly specialised centre with full knowledge of the near-50% maternal mortality.

sections.body:
For the first time in history, more adults than children are living with congenital heart disease. This is entirely a product of surgical success — children who would have died now survive to adulthood, carrying repaired hearts with long-term sequelae that require specialised ongoing care. The ACHD cardiologist must understand both the original anatomy and the surgical history that shaped it.

## The growing ACHD population

Advances in paediatric cardiac surgery since the 1970s have transformed the survival landscape of CHD. In high-income countries, approximately 90% of children with CHD now survive to adulthood. In 2020, the ACHD population exceeded the paediatric CHD population globally for the first time. The spectrum of ACHD includes:

- Simple lesions that were repaired and require only surveillance: small VSD, ASD closure, PDA ligation, mild PS, coarctation repair
- Moderate complexity: TOF repair, transposition of great arteries after atrial switch (Mustard/Senning) or arterial switch, coarctation in adulthood
- Severe complexity: Fontan circulation, cyanotic unrepaired complex CHD, systemic RV (ccTGA, Mustard/Senning)

## Common ACHD presentations and their causes

| Presentation | Underlying anatomy to consider |
| --- | --- |
| New-onset AF or atrial flutter | ASD (RA dilation); Fontan (intra-atrial reentrant tachycardia — IART); repaired TOF; ccTGA; Mustard/Senning |
| Cyanosis in adulthood (new or persistent) | Unrepaired ASD/VSD/PDA with Eisenmenger; TOF with residual RVOTO; Fontan failure; PFO with paradoxical embolism + R-L shunting |
| Ventricular dysfunction | Repaired TOF with chronic PR and RV dilation; systemic RV in ccTGA or Mustard; Fontan ventricular dysfunction; anthracycline cardiotoxicity in CHD patients who had cancer treatment |
| Sudden cardiac death or sustained VT | Repaired TOF (QRS >180 ms, RV dilation); repaired TGA Mustard (systemic RV baffle obstruction → ischaemia); ccTGA; HCM; arrhythmic substrates from ventricular scars |
| Infective endocarditis | Any residual defect, prosthetic valve, intracardiac device, or patch. Any ACHD patient with fever should be evaluated for IE. |
| Heart failure symptoms (dyspnoea, oedema) | Fontan failure; systemic RV failure; residual obstructive lesions; valvular problems (neo-aortic regurgitation post-ASO; systemic AV valve regurgitation in ccTGA) |

## Atrial switch operations — Mustard and Senning (historical D-TGA repair)

Before the arterial switch operation (Jatene, 1975), D-TGA was repaired with atrial-level procedures — redirecting blood flow within the atria using baffles. These operations were performed from the 1960s to 1990s. There is a large cohort of ACHD patients (now aged 30–60) who have had these procedures:

- The Mustard operation: an intra-atrial baffle made of pericardium or Dacron redirects pulmonary venous return to the tricuspid valve → RV → aorta, and systemic venous return to the mitral valve → LV → PA. The circulation is "physiologically correct" but the morphological RV remains the systemic ventricle.
- The Senning operation: similar concept using native atrial tissue rather than a baffle.
- Long-term problems of Mustard/Senning: (1) Systemic RV failure (the RV was not designed for a lifetime of systemic work — EF falls progressively); (2) Baffle obstruction (SVC or IVC limb of the baffle can become obstructed → SVC syndrome or IVC obstruction); (3) Baffle leak (allows R-L or L-R shunting); (4) Arrhythmias — sinus node dysfunction (from surgical injury to the sinus node) and atrial flutter/reentrant tachycardia are very common; (5) Tricuspid valve regurgitation (systemic AV valve — same issues as ccTGA).

## Endocarditis prophylaxis in ACHD

ESC 2023 guidelines: antibiotic prophylaxis before invasive dental procedures (amoxicillin 2g PO 30–60 min before; or clindamycin 600 mg if penicillin-allergic) is recommended only for high-risk CHD patients:

- Prosthetic heart valve (including TAVI/TAVR)
- Previous infective endocarditis
- Any CHD repaired with prosthetic material within 6 months (until endothelialisation)
- Residual defects adjacent to prosthetic patches or devices (permanent endothelialisation not expected)
- Cyanotic CHD — unrepaired or with palliation

Not indicated for: small VSDs, isolated secundum ASDs (after closure without device), repaired coarctation, or bicuspid AV without prosthetic replacement.

Clinical link: The single most important principle for managing any ACHD patient: know their surgical history in detail before making any decision. A patient who says "I had a heart operation as a child" could have had anything from a simple PDA ligation to a Fontan completion or a Rastelli procedure. The surgical history determines what anatomy is present now, what the residual lesions are, what prosthetic materials are in place, and what risks specific interventions carry. Request operative notes, discharge summaries, and prior echo reports. In Indonesia, many ACHD patients have undergone surgery abroad (Singapore, Australia, Malaysia) or at centres that may not have accessible records — imaging (echo, MRI, CT) is often the primary way to reconstruct the anatomy.

Checkpoint: A 38-year-old man presents with palpitations and a heart rate of 180 bpm. He had a Mustard procedure for D-TGA at age 2 months. ECG during tachycardia: regular narrow complex at 180 bpm, no clear P waves. What is the most likely arrhythmia, and what is the management concern unique to his anatomy?
Intra-atrial reentrant tachycardia (IART) — the most common atrial arrhythmia in Mustard/Senning patients. IART is a macro-reentrant circuit around the atrial baffle scar, the surgical incision lines, and the crista terminalis. It is not typical atrial flutter (whose circuit is around the cavotricuspid isthmus) — though it can look similar on ECG. At 180 bpm it is haemodynamically significant. Management concern unique to his anatomy: the systemic ventricle is his morphological RV. In Mustard patients, the RV is already functioning at the limit of its reserve as the systemic ventricle. A rapid IART at 180 bpm imposes additional stress on this already-compromised ventricle — it can precipitate acute systemic RV failure (presenting as systemic heart failure: low BP, elevated JVP, pulmonary oedema). Additionally, cardioversion must be performed carefully — the Mustard baffle can obstruct venous return and make haemodynamic support challenging. Acute management: if haemodynamically unstable → DC cardioversion immediately. If stable: rate control with beta-blocker (preferred) or digoxin (useful in systemic RV failure context). Antiarrhythmic drugs: amiodarone or flecainide (if RV function acceptable). Long-term: catheter ablation of the IART circuit — technically challenging due to the complex atrial anatomy from the Mustard repair. Requires an ACHD electrophysiology specialist. Anticoagulation: start before cardioversion (IART in Mustard carries thromboembolic risk from the static baffle chambers).

sections.body:
As more women with CHD reach reproductive age, managing heart disease in pregnancy has become a core skill for cardiologists. The combination of CHD with the haemodynamic demands of pregnancy — increased CO by 40%, expanded plasma volume, reduced SVR — creates clinical scenarios that range from low-risk (well-repaired simple defects) to the gravest cardiovascular emergency in medicine (Eisenmenger).

## Haemodynamic changes of pregnancy and CHD

Pregnancy imposes substantial cardiovascular demands. For normal hearts, these are accommodated physiologically. For a heart with fixed structural lesions, the changes can be catastrophic:

- ↑ Cardiac output 30–50%: peaks at 28–32 weeks. Achieved via both ↑ HR and ↑ SV from volume expansion. Lesions with fixed obstructions (severe AS, MS, coarctation) cannot increase output across the obstruction → underperfusion of mother and fetus.
- ↓ SVR 20–30%: progesterone → vasodilation + placental low-resistance circuit. In Eisenmenger → more right-to-left shunting → worse cyanosis. In obstructive lesions (AS) → reduced coronary perfusion pressure.
- ↑ Blood volume 50%: ↑ preload → may decompensate impaired ventricles. In valvular regurgitation → temporarily better tolerated. In ventricular dysfunction → HF risk.
- Peripartum: autotransfusion (uterine contractions → 300–500 mL blood return to circulation) + Valsalva-equivalent (pushing during delivery) → sudden preload surge then drop.

## mWHO risk classification for CHD in pregnancy

| mWHO Class | Risk | CHD examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Class I | No detectable risk increase | Repaired simple lesions: PDA ligated, secundum ASD closed, small VSD, mild PS corrected |
| Class II | Small increased risk | Repaired TOF (good function), BAV without significant AS/AR, coarctation repaired without residual, AVSD repaired |
| Class II–III | Moderate risk — specialist assessment required | Mild-moderate systemic ventricular dysfunction, moderate pulmonary stenosis, moderate valve disease |
| Class III | Significant risk — delivery at tertiary CHD centre mandatory | Systemic RV (Mustard, ccTGA), mechanical valve, severe systemic ventricular dysfunction, severe MS, moderately dilated aorta in Marfan (40–45 mm) |
| Class IV | Extremely high risk — pregnancy contraindicated | Eisenmenger syndrome (maternal mortality ~30–50%), severe PAH, severely impaired systemic ventricle (EF <30%), severe symptomatic AS, aorta ≥50 mm Marfan or ≥45 mm with BAV |

## Key lesions in pregnancy

### Repaired TOF — generally well tolerated

Women with repaired TOF with preserved biventricular function (RV EF ≥50%, no severe PR, no severe RVOTO, QRS <160 ms) generally tolerate pregnancy well — mWHO Class II. Key risks: arrhythmias (IART/VT — monitor closely), RV dilation from volume loading of pregnancy (worsened by chronic PR). Pre-pregnancy: optimise RV function, consider PVR before pregnancy if RVEDI approaching threshold.

### Aortic dilation — the emergency

Women with Marfan syndrome or BAV-associated aortopathy are at increased risk of aortic dissection during pregnancy (especially the 3rd trimester and peripartum — peak haemodynamic stress on the aortic wall). Pregnancy contraindicated if aortic root ≥50 mm (Marfan) or ≥50 mm (BAV). Strict BP control (beta-blocker throughout pregnancy), rest, avoidance of Valsalva. Elective caesarean section if aortic root ≥45 mm (to avoid Valsalva of pushing during labour).

### Fontan circulation in pregnancy

Pregnancy in Fontan patients is high-risk (mWHO Class III). The Fontan circuit depends on pulmonary vascular resistance being low — the ↑ CO of pregnancy is accommodated but at the cost of elevated systemic venous (Fontan circuit) pressure. Key risks: HF, arrhythmia, thromboembolic events (Fontan already prothrombotic + pregnancy hypercoagulable state). Fetal outcomes are poor (premature birth, IUGR common). Pre-pregnancy: careful haemodynamic assessment, ensure Fontan pressures and ventricular function are optimal.

### Cyanotic CHD — universal fetal risk

Any degree of maternal cyanosis (SpO₂ <85%) → severe fetal growth restriction and intrauterine death. The fetus depends entirely on the oxygen content of maternal blood. SpO₂ <85% at rest is associated with live birth rates of only 12%. Even SpO₂ 85–89% gives live birth rate ~40%. Women with significant cyanosis should be counselled about fetal outcomes alongside maternal risk.

Exam tip: The ZAHARA and CARPREG II risk scores for ACHD pregnancy: The ZAHARA score (Zwangerschap bij Aangeboren HARtAfwijkingen) and CARPREG II score both estimate maternal cardiac event risk during pregnancy in women with structural heart disease. Key risk factors in both: prior cardiac event, baseline NYHA class >II, cyanosis, left heart obstruction, mechanical valve, systemic ventricular dysfunction, and cardiac medications at baseline. ZAHARA cutoff: score >1.5 = high risk. CARPREG II ≥4 points = event rate >40%. These scores should be calculated before conception counselling in every woman with CHD considering pregnancy. A high score mandates specialist CHD pregnancy centre planning and delivery.

Checkpoint: A 26-year-old woman with repaired AVSD (Down syndrome) and good biventricular function asks about pregnancy. Her echo: EF 62%, mild MR (EROA 0.15 cm²), no residual ASD or VSD, PASP 28 mmHg. She has Down syndrome with mild intellectual disability. Her partner does not have Down syndrome. What are the relevant considerations?
This consultation requires careful attention to medical, genetic, legal, and ethical dimensions. Medical risk assessment: her repaired AVSD with good biventricular function and mild MR (EROA 0.15 — mild, below surgical threshold), normal PASP, and normal LV function places her at mWHO Class II (repaired AVSD with good function — moderate cardiac risk, manageable with appropriate specialist care). The cardiac risk of pregnancy is real but not prohibitive. Genetic counselling is essential: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) has a recurrence risk of approximately 1–2% per pregnancy (higher if either parent carries a Robertsonian translocation — chromosomal analysis of both parents indicated). However, the dominant risk is from advanced maternal age-related nondisjunction — she is 26, so age-related trisomy risk is lower than the general population risk at this age. Prenatal diagnosis: offer detailed counselling about options including non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), amniocentesis, and the options if Trisomy 21 is detected in the fetus. Capacity and supported decision-making: women with Down syndrome have the right to make decisions about reproduction. Mild intellectual disability does not remove legal or ethical capacity to consent to pregnancy. The consultation should assess her understanding of the pregnancy process, medical risks, and parenting demands — and ensure she has access to appropriate support services. Cultural and family context matters. This must be a collaborative, respectful consultation that respects her autonomy while ensuring she has the information and support needed to make an informed decision. Cardiac surveillance plan during pregnancy: echocardiography each trimester, cardiology review each trimester, delivery at a hospital with cardiac and obstetric expertise.

sections.body:
CHD has a set of recognition patterns — combinations of clinical signs, ECG findings, and CXR appearances — that point to the diagnosis before any imaging. Mastering these patterns is the difference between a cardiologist who "knows the answer when they see it" and one who discovers it only after the echo report arrives.

## The 6 essential CHD recognition patterns

### Pattern 1 — Fixed split S2 + pulmonary flow murmur + RV heave in an adult

This triad = secundum ASD until proven otherwise. The fixed split S2 (present in all phases of respiration) is the pathognomonic auscultatory sign of ASD. The pulmonary flow murmur (from increased RV outflow, not from the ASD itself) and RV heave from volume overload complete the picture. A tricuspid mid-diastolic rumble may be audible in large ASDs. Many adults are diagnosed for the first time when they develop AF — RA dilation from chronic volume overload eventually causes AF.

### Pattern 2 — Continuous "machinery" murmur below the left clavicle + bounding pulses

Patent ductus arteriosus. The murmur envelops S2 (does not stop at the second heart sound). Bounding pulses from wide pulse pressure (large SV + diastolic runoff into the PA → low diastolic BP). In an adult with a disappearing continuous murmur → consider Eisenmenger physiology developing (shunt reversing → gradient across the duct falling → murmur shortening to systolic then disappearing).

### Pattern 3 — Left axis deviation + RBBB (incomplete) + prolonged PR in any patient

This ECG combination = AVSD (partial or complete) until proven otherwise. The left axis deviation from abnormal inferior-to-superior depolarisation through the inlet septum is the most distinctive feature. Seen in Down syndrome infants with complete AVSD and in adults with unrepaired or repaired partial AVSD. No other common lesion produces this exact ECG combination.

### Pattern 4 — Central cyanosis + right ventricular hypertrophy + reduced pulmonary vascular markings on CXR

Pulmonary oligaemia + cyanosis = obstruction to pulmonary blood flow + right-to-left shunt. The dominant diagnosis in children: Tetralogy of Fallot (boot-shaped heart, right arch in 25%, concave PA segment). The differential includes: critical PS with ASD, pulmonary atresia with VSD, Ebstein's anomaly with severe TR and right-to-left atrial shunting. Distinguish from D-TGA (cyanosis but increased or normal pulmonary vascular markings — the pulmonary circuit is receiving all the left heart output).

### Pattern 5 — Hypertension in a young person + weak femoral pulses + rib notching on CXR

Coarctation of the aorta. The arm-leg BP gradient, radio-femoral delay, and rib notching (collateral erosion of ribs 3–8 — present only after age 5, never in neonates). The figure-3 sign on CXR. BAV in 50–80% — always look for the aortic valve. Any young person with unexplained hypertension must have blood pressure measured in both arms and one leg. Missing this diagnosis in a 20-year-old condemns them to decades of uncontrolled hypertension, LVH, and premature stroke.

### Pattern 6 — "Egg on a string" CXR + profound neonatal cyanosis + increased pulmonary vascular markings

D-TGA. The narrow mediastinum (parallel great arteries create a thin vascular pedicle) + cardiomegaly + increased pulmonary markings (LV is pumping to the PA → overcirculation). The "egg on a string" appearance is pathognomonic. Contrast with TOF (narrow mediastinum but reduced pulmonary markings, concave PA segment, boot-shaped heart). Any severely cyanotic neonate with increased or normal pulmonary markings requires immediate echo to distinguish TGA from other mixing lesions (TAPVD, HLHS, severe TR).

## 10 critical red flags — dangerous mismanagements to avoid

| # | Dangerous action | Why it kills |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Close an ASD/VSD/PDA in a patient with Eisenmenger physiology (SpO₂ <90%, PVR ≥SVR) | The defect is the RV's only pop-off valve. Closing it → acute RV pressure crisis → right heart failure → death within hours. |
| 2 | Perform phlebotomy routinely for polycythaemia in Eisenmenger without checking iron stores | Iron deficiency in polycythaemia → microcytic, poorly deformable red cells → paradoxically increased stroke risk. Do NOT phlebotomise unless haematocrit >65% AND symptomatic hyperviscosity AND iron stores adequate. |
| 3 | Use IV adenosine or verapamil for a wide complex tachycardia in an ACHD patient with WPW (Ebstein's, ccTGA) | Ebstein's anomaly has right-sided accessory pathways in 25%. WPW + AF → adenosine blocks AV node → all AF conducted via AP → VF. Never adenosine for WCT with possible pre-excitation. |
| 4 | Miss the diagnosis of infective endocarditis in an ACHD patient with fever | Any ACHD patient with prosthetic material, residual defect, or cyanotic lesion is at high IE risk. Three blood cultures before antibiotics — always. Any ACHD + fever of >3 days unexplained = IE until proven otherwise. |
| 5 | Stop PGE1 infusion in a duct-dependent neonate (HLHS, critical coarctation, critical PS/PA, D-TGA) before definitive intervention | Ductal closure in these lesions → rapid cardiovascular collapse. PGE1 must be maintained continuously until surgical/catheter palliation or repair is complete. |
| 6 | Delay repair of AVSD in a Down syndrome infant past 6 months | Pulmonary vascular disease develops faster in Down syndrome AVSD — by 12–18 months PVR may be irreversibly elevated and the window for repair closed. Eisenmenger is preventable if repair is timely. |
| 7 | Cardiovert a patient with Fontan IART without anticoagulation | Slow flow in Fontan circuit → thrombus in static chambers → cardioversion → embolism → stroke. Anticoagulate for ≥3 weeks or exclude thrombus by TOE before any cardioversion. |
| 8 | Allow pregnancy in a woman with Eisenmenger syndrome | Maternal mortality 30–50%. mWHO Class IV = pregnancy contraindicated. Effective contraception (non-oestrogenic) is mandatory. Termination counselling if already pregnant. |
| 9 | Diagnose a neonate with "small VSD" because the murmur is quiet | A quiet or absent murmur in a sick neonate with RV enlargement and increased pulmonary markings may indicate a large NON-restrictive VSD (low velocity across the defect = no turbulence = no murmur). Echo is mandatory — never diagnose VSD severity from murmur loudness alone. |
| 10 | Manage a Mustard/Senning patient's arrhythmia as standard atrial flutter with CTI ablation | IART in Mustard/Senning circulates around the atrial baffle — not the cavotricuspid isthmus. Standard CTI ablation does not work and wastes time. These patients need an ACHD-specific EP specialist who understands the complex atrial anatomy. |

CHD MCQs test anatomical reasoning, genetic associations, haemodynamic logic, and acute management decisions. The framework: identify the anatomy → identify the haemodynamic consequence → identify the correct intervention and contraindications.

## The CHD MCQ framework

1. What is the anatomy? Cyanotic or acyanotic? Left-to-right shunt or obstruction? Which chambers are affected?
2. What is the haemodynamic consequence? Volume overload (which chamber)? Pressure overload (which ventricle)? Right-to-left shunt → cyanosis?
3. What is the genetic or syndromic association? Down → AVSD; Turner → coarctation + BAV; DiGeorge → conotruncal; Noonan → PS (often dysplastic); Williams → supravalvular AS
4. Is there a contraindication? Eisenmenger → no closure; PGE1 → only for duct-dependent; Noonan PS → BPV may fail (dysplastic valve); TOF tet spell → morphine + knee-chest, NOT vasodilators
5. What does the ECG or CXR tell me? LAD + RBBB → AVSD; boot-shaped heart → TOF; egg on string → D-TGA; rib notching → coarctation

## CHD trap library — 15 high-yield traps

| # | Scenario | Trap answer | Correct answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 45-year-old woman with new AF and fixed split S2 | "Investigate for paroxysmal AF — the S2 finding is irrelevant" | Fixed split S2 = ASD until proven otherwise. The AF is from RA dilation — the ASD is the cause, not a coincidence. Echo to confirm, then ASD closure (likely transcatheter). |
| 2 | Infant with quiet precordium, no murmur, but SpO₂ 72%, increased pulmonary markings on CXR, "egg on a string" appearance | "No murmur = no significant cardiac lesion" | D-TGA. The parallel circuits create cyanosis despite high pulmonary blood flow. No shunt murmur because the two circuits don't communicate significantly. Immediate PGE1 + balloon atrial septostomy + arterial switch operation. |
| 3 | 6-month-old with Down syndrome, large AVSD, PASP 65 mmHg, Qp:Qs 1.5:1, parents want to wait until the baby is bigger | "Waiting is reasonable — the baby will grow stronger" | The baby will not grow stronger — the PASP of 65 mmHg at 6 months with falling Qp:Qs indicates rapidly advancing PAH. Each month of delay makes the window for repair narrower. Urgent surgical referral now. |
| 4 | ECG shows left axis deviation, RBBB, and long PR interval in a 25-year-old woman | "Left anterior fascicle block + RBBB + first-degree block — probably idiopathic" | This ECG triad is the hallmark of AVSD (partial or complete). Refer for echo. If partial AVSD: primum ASD + cleft MV → surgical repair. Do not dismiss this ECG pattern in any age group. |
| 5 | Cyanotic CHD patient, SpO₂ 82%, haematocrit 68% — physician orders phlebotomy "to treat polycythaemia" | "Phlebotomy is indicated to reduce hyperviscosity" | Check iron stores first. Phlebotomy in iron-deficient polycythaemia produces microcytic cells with poor O₂ delivery and increased stroke risk. Only phlebotomise if haematocrit >65% AND symptomatic AND iron stores adequate. |
| 6 | Premature infant, PDA 3mm, creatinine 140 µmol/L, platelets 35,000 — physician gives indomethacin | "Indomethacin is first-line for premature PDA" | Indomethacin is contraindicated with renal impairment and thrombocytopenia. Use IV paracetamol (acetaminophen) as the safer alternative for pharmacological ductal closure in this context. |
| 7 | 7-year-old boy, outlet VSD 4mm, Doppler velocity 4.5 m/s, no AR, asymptomatic — doctor says "just watch" | "Small VSD, high velocity, asymptomatic — watch and wait is correct" | Outlet (supracristal/doubly committed subarterial) VSD carries a high risk of aortic cusp prolapse and AR regardless of size. Even small outlet VSDs typically require surgical repair to prevent progressive AR. Refer for surgical assessment. |
| 8 | Child having a tet spell — nurse administers IV GTN (nitroglycerin) to "relax the heart" | "Vasodilators reduce cardiac work during the spell" | Systemic vasodilation in TOF tet spell WORSENS right-to-left shunting (↓ SVR → more blood goes right-to-left across the VSD → more cyanosis). The correct treatment is to INCREASE SVR: knee-chest position, phenylephrine IV, not vasodilators. |
| 9 | Repaired TOF patient, QRS 185 ms on routine ECG, no symptoms, no VT on 24h Holter | "Asymptomatic, no VT — safe to observe" | QRS >180 ms in repaired TOF is an independent risk factor for sustained VT and sudden cardiac death even in asymptomatic patients. Refer for EP study and ICD discussion. This is not a "watch and wait" finding. |
| 10 | Patient with Fontan circulation develops rapid irregular tachycardia. A cardiologist plans CTI ablation for "atrial flutter" | "All atrial flutter is around the cavotricuspid isthmus" | Fontan patients develop intra-atrial reentrant tachycardia (IART) around the atrial scars and the Fontan baffle — not the CTI. Standard CTI ablation will not terminate or prevent it. Requires an ACHD EP specialist with 3D mapping capability. |
| 11 | 14-year-old girl with Noonan syndrome, dysplastic PS (peak gradient 75 mmHg), BPV planned | "BPV is the first-line treatment for all valvular PS" | Dysplastic PS (no commissures to split) responds poorly to BPV. Attempt BPV first (lower risk), but if gradient remains ≥40 mmHg post-BPV → surgical pulmonary valvotomy required. |
| 12 | 22-year-old woman with repaired secundum ASD (device closure 2 years ago) planning dental extraction. Should she receive antibiotic prophylaxis? | "All ACHD patients need endocarditis prophylaxis" | Prophylaxis is NOT indicated for repaired secundum ASD with complete device endothelialisation (device placed >6 months ago with no residual shunt adjacent to prosthetic material). Prophylaxis is only for high-risk CHD lesions per current ESC guidelines. |
| 13 | Mustard procedure survivor, 35 years old, develops complete heart block — cardiologist installs a transvenous RV lead pacemaker | "Standard RV apical pacing is appropriate" | In Mustard patients, the "RV" is the pulmonary ventricle — standard transvenous leads go to the pulmonary ventricle, not the systemic ventricle. The anatomy is reversed. Standard pacing approaches may not work as expected. ACHD pacing requires specialist knowledge of the baffle anatomy and the position of the morphological ventricles. |
| 14 | 25-year-old woman with ccTGA (systemic RV, EF 42%) asks about pregnancy. The cardiologist says: "Your heart condition is corrected, so pregnancy is low risk." | "Congenitally corrected means corrected — low risk" | ccTGA is "physiologically corrected" but the systemic RV (EF 42%) is already at the lower limit of function. Pregnancy (↑ CO demand, ↑ volume load) puts additional stress on the systemic RV → decompensation risk. This is mWHO Class III. The patient needs specialist ACHD pregnancy counselling and delivery at a CHD centre. |
| 15 | A cyanotic 3-year-old, unrepaired TOF, SpO₂ 80%, is scheduled for a non-cardiac procedure (hernia repair). Anaesthesiologist plans to use halothane (a cardiac depressant). Is this appropriate? | "All anaesthetic agents are equally acceptable" | Halothane and other vasodilating or cardiac depressant agents are dangerous in TOF — vasodilation ↓ SVR → worsened right-to-left shunting → acute cyanosis and cardiovascular collapse. Anaesthesia for cyanotic CHD requires a paediatric cardiac anaesthesiologist experienced in maintaining SVR and avoiding agents that worsen R-L shunting. |

## Synthesis vignette — the complete CHD patient

Checkpoint: A 32-year-old Indonesian man with undiagnosed CHD presents to a district hospital with progressive dyspnoea (NYHA III), central cyanosis (SpO₂ 88% at rest), and haemoptysis. He has clubbing, a loud P2, and a grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the left sternal border that is softer than it was "years ago" per an old note. CXR: cardiomegaly with a prominent main PA, enlarged branch PAs, and no rib notching. ECG: RVH pattern with dominant R in V1. He is otherwise unmarried, and his family report he "has always been blue since childhood." Echo: large unrestrictive VSD (1.8 cm, Doppler velocity only 0.8 m/s), PASP 105 mmHg, bidirectional shunt with net right-to-left component, RV markedly dilated and hypertrophied, LV normal size. Identify his diagnosis with anatomical detail, explain the haemodynamic sequence that created this picture, and outline his current management.
Diagnosis: Eisenmenger syndrome secondary to a large unrestrictive VSD. Anatomical detail: The VSD is large (1.8 cm — close to or exceeding the aortic annulus diameter, hence "unrestrictive"), perimembranous in location based on clinical context. The Doppler velocity of 0.8 m/s confirms negligible pressure gradient between LV and RV — essentially systemic-level RV pressure. PASP 105 mmHg = suprasystemic pulmonary arterial hypertension. Haemodynamic sequence: At birth, pulmonary vascular resistance was high → little shunting. As PVR fell physiologically in infancy → massive left-to-right shunt developed (this is when the murmur was loud and he should have been referred for repair). Progressive pulmonary overcirculation → endothelial injury → medial hypertrophy → intimal proliferation → obliterative plexiform lesions → PVR rose progressively over years. When PVR reached SVR → shunt neutralised → murmur became quieter. When PVR exceeded SVR → shunt reversed to right-to-left → cyanosis appeared/worsened (was "always blue since childhood" — the transition likely occurred in early childhood, indicating very early, aggressive PAH development). The small LV (fed only by pulmonary veins, now receiving less flow as less blood reaches the lungs) contrasts with the massive dilated-hypertrophied RV (bearing systemic pressure). Current management: (1) VSD closure is absolutely contraindicated. The VSD is his only RV pop-off valve. Closing it with PVR 105 mmHg → immediate fatal RV failure. Never close. (2) PAH-targeted therapy: Start with a single agent — bosentan 62.5 mg BD for 4 weeks then 125 mg BD (BREATHE-5 trial evidence for Eisenmenger). Assess response at 3 months (6MWT, SpO₂, functional class). Consider adding sildenafil 20–40 mg TDS if inadequate response. Combination therapy for WHO FC III. (3) Haematocrit management: Current SpO₂ 88% → likely haematocrit 55–65%. Check iron stores, ferritin. Supplement iron if deficient. Only phlebotomise if haematocrit >65% AND symptomatic hyperviscosity. (4) Avoid systemic vasodilators (ACEi, nitrates, DHP-CCBs beyond the PAH-targeted context) — reduce SVR → worsen R-L shunting. (5) Avoid pregnancy (mWHO Class IV) — counsel regarding contraception. (6) Haemoptysis evaluation: mild haemoptysis is common from dilated pulmonary vessels. If massive → bronchial arterial embolisation may be needed. (7) Regular surveillance: 6MWT, SpO₂, echo, FBC, iron studies, renal function every 6 months. (8) Heart-lung transplantation discussion: for end-stage disease in appropriate candidates. The transplantation waiting times are long — introduce the concept early while the patient is still a reasonable candidate.

## The final CHD exam checklist

Alert: Before every CHD answer — verify:
✓ Eisenmenger = NEVER close the defect (regardless of what additional "evidence" is given)
✓ Fixed split S2 = ASD (not flow murmur from ASD itself — the split is from RV volume overload)
✓ LAD + RBBB + long PR = AVSD (partial or complete)
✓ Down syndrome → echo mandatory → AVSD in 40%, repair within 3–6 months
✓ Tet spell = knee-chest + morphine + propranolol + phenylephrine. Never vasodilators.
✓ QRS >180 ms in repaired TOF = high SCD risk → EP study ± ICD
✓ PVR threshold for PVR: RVEDI ≥160 mL/m² or RVEF <47% (CMR, not echo, for RV volumes)
✓ D-TGA = egg on string + cyanosis + increased pulmonary markings. Immediate PGE1 + BAS + ASO
✓ Duct-dependent lesions (HLHS, critical coarctation, critical PS, D-TGA without ASD) = PGE1 until repair
✓ Noonan PS + dysplastic valve → BPV may fail → surgical valvotomy
✓ Outlet VSD (supracristal) = repair even if small to prevent AR progression
✓ Perimembranous VSD transcatheter closure → risk of complete heart block (delayed)
✓ Coarctation = young hypertensive + radio-femoral delay + arm-leg BP gradient + rib notching (age >5)
✓ Turner syndrome → BAV (50%) + coarctation (30%) + aortic dissection risk = echo mandatory
✓ Polycythaemia in Eisenmenger → check iron first, do NOT phlebotomise without indication
✓ Fontan IART ≠ typical atrial flutter → not CTI ablation → ACHD EP specialist required
✓ Pregnancy contraindicated: Eisenmenger (50% maternal mortality), severe PAH, EF <30%, aorta ≥50 mm
✓ Endocarditis prophylaxis: only high-risk CHD (prosthetic valve, prior IE, cyanotic unrepaired, prosthetic material <6 months)
✓ ccTGA = double discordance (AV + VA) = physiologically corrected but systemic RV → progressive RV failure + complete heart block risk

sections.body:
Diagnosing CHD requires a systematic integration of clinical findings, chest X-ray, ECG, and echocardiography. Each investigation provides a different dimension of information — and together they build the complete haemodynamic picture before intervention.

## Clinical examination in CHD

### Cyanosis — central vs peripheral

Central cyanosis: bluish discolouration of tongue, mucous membranes, and nail beds — signifies arterial hypoxaemia (SpO₂ typically <85%). Seen in right-to-left shunts, pulmonary disease with V/Q mismatch, or severe alveolar hypoventilation. Peripheral cyanosis: bluish extremities with pink mucous membranes — from reduced peripheral perfusion (low cardiac output, cold environment, Raynaud's). Only central cyanosis implies a cardiac structural lesion with right-to-left shunting.

Differential cyanosis: lower body more cyanotic than upper body (or vice versa). Lower body cyanosis with pink upper body → PDA with Eisenmenger physiology (right-to-left shunt at ductal level — deoxygenated blood enters the descending aorta below the left subclavian → legs cyanotic; pre-ductal arch supplies head/arms with oxygenated blood). Upper body cyanosis with pink lower body → D-TGA with PDA (deoxygenated blood from the RV-aorta supplies the head; PDA allows oxygenated pulmonary blood to enter the descending aorta).

### Clubbing

Chronic arterial hypoxaemia → loss of nail angle (Lovibond angle >180°), drumstick fingertips, sponginess of the nail bed. Develops over months to years of sustained cyanosis. Absent in acute right-to-left shunts. Clubbing in CHD = long-standing significant cyanosis = Eisenmenger or unrepaired cyanotic CHD.

### Precordial examination

- Right ventricular heave (parasternal lift): palpable impulse along the left sternal edge — RV volume or pressure overload. Seen in ASD (volume), pulmonary hypertension (pressure), PS (pressure)
- Left ventricular apex displacement: LV volume overload (VSD, PDA, MR) displaces the apex laterally and inferiorly
- Thrill: palpable vibration from a turbulent murmur — indicates a grade 4+ murmur. In CHD: thrill at lower left sternal border → VSD; at upper left sternal edge → PS; at upper right sternal edge → AS

## Chest X-ray in CHD — the systematic approach

| Feature | What it means | Associated conditions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cardiomegaly (CTR >0.5) | Volume-overloaded or dilated heart | Large VSD, PDA, AVSD (biventricular enlargement); Ebstein's anomaly (massively enlarged RA) |
| Increased pulmonary vascular markings | Pulmonary overcirculation — large L→R shunt | Large ASD, VSD, PDA, AVSD, TGA with VSD |
| Reduced pulmonary vascular markings (oligaemia) | Reduced pulmonary blood flow | TOF (classic — "black lung fields"), severe PS/PA with IVS, Ebstein's with PS |
| Pulmonary oedema pattern | Elevated pulmonary venous pressure | Total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (TAPVD) — especially obstructed type |
| Boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot) | RV hypertrophy + small main PA + normal-sized heart | Tetralogy of Fallot (classic CXR sign) |
| "Egg on a string" or narrow mediastinum | Parallel great arteries in D-TGA → narrow vascular pedicle on PA view | D-Transposition of the great arteries |
| Right-sided aortic arch | Aorta arches to the right instead of left | TOF (25%), truncus arteriosus, DiGeorge syndrome — "right arch in cyanotic CHD = TOF until proven otherwise" |
| Rib notching | Collateral intercostal artery erosion of inferior rib margins (ribs 3–8) | Coarctation of the aorta (>5 years of age when collaterals develop — not present in neonates) |
| Snowman/figure-of-8 sign | Dilated SVC + vertical vein + RA forming snowman shape | Supracardiac TAPVD |

## ECG in CHD

| ECG pattern | Interpretation | CHD association |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Right axis deviation + RBBB + RVH | RV pressure overload | ASD (volume → RBBB common; RAD); PS; TOF post-repair (RBBB almost universal) |
| Left axis deviation + RBBB | Inferior conduction delay + left anterior fascicle block | AVSD (primum ASD) — the pathognomonic ECG of AV canal defects |
| Left axis deviation (extreme) + RBBB | Same, more pronounced | Complete AVSD (Down syndrome) |
| RVH dominant R in V1 | RV pressure overload | Pulmonary hypertension, severe PS, D-TGA (neonatal) |
| Sinus venosus ASD | Often normal or P wave axis changes (low ectopic atrial rhythm from posterior sinus node displacement) | Sinus venosus ASD — P wave negative in inferior leads (coronary sinus displacement) |
| Delta waves | Pre-excitation | Ebstein's anomaly (WPW in 25%, right-sided AP), L-TGA (accessory pathway common) |

## Echocardiography in CHD — the segmental approach

Complex CHD requires systematic segmental analysis rather than direct structural labelling. The segmental approach describes three cardiac segments and two junctions in sequence:

1. Atrial situs: which side is the morphological right atrium vs left atrium? (Right atrium = broad-based appendage, eustachian valve; LA = narrow tubular appendage). Normally the right atrium is on the right (situs solitus). In situs inversus (mirror image), everything is reversed. In heterotaxy (situs ambiguus): bilateral right or bilateral left atria.
2. AV junction: are the atria concordant with the ventricles? (RA → RV = normal concordance). Discordance: RA connects to the morphological LV and LA to the RV — as in L-TGA.
3. Ventricular identification: morphological RV (trabecular, apical moderator band) vs LV (smooth walls, two papillary muscles). Which is the subpulmonary ventricle and which is subaortic?
4. Ventriculo-arterial junction: concordant (RV→PA, LV→Ao) or discordant (RV→Ao, LV→PA = D-TGA)?
5. Additional lesions: ASD, VSD, valvular abnormalities, arch anomalies, coronary origins.

Clinical link: The pre-echo clinical assessment determines which echo views to prioritise. A cyanotic neonate with a single loud S2 and no murmur, CXR showing increased vascular markings and a narrow mediastinum → probable D-TGA → prioritise parasternal long axis view (demonstrates great artery relationship: parallel rather than crossing great arteries) and subcostal views (atrial septum, ductal anatomy). A child with a pansystolic murmur, thrill at the lower left sternal border, and biventricular enlargement on CXR → probable large VSD → prioritise parasternal views showing the interventricular septum and Doppler across the VSD. The clinical and radiological information should always guide the echo rather than performing a standardised study alone.

Checkpoint: A 6-week-old baby has been feeding poorly, sweating during feeds, and gaining weight slowly since birth. On examination: tachycardia (HR 165 bpm), tachypnoea (RR 56 breaths/min), mild perioral cyanosis during feeds only, hepatomegaly 3 cm. There is a pansystolic murmur grade 3/6 at the lower left sternal border with a thrill. CXR: cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary vascular markings. What is the diagnosis and the haemodynamic explanation for his symptoms?
Large VSD with heart failure from pulmonary overcirculation. Haemodynamic explanation: A large non-restrictive VSD creates a free communication between the left and right ventricles. In the first weeks of life, the elevated fetal pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) limits left-to-right shunting — symptoms are minimal. As PVR falls physiologically over weeks 2–8, the shunt increases dramatically. By 6 weeks, a large Qp:Qs (2:1 to 3:1) means the right ventricle, pulmonary vasculature, and left atrium/ventricle are handling 2–3× the normal blood volume. The consequences: (1) Pulmonary overcirculation → tachypnoea (the lungs are wet and stiff from engorgement — the baby breathes fast to compensate); (2) High metabolic demand → feeding intolerance and sweating (the effort of breathing fast leaves no reserve for the mechanics of suckling; sweating from catecholamine activation); (3) Right heart dilation + RV pressure elevation → hepatomegaly; (4) Perioral cyanosis during feeds from increased metabolic demand + temporary mixing. Management priorities: (1) Acute: diuretics (furosemide) to reduce pulmonary oedema; nasogastric feeds to reduce caloric expenditure of suckling; digoxin (in some centres) for inotropy. (2) Definitive: VSD closure — surgical patch closure at 3–6 months, or transcatheter closure if anatomy permits, before pulmonary vascular disease develops.
