sections.body:
ASD is the most common congenital heart defect presenting in adulthood — often discovered incidentally on a murmur or ECG. The key to ASD management is understanding why right heart volume overload develops, how to classify the defect type, and when to close it before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease or AF develops.

## ASD types and anatomy

| Type | Location | Frequency | Key associations |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Secundum ASD | Central fossa ovalis region — resorption of septum primum creates the hole | ~70% of ASD | Most amenable to transcatheter closure (Amplatzer device). Holt-Oram syndrome (TBX5 mutation). |
| Primum ASD | Lower atrial septum, above the AV valves — failure of septum primum to fuse with endocardial cushions | ~15–20% | Part of AV septal defect spectrum. Cleft anterior mitral leaflet → MR. Pathognomonic ECG: left axis deviation + RBBB. Cannot be closed percutaneously — surgical repair required. |
| Sinus venosus ASD | Upper or posterior atrial septum — at SVC-RA or IVC-RA junction | ~5–10% | Almost always associated with partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (PAPVD) — right upper pulmonary vein drains to SVC. Surgical repair required (transcatheter not feasible). P-wave axis changes on ECG (ectopic atrial pacemaker from posterior displacement). |
| Coronary sinus ASD | Unroofing of the coronary sinus — LA communicates with RA via the CS orifice | <1% | Often associated with persistent left SVC draining to the coronary sinus. Surgical repair. |
| Patent foramen ovale (PFO) | Probe-patent foramen ovale — flap not fused | 25% of adults (not a "true" ASD) | No haemodynamic significance. Associated with cryptogenic stroke (paradoxical embolism). PFO closure after cryptogenic stroke in patients <60 years: RESPECT, REDUCE, GORE-REDUCE trials all show reduced recurrent stroke vs medical therapy alone. |

## Haemodynamics of ASD

In ASD, the driving force for the left-to-right shunt is not a pressure difference (LA and RA pressures are nearly equal at rest) but rather the differential compliance of the two ventricles. The right ventricle is more compliant (thinner, lower resistance) than the left — it accepts blood more readily during diastole. This preferential filling of the RV drives flow from the LA across the ASD into the RA and then to the RV — even without a pressure gradient. The result: right heart dilation (RA, RV), pulmonary overcirculation (Qp > Qs), and enlarged main pulmonary artery.

Key concept: The ASD murmur is not from flow through the defect itself — it is a pulmonary flow murmur from increased flow across a normal pulmonary valve, and a fixed split S2
The flow velocity across an ASD is too low to generate turbulence and audible murmur — the pressure differential is minimal. What you hear instead: (1) An ejection systolic murmur in the left 2nd ICS from the increased flow across the pulmonary valve (like a pulmonary flow murmur, grade 2–3/6); (2) A fixed split S2 — the most characteristic auscultatory sign of ASD. Normally, S2 splits with inspiration (right-sided filling delays PV closure) and merges in expiration. In ASD: the right heart is always volume-overloaded → PV closure is always delayed → S2 is split throughout the respiratory cycle ("fixed"). The fixed split S2 distinguishes ASD from all other causes of split S2. Additional finding in large ASD: tricuspid mid-diastolic rumble (increased tricuspid flow from RV volume overload — analogous to the diastolic rumble of MS but from increased flow not obstruction).

## Clinical features by age

- Children: Often asymptomatic. Incidental murmur. Exercise tolerance may be mildly reduced. Recurrent respiratory infections from pulmonary overcirculation.
- Young adults (20–40s): Exertional dyspnoea, palpitations. Paradoxical embolism (stroke/TIA) if right-to-left shunting occurs during Valsalva.
- Older adults (40s–60s): AF or flutter (from RA dilation) is the presenting feature in 10–15%. New right heart failure. Pulmonary hypertension developing. Those who reach their 60s without closure have ~75% with AF, reduced exercise tolerance, and RV dysfunction.

## When to close — indications (ESC 2020 ACHD guidelines)

| Indication | Class |
| --- | --- |
| Significant ASD: Qp:Qs ≥1.5:1 OR evidence of RV volume overload (RV dilation) regardless of symptoms | Class I — close the defect |
| Symptomatic ASD at any Qp:Qs ratio | Class I |
| Paradoxical embolism through ASD or large PFO | Class IIa — closure |
| ASD with PVR ≥5 Wood units (moderate PAH) — closure possible if still net left-to-right | Class IIb — careful patient selection, cover test recommended (balloon occlusion) |
| ASD with Eisenmenger physiology (net right-to-left shunt, SpO₂ <90% at rest) | Contraindicated — do NOT close |

## Transcatheter vs surgical closure

Transcatheter (Amplatzer/Occlutech septal occluder): suitable for secundum ASD with adequate rim of tissue around the defect (rim ≥5 mm from key structures — AV valves, pulmonary veins, SVC, IVC). Defect diameter ≤38–40 mm (device sizing limit). Contraindicated: primum ASD, sinus venosus ASD, deficient rims. Procedure: transseptal catheter, device deployed under TOE and fluoroscopic guidance. Success rate >98%, complication rate <1% (device erosion — rare but can cause aortic or atrial perforation — most dangerous late complication, presents with pericardial tamponade weeks to years after implant).

Surgical closure: open repair under cardiopulmonary bypass. Required for: primum ASD (cleft mitral valve repair needed simultaneously), sinus venosus ASD (PAPVD repair needed), coronary sinus ASD, large secundum ASD with inadequate rims. Mortality <0.5% for isolated ASD repair in experienced centres.

Indonesian context: ASD in Indonesia: ASD is one of the most commonly diagnosed CHD lesions in Indonesia and represents a significant proportion of the adult CHD referral workload. Many patients in Indonesia with ASD are diagnosed for the first time in adulthood — presenting with AF, dyspnoea, or incidental murmur. By the time of diagnosis, some have already developed significant pulmonary hypertension. The availability of transcatheter ASD closure (Amplatzer) at major cardiac centres (PJNHK Jakarta, RS Harapan Kita) under BPJS coverage has improved access to closure without the need for open-heart surgery. However, device availability and the catheterisation laboratory capacity remain limiting factors outside Jakarta and Denpasar. For patients in remote areas with hemodynamically significant ASD: refer to the nearest tertiary cardiac centre before the window for safe closure (before irreversible PAH) is lost.

Checkpoint: A 45-year-old woman is referred with new-onset AF and dyspnoea NYHA II. Echo shows: secundum ASD 22 mm with adequate rims all around, right atrial dilation (RA area 28 cm²), RV dilation with preserved RV function, estimated PASP 42 mmHg, Qp:Qs 2.1:1. She is on anticoagulation for AF. Should her ASD be closed, and which technique is appropriate?
Yes — ASD closure is indicated. She meets Class I criteria: Qp:Qs ≥1.5:1 (2.1:1) with RV dilation and symptoms (NYHA II + new AF from RA dilation). The PASP of 42 mmHg (borderline elevated) must be assessed further — 42 mmHg is below the Eisenmenger threshold, and with a Qp:Qs still left-to-right at 2.1:1, the shunt is still predominantly left-to-right, making closure appropriate. Technique: transcatheter closure (Amplatzer or equivalent device) is the preferred approach. Criteria met: secundum type, 22 mm diameter (well within the ≤38–40 mm device limit), adequate rims confirmed. TOE guidance during the procedure. Pre-procedure: confirm AF is rate-controlled; ensure at least 3 weeks anticoagulation before any cardioversion or procedure. Continue anticoagulation after closure — AF persists after ASD closure in many adult patients (the AF substrate is RA dilation, which partially regresses but does not fully normalise). Post-closure: reassess PASP at 3–6 months echo. Important prognostic point: ASD closure in adults with established AF partially reduces AF burden (RA volume reduces) but does not reliably restore sinus rhythm — AF ablation may be needed subsequently if sinus rhythm is the goal.

sections.body:
VSD is the most common congenital heart defect overall — present in 30–40% of all CHD. Its haemodynamic impact spans a spectrum from the trivial muscular VSD that closes spontaneously in infancy to the large perimembranous defect that causes heart failure and irreversible pulmonary vascular disease within months of birth if uncorrected.

## Anatomical classification

| Type | Location | Frequency | Key features |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Perimembranous (paramembranous) | Membranous septum, just below the aortic valve — involves fibrous continuity between AV and semilunar valves | ~70–80% | Most common type. Risk of aortic valve prolapse into the VSD (especially right coronary cusp) → AR development over time. Partial spontaneous closure by fibrous "aneurysm" tissue (~30% of small defects close spontaneously by age 5). |
| Muscular | Anywhere in the muscular ventricular septum — apical, mid, anterior, posterior | ~10–15% | Often multiple ("Swiss cheese" septum). Highest rate of spontaneous closure (up to 80% by age 2). The muscular walls contract during systole → VSD dynamically narrows → less shunting than size suggests at rest. |
| Outlet (supracristal, doubly committed subarterial) | Outlet septum — directly below both semilunar valves | ~5–7% (higher in Asian populations — ~30% in East/SE Asian CHD) | High risk of aortic cusp prolapse → progressive AR regardless of VSD haemodynamics. Rarely closes spontaneously. Surgical repair usually recommended even when small, to prevent AR progression. Higher prevalence in Asian (including Indonesian) patients compared to Western populations. |
| Inlet (AV canal type) | Inlet septum, below the AV valves | ~5% | Component of complete AVSD. If isolated (without ASD), associated with Down syndrome. Same ECG pattern as AVSD: left axis deviation. |

## Haemodynamic consequences — size-dependent

The key determinant of haemodynamic impact is the size of the VSD relative to the aortic annulus:

- Restrictive VSD: small defect — maintains a pressure gradient between LV and RV (RV pressure remains normal or near-normal). The Doppler velocity across the VSD is high (4–5 m/s) precisely because the pressure difference is large. Minimal haemodynamic impact. No pulmonary hypertension development.
- Moderately restrictive VSD: intermediate. LV-RV pressure difference is partially maintained. Some pulmonary overcirculation — RV and PA pressure mildly elevated.
- Non-restrictive (large) VSD: size equals or exceeds the aortic annulus. LV and RV pressures equalise — the RV operates at systemic pressure. Massive pulmonary overcirculation → rapid development of pulmonary arterial hypertension. Without repair, progresses to Eisenmenger by age 1–2 years in many patients. The Doppler velocity across a large non-restrictive VSD is LOW (1–2 m/s) because the pressure difference is minimal — do not be reassured by a "low-velocity" VSD in an infant with HF symptoms.

Key concept: A small VSD has a loud murmur; a large VSD may have a quiet murmur — the paradox of restrictive vs non-restrictive VSDs
This is one of the most counterintuitive principles in CHD. A small restrictive VSD generates a loud holosystolic murmur because the high velocity (4–5 m/s) jet through a narrow orifice produces intense turbulence. A large non-restrictive VSD may have a soft or even absent systolic murmur because the large orifice allows low-velocity equalisation of pressures — minimal turbulence. Clinical implication: a quiet murmur or no murmur in a cyanotic or tachypnoeic neonate does NOT mean no VSD. Conversely, a loud murmur in a thriving infant likely means a small, haemodynamically insignificant VSD. Always integrate echo findings with haemodynamic status — never use murmur loudness alone to grade severity in VSDs.

## Indications for VSD closure (ESC 2020)

| Indication | Class |
| --- | --- |
| Qp:Qs ≥2:1 with evidence of LV volume overload | Class I |
| History of infective endocarditis | Class I |
| Outlet VSD with any degree of AR progression | Class I (repair to prevent AR regardless of haemodynamics) |
| Qp:Qs 1.5–2:1 with LV dilation OR symptoms | Class IIa |
| Small restrictive VSD with no LV dilation, no PAH, no AR — asymptomatic | No intervention — annual surveillance |
| VSD with Eisenmenger (net right-to-left shunt, SpO₂ <90%) | Contraindicated — no closure |

## Transcatheter vs surgical VSD closure

Transcatheter closure: muscular VSDs and some perimembranous VSDs (with specific device designs) can be closed percutaneously. Not suitable for: outlet VSDs (too close to aortic valve), inlet VSDs, very large defects. Complication specific to perimembranous VSD transcatheter closure: complete heart block — the conduction system (AV node and bundle of His) runs along the posterior-inferior rim of the perimembranous septum → device deployment near this area → delayed complete heart block (may occur days to weeks after device implantation). Incidence ~1–5%. Requires PPM. This risk must be carefully weighed in perimembranous VSD device closure vs surgical repair.

Surgical closure: patch closure (Dacron or pericardium) under cardiopulmonary bypass. Gold standard for most VSDs, especially perimembranous, outlet, inlet, and multiple muscular VSDs ("Swiss cheese"). Operative mortality <1% in experienced paediatric cardiac centres for isolated VSD.

Checkpoint: A 7-year-old Indonesian boy is referred for a VSD detected at birth. He has never had symptoms. Echo now shows: perimembranous VSD 5 mm, Doppler velocity 4.2 m/s, estimated RV pressure 35 mmHg (normal PASP), normal LV size, no AR, Qp:Qs 1.3:1. What is your assessment and recommendation?
Small restrictive perimembranous VSD — haemodynamically insignificant. Evidence: high Doppler velocity (4.2 m/s = large LV-RV pressure gradient = restrictive), estimated PASP 35 mmHg (normal), normal LV size (no volume overload), Qp:Qs 1.3:1 (barely above 1:1 — minimal shunt). Current ESC indications for closure are NOT met: no LV dilation, no PAH, no AR, no IE history, Qp:Qs <1.5:1. Management: conservative surveillance, no closure. Two important monitoring points: (1) AR development — perimembranous VSDs are at risk for right coronary cusp prolapse into the defect → AR. Annual echo specifically assessing the aortic valve is mandatory. If AR develops and progresses to even mild-moderate AR → surgical repair indicated (to prevent AR becoming severe and causing LV dilation). (2) Endocarditis prophylaxis: IE risk with VSD is real — high-velocity jet causes endothelial damage. He should receive antibiotic prophylaxis for invasive dental procedures (amoxicillin 50 mg/kg 1 hour before) per current guidelines. (3) Activity: no restriction needed for a restrictive VSD with normal RV pressure and normal LV size. He can participate in all normal physical activities. Follow-up echo: annually while the VSD is present.

sections.body:
The ductus arteriosus is essential in fetal life — it bypasses the fluid-filled lungs and delivers right heart output to the systemic circulation. After birth, it should close within 24–72 hours. When it remains patent, it creates a direct communication between the high-pressure aorta and the low-pressure pulmonary artery — with consequences that range from trivial to catastrophic depending on its size.

## Fetal circulation and ductal function

In fetal circulation, the placenta performs gas exchange — the lungs are fluid-filled and receive only 10% of combined ventricular output. The ductus arteriosus (DA) connects the main pulmonary artery to the descending aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery, allowing 90% of RV output to bypass the lungs and enter systemic circulation. Three shunts characterise fetal circulation:

1. Ductus venosus: umbilical vein → IVC (bypasses liver)
2. Foramen ovale: IVC blood → LA → LV → ascending aorta/brain (oxygen-rich blood preferentially to brain)
3. Ductus arteriosus: RV → PA → aorta (bypasses lungs)

At birth: cord clamping → placental circulation ends → arterial PO₂ rises → oxygen triggers ductal smooth muscle constriction (via prostaglandin E2 pathway being removed). Functional closure within 10–15 hours in term neonates; anatomical fibrous obliteration by 2–3 weeks (ligamentum arteriosum). Premature infants: immature ductal smooth muscle responds poorly to oxygen → PDA very common (>30% of infants <30 weeks). The neonatal DA is prostaglandin E2-dependent (high PGE2 keeps it open) — indomethacin (COX inhibitor → ↓PGE2) closes it pharmacologically.

## Haemodynamics of PDA

Blood flows continuously from the aorta (high pressure throughout systole and diastole) to the pulmonary artery (lower pressure). This creates a continuous shunt — unlike VSD (only during systole) or ASD (diastolic). Consequences:

- Pulmonary overcirculation (the PA receives extra flow from the aorta throughout the cardiac cycle)
- Left atrial and left ventricular volume overload (all the extra pulmonary return comes back to the left heart) — LA and LV dilation are hallmarks
- "Steal" phenomenon: diastolic runoff into the PA → reduced diastolic pressure → reduced diastolic coronary perfusion (particularly problematic in premature neonates)
- Wide pulse pressure: large SV from volume-overloaded LV + diastolic runoff into PA → low diastolic BP → wide pulse pressure → "bounding pulses"

## Clinical examination

The continuous "machinery" murmur — the classic auscultatory finding of PDA. It begins in systole, peaks around S2, and continues into diastole (because the aorta-to-PA pressure gradient exists throughout the cardiac cycle). Best heard in the left infraclavicular region (under the left clavicle, below the clavicle) and left upper sternal border. The murmur "envelops" S2 — it does not stop at S2 and restart (as would two separate systolic/diastolic murmurs). Additional findings: bounding peripheral pulses (wide pulse pressure); active precordium; apical displaced LV apex (LV volume overload).

When the murmur disappears: as PAH develops and pulmonary arterial pressure approaches aortic pressure, the pressure gradient decreases → murmur shortens to systolic only → eventually disappears when Eisenmenger physiology establishes (PVR = SVR). A disappearing PDA murmur in a patient with CHD may signal Eisenmenger development — a dangerous late sign.

## Management

### Premature neonatal PDA

- Indomethacin IV: COX-1 inhibitor → ↓PGE2 → ductal constriction. Success rate ~70–80% in premature neonates. Side effects: renal impairment (reduces renal prostaglandin-mediated perfusion), GI: NEC risk, platelet dysfunction.
- Ibuprofen IV: similar efficacy to indomethacin, potentially fewer renal side effects — alternative pharmacological option.
- Acetaminophen (paracetamol) IV: emerging evidence as an alternative for ductal closure in premature neonates with contraindications to indomethacin/ibuprofen (NEC, renal failure).
- Surgical ligation: if pharmacological closure fails and PDA remains haemodynamically significant — video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) ligation in many centres.

### Term infant and childhood PDA

Indomethacin is ineffective in term infants (ductal muscle is mature and responds poorly to PGE2 manipulation after a few days). Transcatheter coil or device occlusion is the treatment of choice — Amplatzer ductal occluder or coil deployment via femoral artery catheter. Success rate >98%, extremely low complication rate. Surgical ligation reserved for very large ducts not amenable to device closure or premature neonates requiring surgery for other reasons.

### Adults with PDA

Small, silent (no murmur — too small for turbulence) PDAs may be found incidentally on echo. Even small PDAs carry endocarditis risk (endarteritis at the ductal pulmonary end) — closure recommended for all PDAs that can be safely accessed. Large PDAs in adults who have escaped earlier diagnosis may present with Eisenmenger physiology (see Chapter 12).

Exam tip: The differential diagnosis of a continuous murmur: PDA: left infraclavicular, envelops S2, bounding pulses
Coronary AV fistula: continuous murmur over the heart, may be anywhere — Doppler echo shows abnormal coronary vessel
Ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm: sudden-onset continuous murmur (aortic sinus communicates with RA or RV), acute haemodynamic deterioration, usually in a young adult
Venous hum: benign childhood murmur, disappears with lying down or turning the head — not pathological
Mammary souffle: pregnancy/lactation — bilateral, systolic + diastolic, breast vessels
Key distinguishing test: disappears when the patient lies flat or the neck is compressed (venous hum) vs persists regardless of position (PDA, fistula).

Checkpoint: A 28-week premature neonate on ventilator support has worsening respiratory requirements at day 4. Echocardiogram confirms a large PDA (2.8 mm) with left-to-right flow, LV/LA dilation, LA:Ao ratio 1.8:1. Renal function: creatinine 120 µmol/L (elevated for age). Platelet count: 48,000/µL. What pharmacological option is preferred and why?
This premature neonate has a haemodynamically significant PDA (large size, left-to-right flow with LA:Ao ratio ≥1.4:1 confirming volume overload) requiring pharmacological closure. The two conventional options — indomethacin and ibuprofen — are problematic here: (1) Indomethacin: contraindicated in active renal impairment (creatinine 120 µmol/L elevated, and indomethacin reduces renal prostaglandin-mediated perfusion → risk of worsening AKI); also causes platelet dysfunction (already thrombocytopenic at 48,000/µL → bleeding risk). (2) Ibuprofen: similar renal and platelet concerns. The preferred option in this case: intravenous paracetamol (acetaminophen) 15 mg/kg q6h for 3–7 days. The mechanism is different from indomethacin/ibuprofen — paracetamol inhibits prostaglandin synthesis via peroxidase inhibition rather than COX inhibition, with minimal effects on renal prostaglandins or platelet function. Multiple RCTs and meta-analyses show comparable ductal closure rates to indomethacin/ibuprofen with a more favourable safety profile in neonates with renal impairment and thrombocytopenia. If pharmacological closure fails: surgical ligation consultation, weighing the extreme prematurity risks of surgery against the haemodynamic impact of the persistent PDA.
sections.title: Study text

sections.body:
AVSD — also called AV canal defect — is the definitive lesion of endocardial cushion failure. It combines an atrial and ventricular defect with a common AV valve, creating haemodynamic chaos at both levels. Its strong association with Down syndrome makes it the most important CHD to diagnose early in Indonesian clinical practice.

## Anatomy and spectrum

Partial AVSD (partial AV canal): Primum ASD only (no VSD component). Two separate but abnormal AV valve orifices. The mitral valve has a cleft anterior leaflet → typically causes mitral regurgitation. ECG: left axis deviation + RBBB (the hallmark). Management: primum ASD closure + cleft mitral valve repair at surgery.

Complete AVSD (complete AV canal): Primum ASD + inlet VSD + a single common AV valve with five leaflets (superior and inferior bridging leaflets + left and right mural leaflets + right anterosuperior leaflet). Massive left-to-right shunting at both levels. Common in Down syndrome. Rapid progression to PAH. Requires surgical repair within 3–6 months of life.

## The common AV valve — Rastelli classification

For complete AVSD, the superior bridging leaflet attachment determines the Rastelli type — relevant for surgical planning:

- Type A (most common, ~70%): superior bridging leaflet is divided and attached to the ventricular septum by chordae. Most amenable to surgical repair.
- Type B: superior bridging leaflet extends to the RV with anomalous papillary muscle attachments. Uncommon.
- Type C: superior bridging leaflet is a free-floating "tongue" with no septal attachment — most challenging anatomically. Associated with asplenia (right isomerism).

## Haemodynamics

In complete AVSD: shunting occurs at both atrial and ventricular levels. The common AV valve may also be regurgitant, adding volume overload to both ventricles. The net effect: massive biventricular volume overload + pulmonary overcirculation. In Down syndrome, the pulmonary vasculature may be intrinsically more reactive → PAH develops faster (by 6–12 months) than in non-Down syndrome AVSD. This is the primary reason repair must occur early.

## The pathognomonic ECG of AVSD

The ECG of AVSD (both partial and complete) is so distinctive that it can strongly suggest the diagnosis before echo:

- Left axis deviation (LAD): the superior and leftward direction of initial ventricular depolarisation from the abnormal conduction through the inlet septum. The axis is typically −30° to −90° (extreme LAD).
- RBBB pattern: usually incomplete RBBB (rSR' in V1) from RV volume overload or conduction tissue anomaly
- Prolonged PR interval: the displaced AV node (inferiorly displaced in AVSD) lengthens conduction time

The combination LAD + RBBB + long PR in any patient is AVSD until proven otherwise.

## Surgical repair

Complete AVSD repair: one-stage repair at 3–6 months using the single-patch or two-patch technique. Goals: (1) close the VSD component with a pericardial or Dacron patch, (2) close the ASD component, (3) divide and reconstruct the common AV valve into a competent left AV valve and right AV valve. The cleft in the left AV valve is closed primarily (suture approximation of the cleft edges). Post-repair: residual left AV valve regurgitation is the most common long-term problem — present in 10–20% and may require re-operation. Conduction disturbances (heart block) are an important surgical risk given the proximity of the repair to the AV node and bundle of His.

Indonesian context: AVSD and Down syndrome in Indonesia: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) is the most common chromosomal abnormality in Indonesia, with approximately 1 in 700–1,000 live births. The combination of increasing maternal age and limited access to prenatal diagnosis (amniocentesis and chromosomal analysis are not universally available or accessed) means many Down syndrome babies are born without prenatal awareness. The cardiac manifestation — complete AVSD in ~40% — is often the presenting diagnosis. The critical issue: many Indonesian children with Down syndrome + AVSD are referred too late for repair. The ideal surgical window is 3–6 months. By 12–18 months, PVR may be elevated beyond the safe closure threshold. The pattern of late referral is driven by: delayed diagnosis at primary care level, parental acceptance time after Down syndrome diagnosis, and long waiting lists at the limited number of paediatric cardiac surgery centres. Any infant with Down syndrome and clinical signs of heart failure (poor feeding, tachypnoea, failure to thrive, hepatomegaly) must be referred urgently for echo and surgical evaluation — do not wait for growth or weight gain before acting.

Checkpoint: A 14-month-old girl with Down syndrome is referred with failure to thrive and dyspnoea. Echo shows: complete AVSD (Rastelli type A), estimated PASP 65 mmHg, Qp:Qs 1.4:1 (previously estimated Qp:Qs 2.8:1 at 4 months when initially diagnosed — parents refused surgery). SpO₂ 92% at rest. What has happened, and is surgical repair still possible?
This is a delayed presentation of complete AVSD with advanced pulmonary arterial hypertension. The critical change: Qp:Qs has fallen from 2.8:1 to 1.4:1 over 10 months while PASP has risen to 65 mmHg — classic progression toward Eisenmenger physiology. The falling Qp:Qs does not mean the lesion has improved; it means the rising PVR is now opposing the left-to-right shunt and reducing the shunt fraction. SpO₂ 92% at rest confirms early right-to-left component. The question of operability requires: (1) Cardiac catheterisation with oxygen reactivity testing: measure PVR in room air, then with 100% O₂ (and NO if available). If PVR falls significantly with O₂/NO (reactive PAH) and falls to <6–8 Wood units → repair may still be feasible with acceptable risk (higher than ideal timing, but not impossible). If PVR is fixed (>8 Wood units, no reactivity) → inoperable (Eisenmenger equivalent). (2) In Down syndrome patients, the pulmonary vasculature tends to be more reactive than in non-DS patients at equivalent PVR levels — so cautious optimism is warranted pending catheterisation data. This case illustrates the cost of the 10-month delay: a child who was easily repairable at 4 months (Qp:Qs 2.8:1, presumably normal PVR at that time) may now be at or near the limit of operability. Outcome with surgical repair at this stage carries substantially higher risk. The lesson for clinical practice: early cardiac surgery referral for complete AVSD in Down syndrome is urgent — defer only for genuine medical instability, not parental hesitation or waiting list delays.

sections.body:
Pulmonary stenosis is almost always congenital, almost always isolated, and almost always curable with a single balloon valvuloplasty. But the spectrum of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction — from valvular PS to infundibular, supravalvular, and branch pulmonary artery stenoses — requires careful anatomical localisation before intervention.

## Anatomy of RVOT obstruction

Obstruction can occur at multiple levels within the right ventricular outflow tract:

- Valvular PS: most common (~80% of isolated PS). Fusion of pulmonary valve leaflets → domed, fish-mouth morphology during systole. Leaflets are usually mobile (as opposed to calcific — which is rare in the young). Preceded by a pulmonary ejection click (the domed leaflet snapping upward at the onset of systole — unique to valvular PS and absent in subvalvular or supravalvular obstruction).
- Subvalvular (infundibular) PS: muscular hypertrophy of the RVOT ("infundibular stenosis"). Can be primary (rare) or secondary (develops in response to valvular PS or VSD-related RVOT remodelling). In TOF, the infundibular obstruction is the primary RVOT component.
- Supravalvular PS: narrowing of the main pulmonary artery trunk above the valve. Associated with Williams syndrome, Noonan syndrome, congenital rubella syndrome.
- Branch pulmonary artery stenosis: stenosis of the right or left PA branch. Can be isolated, part of a syndrome (Williams, Alagille), or post-surgical (after Blalock-Taussig shunt or unifocalisation operations). Bilateral branch PA stenosis is a sign of Rubella syndrome ("rubella pulmonary stenosis").

## Grading of pulmonary stenosis

| Severity | Peak Doppler gradient | Management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mild PS | <36 mmHg (peak velocity <3 m/s) | No intervention. Annual surveillance echo. No activity restriction. |
| Moderate PS | 36–64 mmHg | Asymptomatic: close surveillance. Symptomatic or with RV dysfunction: balloon valvuloplasty. |
| Severe PS | ≥64 mmHg | Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty (BPV) regardless of symptoms (prevent RV dysfunction). |

## Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty (BPV)

BPV is the gold standard treatment for valvular PS. A balloon catheter is advanced from the femoral vein, across the tricuspid valve, into the RVOT, and positioned across the pulmonary valve. Balloon inflation splits the fused commissures → reduces the gradient dramatically. Outcomes:

- Immediate gradient reduction from ~70–80 mmHg to <20 mmHg in most patients
- Success rate >95% for typical dome-shaped valvular PS
- Complication rate <1%: transient bradycardia or arrhythmia during balloon inflation, rare right heart perforation, rare severe PR
- Long-term results excellent — restenosis is uncommon (<10% over 10 years)
- Mild PR is expected post-BPV (deliberate commissure splitting) — well tolerated long-term unless severe

Dysplastic pulmonary valve: a thickened, myxomatous, immobile valve with no commissural fusion (as seen in Noonan syndrome). Does NOT respond to BPV (there are no commissures to split). Requires surgical valvotomy or valvuloplasty. Suspect dysplastic valve when BPV fails or is expected to fail in Noonan syndrome patients.

## Noonan syndrome and pulmonary stenosis

Noonan syndrome (PTPN11 mutation in ~50%) is associated with PS in 50–70% of cases. The PS is often due to a dysplastic valve — hence the lower BPV success rate (vs typical dome-shaped PS). Noonan syndrome features: short stature, webbed neck, pectus excavatum or carinatum, widely spaced nipples, ptosis, low-set ears, hypertelorism. Often described as "male Turner syndrome" — important distinction: Turner syndrome has 45,X karyotype and affects only females; Noonan syndrome is autosomal dominant affecting both sexes. HCM occurs in ~20% of Noonan syndrome — important to assess the LV simultaneously when evaluating PS in this context.

## Critical pulmonary stenosis in the neonate

Severe PS at birth — where the RV is dependent on the PDA to supply some pulmonary blood flow — is a "duct-dependent" lesion. Neonates present with severe cyanosis when the ductus closes. Management: urgent IV prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) to maintain ductal patency → urgent BPV (the RV is often hypertensive and the valve nearly atretic). Even after BPV, the hypoplastic RV may take months to grow into adequate function. Differentiate from pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum (PA-IVS) — discussed in the single ventricle chapter.

Checkpoint: A 14-year-old girl with Noonan syndrome is found to have a peak pulmonary valve gradient of 78 mmHg on echo. The pulmonary valve appears thick and immobile with no visible commissures. She is asymptomatic but has mild RV hypertrophy. Her cardiologist plans balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty. What is the expected outcome, and is there an alternative?
The expected outcome of BPV for a dysplastic pulmonary valve (thick, immobile, no commissures — as in Noonan syndrome) is suboptimal. BPV works by splitting commissures — in a dysplastic valve with no commissures to split, the balloon simply compresses the myxomatous tissue temporarily, achieving minimal sustained gradient reduction. BPV success rates for dysplastic PS in Noonan syndrome are approximately 30–50% (vs >95% for typical dome-shaped PS). It is reasonable to attempt BPV first given its lower risk profile: if gradient drops to <36 mmHg → acceptable result, monitor. If gradient remains ≥36–40 mmHg post-BPV → proceed to surgical pulmonary valvotomy. Surgical pulmonary valvotomy (or valvuloplasty): open surgical relief of RVOT obstruction under cardiopulmonary bypass — allows direct inspection, excision of obstructing muscle bundles, pericardial widening of the RVOT, and repair of the dysplastic valve. In Noonan syndrome with dysplastic PS failing BPV, this is the definitive treatment. The RV hypertrophy will gradually regress after gradient relief — typically taking 1–2 years to normalise. Also: ensure she has been assessed for HCM (present in 20% of Noonan syndrome) — echo of LV wall thickness and outflow tract is mandatory before any cardiac procedure.

sections.body:
Congenital left heart obstructions range from the bicuspid aortic valve — the most common congenital heart defect in adults — to the neonatal emergency of critical coarctation and hypoplastic aortic arch. Understanding each level of obstruction (subvalvular, valvular, supravalvular, and arch) determines the diagnosis and the intervention.

## Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) — the most common CHD in adults

BAV affects 1–2% of the general population — approximately 1 in 50 people. Two aortic valve leaflets instead of three, usually from fusion of the right and left coronary cusps (most common, ~70%), or right and non-coronary cusps. The abnormal valve geometry creates turbulent flow → accelerated leaflet calcification → aortic stenosis developing 10–20 years earlier than tricuspid calcific AS. BAV is also associated with aortopathy (medial degeneration independent of haemodynamic factors) — 30–50% of BAV patients have an enlarged aortic root or ascending aorta (same surveillance and surgical thresholds as Marfan-associated aortopathy: surgery at ≥55 mm, or ≥50 mm with additional risk factors).

## Congenital subvalvular AS (subaortic stenosis)

Fibromuscular ridge or membrane in the LVOT, typically 5–10 mm below the aortic valve. Creates a fixed obstruction in the LVOT independent of the valve leaflets themselves. The turbulent jet from the subaortic obstruction strikes the aortic valve leaflets → secondary valve damage and AR (in 50–60% of patients over time). Key points:

- No ejection click (unlike valvular AS — the click requires mobile, dome-shaped leaflets snapping open)
- AR develops and progresses even in mild cases — unlike valvular AS, subaortic membrane causes progressive AR regardless of gradient severity
- Surgical excision recommended at relatively lower gradients than valvular AS — to prevent AR progression. Most guidelines: operate if gradient ≥30–40 mmHg or AR developing
- Recurrence after surgical excision: ~10–20% — membranous forms more likely to recur than tunnel-type

## Supravalvular AS

Narrowing of the ascending aorta above the sinus of Valsalva. Three morphological types: hourglass (most common), diffuse hypoplasia, and discrete membrane. Associated with Williams syndrome (elastin gene deletion — the elastic tissue in the aortic wall is abnormal → chronic fibrotic narrowing). Features of Williams syndrome: elfin facies, intellectual disability, hypercalcaemia, friendly/loquacious personality, good musical memory. Coronary arteries are at high risk in supravalvular AS — the coronary ostia are in the high-pressure zone below the obstruction → coronary overdistension and accelerated atherosclerosis.

## Coarctation of the aorta

Discrete narrowing of the aorta at or just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery (at the ductal insertion site). Mechanism: constriction of ductal smooth muscle tissue that extends into the aortic wall — hence the coarctation is located at the ductal/juxtaductal position. Pathophysiology:

- Hypertension proximal to the coarctation (head, arms) — persistent, often severe, driving LVH
- Hypotension distal to the coarctation (legs) — reduced lower limb pulses, cool legs, claudication in severe cases
- Collateral circulation development: intercostal arteries enlarge to bypass the obstruction → rib notching on CXR (ribs 3–8 — inferior margins eroded; not present in neonates, develops after 5 years)
- Figure-3 sign on CXR: the aortic knuckle → indentation at the coarctation → post-stenotic dilation → three bumps forming a "3" shape on the left mediastinal border

### Clinical diagnosis — the arm-leg blood pressure gradient

The hallmark clinical sign: systolic BP in the right arm significantly higher than in the legs (or left arm if left subclavian is involved). A gradient >20 mmHg between right arm and leg suggests significant coarctation. Femoral pulse is typically weak and delayed (radio-femoral delay). In severe coarctation, the femoral pulse may be absent. Any young hypertensive patient — especially without a family history of hypertension — should have leg BPs measured to exclude coarctation.

### Neonatal presentation — duct-dependent critical coarctation

Severe neonatal coarctation: the fetus compensates with ductal flow supplying the lower body. When the ductus closes at birth → sudden loss of lower body perfusion → profound shock, acidosis, circulatory collapse. This is a life-threatening emergency within the first 2 weeks of life. Treatment: IV prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) to re-open the ductus → stabilise → urgent surgical repair (end-to-end anastomosis or subclavian flap aortoplasty).

### Repair options for coarctation

| Approach | Indication | Key considerations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Surgical resection and end-to-end anastomosis | Native coarctation in neonates and infants; discrete coarctation in older children | Gold standard for neonates. Allows concomitant arch repair if arch is hypoplastic. Risk: paradoxical hypertension post-repair (sympathetic surge), spinal cord ischaemia during cross-clamp. |
| Balloon angioplasty | Native coarctation in older children as primary treatment; recurrent (re-coarctation) after surgical repair | Risk of aortic dissection (~1% for native). Higher recurrence than surgery for primary native coarctation. |
| Stent implantation | Adolescents and adults with discrete native or recurrent coarctation | Covered stents (e.g. CP stent, Andrastent) can be expanded later as the patient grows. Preferred over surgery in adults. Risk: stent fracture, aortic wall injury. |

Exam tip: Turner syndrome and coarctation — the mandatory cardiac checklist: Turner syndrome (45,X) is present in approximately 1 in 2,500 female live births. Cardiovascular anomalies occur in 25–50%: Bicuspid aortic valve: ~50% — with all the associated AS and aortopathy risks
Coarctation of the aorta: ~30% — classically infantile (tubular hypoplastic arch)
Hypoplastic left heart variants: rare
Aortic dilation and dissection: significantly elevated lifetime risk — dissection has been reported at aortic root sizes smaller than in Marfan syndrome. Aortic index (aortic root area / BSA) >10 cm²/m² → high risk for dissection
Every Turner syndrome diagnosis requires echo assessment. Pregnancy in Turner syndrome with a bicuspid AV or dilated aorta carries an extremely high dissection risk — carefully assessed by a specialist centre before conception.

Checkpoint: A 22-year-old man is referred for investigation of hypertension (BP right arm 172/95 mmHg) discovered on a pre-employment medical. He has no symptoms. Examination: radio-femoral delay, right arm-left leg BP gradient 48 mmHg. Echo shows BAV with mild AS, normal LV function, and a Doppler gradient of 35 mmHg across the descending aorta. CXR: rib notching ribs 4–6 bilaterally. What is the diagnosis, what further imaging is needed, and what is the management plan?
Coarctation of the aorta with bicuspid aortic valve — the classic association (BAV occurs in 50–80% of coarctation patients). The arm-leg gradient of 48 mmHg, radio-femoral delay, Doppler gradient of 35 mmHg across the descending aorta, and rib notching (from intercostal collaterals developed over years) all confirm significant coarctation. Further imaging: CT aortogram or MR aortography — mandatory before any intervention. Goals: define the exact anatomy (discrete vs long-segment), measure the minimum lumen diameter, assess arch anatomy (hypoplastic arch vs discrete juxtaductal), evaluate collateral vessels, assess the entire aorta including the aortic root and ascending aorta (BAV-associated aortopathy evaluation). Management: (1) Antihypertensive therapy immediately: start beta-blocker (reduces LV afterload and aortic wall stress) while awaiting catheterisation. (2) Transcatheter stent implantation: the treatment of choice for this age and anatomy — discrete native coarctation in an adolescent/adult. A covered stent (e.g. CP stent or Andrastent XL) is implanted across the coarctation under fluoroscopic guidance, eliminating the gradient. Target: post-stent gradient <10 mmHg. Surgery is an alternative if anatomy is not stent-suitable (long-segment, complex arch). (3) BAV surveillance: mild AS now, but will require long-term echo follow-up (every 2–3 years) for AS and AR progression, and aorta monitoring (CT/MR every 3–5 years). (4) Warn about paradoxical hypertension post-coarctation repair — may require antihypertensive drugs long-term even after gradient elimination; persistent hypertension is common in adults repaired late.

sections.body:
Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic CHD — and the prototype for understanding right ventricular outflow tract obstruction with ventricular mixing. Its anatomy flows logically from a single embryological event, its acute management involves a counterintuitive knee-chest position, and its repaired adults constitute the largest cohort of congenital heart disease patients seen by adult cardiologists worldwide.

## The single embryological defect that explains all four components

TOF results from a single developmental error: anterior and superior malalignment of the conal (outlet) septum relative to the muscular ventricular septum. This one displacement produces all four structural features simultaneously:

1. Ventricular septal defect (outlet/perimembranous): the malaligned conal septum fails to meet the muscular septum → VSD at the outlet level, typically large and non-restrictive
2. Overriding aorta: the aortic valve, which sits on the conal septum, "overrides" to the right across the VSD — receiving blood from both ventricles
3. Right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (RVOTO): the anteriorly displaced conal septum narrows the RVOT (infundibular stenosis); the pulmonary valve is also commonly stenotic or hypoplastic; pulmonary artery branches may be small
4. Right ventricular hypertrophy: secondary to the RVOTO and systemic-level RV pressure through the non-restrictive VSD

Mental model: Think of TOF as building a house where the dividing wall was placed too far to the right. The wall (conal septum) doesn't reach the foundation (muscular septum) → gap (VSD). The main gate (aorta) sits over the gap instead of being fully on the left side → overriding aorta. The right corridor (RVOT) is cramped by the misplaced wall → obstruction. The right room (RV) has to work harder against the cramped corridor → hypertrophy. One misplaced wall, four consequences — this is the elegance of TOF anatomy.

## Haemodynamics — the RVOTO determines the phenotype

The degree of RVOTO determines the direction of shunting through the VSD:

- Severe RVOTO: RV pressure > LV pressure → right-to-left shunt through the VSD → deoxygenated blood enters the overriding aorta → cyanosis. This is the classic "blue" TOF.
- Mild RVOTO ("pink TOF" or acyanotic TOF): RVOTO insufficient to raise RV pressure above LV → net left-to-right shunt → no cyanosis. These infants may present like a VSD with pulmonary overcirculation. They become cyanotic as the infundibular obstruction progresses (infundibular muscle hypertrophies over time in response to the obstruction — a vicious cycle).

## Hypercyanotic spells ("tet spells")

Hypercyanotic spells are acute, potentially fatal episodes of severe cyanosis from dynamic RVOTO. They typically occur in infants aged 2–4 months in the morning after waking, during crying, feeding, or defecation. The mechanism:

1. Trigger (crying, agitation, fever, exertion) → ↓ SVR (vasodilation from catecholamines) or ↑ RV infundibular spasm
2. Reduced SVR → increased right-to-left shunt through VSD
3. Simultaneous infundibular muscle spasm (dynamic RVOTO worsens acutely) → further reduction in pulmonary blood flow
4. Profound cyanosis → hypoxia → acidosis → further ↑ heart rate → more infundibular spasm (a vicious, self-amplifying cycle)
5. If uncorrected: loss of consciousness, seizures, cerebrovascular accident, death

### Immediate management of tet spell

Alert: Tet spell emergency management — remember the mechanism: reduce dynamic RVOTO + increase SVR:
1. Knee-chest position (or squatting in older children): flexing the knees compresses the femoral vessels → ↑ SVR → reduces right-to-left shunt. This is why children with TOF spontaneously squat — they are self-treating.
2. 100% oxygen: reduces hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (though limited benefit once profound right-to-left shunt is established)
3. IV/IM morphine 0.1–0.2 mg/kg: reduces RV infundibular spasm (central opioid effect + sedation reduces sympathetic drive)
4. IV propranolol 0.1 mg/kg: reduces heart rate and infundibular spasm (β1 blockade of the infundibular muscle)
5. IV phenylephrine (pure α-agonist) or IV noradrenaline: increases SVR → reduces right-to-left shunt
6. IV sodium bicarbonate: correct metabolic acidosis (acidosis worsens infundibular spasm)
7. Urgent surgical or catheter repair: after stabilisation — tet spells indicate severe RVOTO requiring urgent repair

## Surgical repair of TOF

Complete repair is performed under cardiopulmonary bypass, typically at 3–6 months (earlier if severe cyanosis or recurrent tet spells). Components of repair:

1. VSD patch closure: Dacron or pericardial patch closing the outlet VSD. Careful preservation of the conduction system (AV node and bundle of His run along the posterior-inferior VSD rim)
2. RVOT reconstruction: relief of infundibular obstruction (muscle bundle resection), pulmonary valve repair or replacement, transannular patch (TAP) if the pulmonary annulus is too small — TAP sacrifices pulmonary valve competence → inevitable pulmonary regurgitation

The transannular patch dilemma: Using a TAP effectively eliminates the pulmonary valve → free pulmonary regurgitation (PR) from the outset. This is necessary when the PA annulus is severely hypoplastic, but it sets up a lifetime of progressive RV volume overload from chronic PR. The outcome: most TAP patients require pulmonary valve replacement (PVR) in adolescence or adulthood when RV dilation reaches the intervention threshold (RVEDI ≥160 mL/m² or RV EF falling below 47%).

## Long-term issues in repaired TOF

- Right bundle branch block (RBBB): nearly universal after repair — from right ventriculotomy or VSD patch placement near the RBBB. A wide QRS (>180 ms) is an independent predictor of sustained VT and sudden cardiac death
- Pulmonary regurgitation (PR): if TAP was used — chronic RV volume overload → progressive RV dilation → arrhythmia → RV failure → indication for PVR
- Residual RVOTO: branch PA stenosis, residual infundibular obstruction — requires surveillance and sometimes catheter dilation
- Ventricular tachycardia and sudden cardiac death: macro-re-entry VT around the RV incision scar. Risk factors: wide QRS >180 ms, severe RV dilation, residual RVOTO, systolic dysfunction. ICD implantation for high-risk patients.
- Aortic root dilation: the overriding aorta often dilates progressively — surveillance needed

Exam tip: The three most tested facts about repaired TOF in ACHD examinations: QRS duration >180 ms post-repair = high risk for sustained VT and sudden death. This is the single most important prognostic ECG parameter in repaired TOF. Monitor QRS width at every annual visit.
Pulmonary valve replacement (PVR) threshold: RVEDI ≥160 mL/m² (CMR is gold standard for RV volumes — not echo) OR RV EF <47% OR any of: sustained VT, severe TR, RVOTO with RV pressure ≥two-thirds systemic. Transcatheter PVR (Melody, Sapien XT) is preferred over surgical PVR for failed conduit or bioprosthesis.
The CXR of unrepaired TOF: "coeur en sabot" (boot-shaped heart) — elevated cardiac apex (from RVH), concave main PA segment (hypoplastic PA), narrow waist. Right aortic arch in 25%.

Checkpoint: A 28-year-old man had TOF repair with transannular patch at age 4 months. He is now NYHA II with exertional dyspnoea. CMR: RVEDI 188 mL/m² (severely dilated), RVEF 42% (reduced), severe free PR on Doppler. ECG: RBBB, QRS 172 ms. No VT on 48h Holter. What is indicated and what specific risk does his QRS duration imply?
Pulmonary valve replacement (PVR) is clearly indicated. He meets multiple Class I criteria simultaneously: RVEDI 188 mL/m² (≥160 mL/m²), RVEF 42% (<47%), symptomatic (NYHA II), severe PR. These are all independent and cumulative indications. Transcatheter PVR (if he has a conduit or previous bioprosthesis in the pulmonary position) vs surgical PVR — assess the anatomy of his RVOT (CT or fluoroscopy). If no existing conduit/bioprosthesis, surgical PVR required. QRS duration 172 ms — approaching but not yet exceeding the 180 ms threshold. This implies he is at intermediate-high risk for sustained VT. The 180 ms threshold does not mean "safe below, dangerous above" — it is a risk gradient. At 172 ms, his VT risk is already elevated. Additionally, PVR may reduce QRS duration by reducing RV volume (removing the RV dilation that contributes to conduction delay) — some patients see QRS shortening after PVR. Monitor QRS duration post-PVR. If QRS widens beyond 180 ms post-PVR or if sustained VT documented → ICD discussion with electrophysiology. The absence of VT on a 48h Holter is reassuring but not definitive — programmed ventricular stimulation (invasive EP study) should be considered at the time of PVR for a comprehensive arrhythmia risk assessment. This patient needs combined surgical/EP team input: PVR ± concomitant VT substrate ablation ± ICD implantation depending on EP study findings.

sections.body:
The first five minutes of any cardiovascular emergency determine whether the next five hours are a recovery or a resuscitation. A structured, repeatable approach — regardless of the specific diagnosis — prevents the most dangerous error in emergency medicine: treating an impression rather than a patient.

Case: The Unresponsive Patient in the Emergency Department
A 67-year-old man is brought in by ambulance, unresponsive. His wife says he collapsed suddenly at home 20 minutes ago. He has known hypertension and DM. On arrival: GCS 8, BP 78/50 mmHg, HR 42 bpm irregular, RR 28 breaths/min, SpO₂ 84% on room air, cold clammy peripheries, skin mottled from knees downward. Two large-bore IV cannulas are placed. ECG is being attached.
Before the ECG prints — what do you do first, and what is your immediate diagnostic framework?

## The ABCDE primary survey — adapted for cardiovascular emergencies

The ABCDE approach (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure) structures the initial assessment of any critically ill patient. In cardiovascular emergencies, the priority shifts heavily to C — but A and B must always be secured first:

Algorithm: Cardiovascular Emergency — Primary Survey
A. Airway: Is it patent? If GCS ≤8 or inadequate airway reflexes → immediate airway protection (jaw thrust, oropharyngeal airway, intubation). A dead airway kills before any cardiac cause.
B. Breathing: SpO₂, RR, accessory muscle use, air entry. SpO₂ <94% → supplement O₂ (target 94–98%; 88–92% if COPD risk). Wheeze or absent breath sounds → exclude tension pneumothorax. Crepitations → pulmonary oedema.
C. Circulation: HR, rhythm, BP, pulse character, capillary refill, JVP, skin temperature/colour. Identify the haemodynamic state: Is this patient in shock? If no pulse → immediate CPR. If pulse present but BP critically low → initiate vasopressors while determining cause.
D. Disability: GCS, pupils, glucose (always check — hypoglycaemia mimics cardiovascular collapse). Blood glucose <3.5 mmol/L → IV dextrose immediately.
E. Exposure + investigations: 12-lead ECG, CXR, urgent bloods (FBC, U&E, Mg²⁺, lactate, troponin, BNP, ABG, coagulation), bedside echo if available.

## Shock — definition and classification

Shock is a state of acute circulatory failure with inadequate cellular oxygen delivery, leading to cellular dysfunction and — if untreated — organ failure and death. The hallmark: signs of organ hypoperfusion (altered consciousness, oliguria, cold extremities, elevated lactate) despite the specific haemodynamic mechanism.

| Type | Mechanism | Clinical clues | Haemodynamic signature | Initial treatment direction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cardiogenic | Pump failure → ↓ CO | Pulmonary oedema, S3, elevated JVP, cold peripheries, poor pulse volume | ↓CO, ↑SVR (compensatory vasoconstriction), ↑PCWP, ↓SvO₂ | Inotropes (dobutamine), vasopressors if BP critical, mechanical support |
| Distributive | ↓ SVR → relative hypovolaemia (sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic) | Warm flushed peripheries, wide pulse pressure, bounding pulse (sepsis early), anaphylaxis history | ↑CO (or normal), ↓SVR, low PCWP, ↑SvO₂ (maldistribution) | Fluid resuscitation + vasopressors (noradrenaline) |
| Hypovolaemic | ↓ Preload from volume loss | Bleeding history, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure | ↓CO, ↑SVR, ↓CVP/PCWP, ↓SvO₂ | Fluid resuscitation, stop the bleeding, transfuse |
| Obstructive | Mechanical obstruction to flow (tamponade, massive PE, tension pneumothorax) | Elevated JVP without pulmonary oedema (tamponade, PE, tension PTX); muffled heart sounds; tracheal deviation | ↓CO, ↑SVR, ↑CVP, low PCWP (except tamponade) | Relieve the obstruction: drain tamponade, thrombolyse/embolectomy for PE, decompress PTX |

## Bedside tools to determine shock type rapidly

- JVP assessment: elevated JVP → cardiogenic, obstructive (tamponade, PE, tension PTX), or distributive (only if fluid-overloaded). Flat JVP → hypovolaemic or early distributive.
- Lung auscultation and SpO₂: pulmonary crepitations + SpO₂ ↓ → cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (high PCWP). Clear lungs with low SpO₂ → obstructive (PE, tamponade) or distributive.
- Peripheral temperature: cold clammy → cardiogenic or hypovolaemic (↑SVR). Warm flushed → distributive (↓SVR).
- Bedside echo (POCUS — point-of-care ultrasound): the single most useful rapid assessment tool in undifferentiated shock. Five views: subcostal (pericardial effusion/tamponade, RV size), parasternal long axis (LV function), IVC (volume status — <2.1 cm and collapsible = hypovolaemic), lung (B-lines = pulmonary oedema; absent lung sliding = pneumothorax).

## Vasopressors vs inotropes — the critical distinction

Vasopressors — increase vascular resistance: Used when BP is critically low due to ↓ SVR. Mechanically increase afterload to raise MAP. Examples: noradrenaline (α1 > β1 — first choice for distributive shock), vasopressin (V1 receptor — add-on in refractory shock), phenylephrine (pure α1 — raises BP but may reduce CO if LV is impaired). Risk: in cardiogenic shock, adding vasopressors without inotropy → ↑ afterload on a failing heart → worsens CO.

Inotropes — increase cardiac contractility: Used when CO is inadequate from pump failure. Examples: dobutamine (β1 > β2 — inotropy + mild vasodilation, first-line for cardiogenic shock without extreme hypotension), milrinone (PDE3 inhibitor — inotropy + pulmonary vasodilation, useful in RV failure), adrenaline (β1 + β2 + α1 at high dose — powerful but increases myocardial O₂ demand and arrhythmia risk). Risk: inotropes increase myocardial O₂ demand and can worsen ischaemia in the context of acute MI.

## Returning to the case

The patient is in shock — BP 78/50, HR 42, SpO₂ 84%, cold mottled peripheries. The primary survey: airway is maintainable (GCS 8, not 3 — bag-mask ventilation + airway adjuncts). Breathing: supplement O₂ immediately, target SpO₂ ≥94%. Circulation: HR 42 irregular with very low BP — symptomatic bradycardia with haemodynamic compromise. The ECG (about to print) will determine whether this is complete heart block, severe sinus bradycardia, or something else. While the ECG is printing:

- IV atropine 0.5 mg bolus (may repeat to 3 mg total) — treat the bradycardia empirically
- Prepare transcutaneous pacing (apply pads while IV access is secured)
- Blood glucose: check immediately — this is a "D" emergency too
- Bedside echo: immediately check for pericardial effusion, RV dilation (PE?), wall motion abnormality (inferior MI + AV block is the classic story)

sections.body:
Acute aortic dissection kills faster than almost any other cardiovascular condition — Type A dissection has a mortality of 1–2% per hour without surgery. Its mimicry of ACS, PE, and stroke makes it the most dangerous missed diagnosis in the emergency department. One clinical question can save a life: does this chest pain have a tearing or ripping quality and does it radiate to the back?

Case: The Hypertensive Man with Unequal Blood Pressures
A 58-year-old man with known hypertension (often poorly controlled) presents with sudden onset severe chest pain radiating to his back and neck, described as "tearing." Onset was 45 minutes ago. BP right arm 182/104 mmHg, BP left arm 138/90 mmHg (asymmetry of 44 mmHg systolic). HR 112 bpm. He is pale and diaphoretic. ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ST changes. CXR: widened mediastinum (superior mediastinum 8 cm width). Troponin sent but not yet resulted. He is not allergic to contrast. GCS 15.
The clinical picture strongly suggests acute aortic dissection. What is the immediate management while CT is being arranged, and what is the single most important drug-sequencing error to avoid?

## Acute aortic syndrome spectrum

- Type A dissection: involves the ascending aorta (regardless of where the intimal tear starts). Surgical emergency — immediate surgery is required. Mortality without surgery: 1–2% per hour, reaching 50% at 48h. Complications: aortic regurgitation (Type A dissection shears the aortic root), coronary ostium involvement → inferior STEMI (RCA is posterior → Type A can occlude it), pericardial effusion → tamponade, stroke (carotid involvement), spinal cord ischaemia.
- Type B dissection: confined to the descending aorta beyond the left subclavian. Medical management (BP and HR control) is standard unless "complicated" (end-organ ischaemia, uncontrollable pain, rupture). Endovascular repair (TEVAR) for complicated Type B.
- Intramural haematoma (IMH): haemorrhage within the aortic wall without a visible intimal tear on CT. Classified as Type A or B by location. Similar management principles to dissection.
- Penetrating aortic ulcer (PAU): an atherosclerotic plaque ulcerates through the intima into the media. Localised. Can progress to IMH or rupture. Typically in elderly hypertensives with severe aortic atherosclerosis.

## Clinical features of aortic dissection — the diagnostic approach

| Feature | Sensitivity for dissection | Clinical note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tearing/ripping pain | ~70% | The classic "worst of life" sudden-onset tearing sensation, often described as a "knife going through" the chest to the back. |
| Interarm BP differential >20 mmHg | ~38% | Dissection flap occludes one subclavian → lower BP in that arm. Absent on one side if subclavian involved. |
| Widened mediastinum on CXR | ~62% | Not diagnostic alone — also seen in obesity, tortuous aorta. Sensitivity low; specificity poor. Do NOT exclude dissection on normal CXR. |
| Aortic regurgitation murmur | ~20% | Early diastolic murmur from aortic root involvement in Type A. Pulsus paradoxus if tamponade. |
| Neurological deficits | ~15% | Stroke (carotid involvement), spinal cord ischaemia (paraplegia from intercostal artery involvement), Horner syndrome. |
| D-dimer (<500 µg/L) | High NPV (>97%) | A D-dimer <500 µg/L in a low-probability patient effectively rules out dissection. Positive D-dimer non-specific. |

Warning: NEVER give thrombolytics or anticoagulants for suspected STEMI before excluding aortic dissection. Type A dissection can occlude the right coronary artery → inferior ST elevation on ECG. If this is mistaken for STEMI and the patient receives thrombolytics → haemorrhagic dissection of the aortic wall → rapid death. The key clinical features that should trigger aortic dissection consideration before any thrombolysis: tearing/ripping character of the pain; radiation to the back or interscapular region; interarm BP asymmetry; widened mediastinum on CXR; new aortic regurgitation murmur; history of Marfan syndrome or known aortic aneurysm. When in doubt: CT aorta before thrombolysis.

## Immediate medical management — the β-blocker first rule

Algorithm: Acute Aortic Dissection — Immediate Medical Management
1. IV esmolol (or IV labetalol) FIRST to reduce HR to 50–60 bpm. Esmolol: 500 mcg/kg bolus over 1 min, then 50–300 mcg/kg/min infusion. Labetalol: 20 mg IV bolus, repeat to control HR. Rationale: reducing dP/dt (the force of each heartbeat on the aortic wall) is the most critical immediate goal — it limits propagation of the dissection flap.
2. IV vasodilator to target SBP <120 mmHg — ONLY after beta-blocker is established. IV nicardipine infusion 5→15 mg/h, or IV sodium nitroprusside 0.3→5 mcg/kg/min. Never start vasodilator without beta-blocker first — vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia → increases dP/dt → propagates the dissection.
3. IV morphine 4–6 mg → reduces pain-mediated sympathetic activation → helps HR and BP control; reduces dP/dt indirectly.
4. Urgent CT aortogram (without and with contrast, ECG-gated for aortic root imaging): confirms diagnosis, classifies Type A vs B, identifies extent, complications (pericardial effusion, involvement of branch vessels). This is the diagnostic gold standard. Arrange immediately after initial medical stabilisation — do not delay CT for blood results.
5. Type A confirmed → immediate cardiac surgery referral: call the on-call cardiac surgeon immediately. Every minute from CT confirmation to OR decision matters. Type B without complications → ICU admission, continue medical therapy (BP/HR control), serial CT at 24h and 1 week.

sections.body:
Massive PE kills through acute RV failure, not through hypoxaemia. The clot load in the pulmonary arteries suddenly doubles RV afterload — the thin-walled RV is not built for pressure and fails acutely. Recognising the haemodynamic signature of RV failure, and deciding whether to lyse or anticoagulate, is the emergency decision that determines survival.

Case: The Post-Surgical Patient Who Suddenly Collapsed
A 48-year-old woman, day 4 post-hysterectomy for uterine fibroids, suddenly develops severe dyspnoea, chest pain, and almost collapses while mobilising. HR 128 bpm, BP 86/58 mmHg, SpO₂ 83% on room air. RR 32 breaths/min. She has had no DVT prophylaxis (the surgeon's oversight). ECG: sinus tachycardia, new S1Q3T3 pattern, right bundle branch block (new). Bedside echo: RV dilation with D-sign (flattening of the interventricular septum indicating RV pressure overloading the LV) and McConnell's sign (RV free wall akinesis with preserved apical RV motion).
Massive PE with haemodynamic instability. She is post-surgical (4 days). What is the reperfusion decision and what modality do you choose?

## PE severity classification

| Classification | Definition | Management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Massive (high-risk) | Acute PE + sustained hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg for ≥15 min) OR cardiac arrest OR haemodynamic compromise requiring vasopressors | Systemic thrombolysis if no absolute contraindication. Catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy if thrombolysis contraindicated. |
| Submassive (intermediate-high risk) | Normotensive but with RV dysfunction on echo + positive troponin and/or BNP | Anticoagulate with heparin; consider thrombolysis if haemodynamic deterioration. PEITHO trial: thrombolysis prevents haemodynamic collapse but increases bleeding, especially ICH. |
| Low-risk | Normotensive, no RV dysfunction, normal biomarkers (PESI score low) | Anticoagulate (DOAC preferred). Early discharge possible in very-low-risk patients (Hestia criteria). |

## Immediate management of massive PE

Drug: IV Unfractionated Heparin — give immediately at diagnosis (even before CT if clinical diagnosis is confident)
Bolus: 80 U/kg IV (max 8,000–10,000 U).
Infusion: 18 U/kg/h (max 1,200–1,500 U/h). Titrate to aPTT 60–100 seconds (2–3× control).
Heparin prevents clot extension; allows the patient's endogenous fibrinolytic system to begin working; is reversible with protamine if thrombolysis or surgery is subsequently needed.

Drug: Vasopressors for haemodynamic support — bridge to reperfusion
Noradrenaline 0.1–0.5 mcg/kg/min: maintains MAP ≥65 mmHg; α-agonist increases systemic resistance → maintains coronary perfusion of the failing RV. First-choice vasopressor for massive PE.
Vasopressin 0.03 U/min: add-on in refractory shock; reduces PVR relatively (vs noradrenaline) — beneficial for RV failure.
Caution with fluids: do NOT give large fluid boluses for massive PE. The RV is already volume-overloaded and critically pressure-overloaded. 250–500 mL cautious bolus only if CVP <5 mmHg. Excess fluids worsen RV dilation, push the septum leftward, and reduce LV output further (ventricular interdependence).

## Reperfusion in massive PE — three modalities

### 1. Systemic thrombolysis (alteplase)

Drug: Alteplase (tPA) for massive PE — standard systemic thrombolysis
100 mg IV over 2 hours (most common regimen).
OR accelerated regimen if cardiac arrest: 50 mg IV bolus over 2 minutes → continue CPR → reassess for ROSC.
After tPA: restart heparin infusion once aPTT <80 seconds (2–4h after tPA completion).
Hold other anticoagulants during tPA infusion.

The patient is 4 days post-surgery — this is a relative contraindication to systemic thrombolysis (major surgery within 10 days is a relative contraindication). In massive PE with haemodynamic collapse, the risk of thrombolysis may still be outweighed by the risk of death from obstructive shock — a shared decision with senior clinical input is required urgently.

### 2. Catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) / catheter embolectomy

A catheter is placed directly in the pulmonary artery via femoral vein → tPA infused locally (lower dose: 20–24 mg over 12–24h rather than 100 mg systemically) → higher thrombus concentration with less systemic exposure → potentially lower bleeding risk. Also: mechanical aspiration embolectomy (FlowTriever, Inari device) allows mechanical clot removal without thrombolytics — ideal for patients with bleeding contraindications.

### 3. Surgical pulmonary embolectomy

Open surgical extraction of the clot under cardiopulmonary bypass. Reserved for: thrombolytics contraindicated AND catheter techniques not available or failed. High surgical mortality in the haemodynamically unstable patient but can be lifesaving. Requires immediate cardiac surgical team.

## Returning to the case — the surgical contraindication decision

This patient is post-surgical day 4 — major absolute contraindication to systemic thrombolysis does not apply (major surgery <3 weeks is relative, not absolute, contraindication). Given haemodynamic collapse (BP 86/58 mmHg) and bedside echo confirmation of massive PE: the risk of death from untreated massive PE (~30–60% without reperfusion) exceeds the risk of post-surgical bleeding from thrombolysis. Decision: systemic alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours is indicated, with surgical team on notice for post-thrombolysis re-evaluation. If the surgical team objects to systemic thrombolysis at day 4 post-hysterectomy → catheter-directed mechanical embolectomy (if available) is the alternative — clot removal without systemic thrombolytic exposure.

sections.body:
Cardiac tamponade is haemodynamic obstructive shock from pericardial compression. The pressure builds slowly or rapidly depending on the cause — what matters clinically is whether compensatory mechanisms have been overwhelmed. The treatment is a needle in the pericardial space, and it works within seconds of correct placement.

Case: The Breathless Man After a Procedure
A 65-year-old man with atrial fibrillation underwent electrophysiology study and catheter ablation 3 hours ago. He is now increasingly short of breath, pale, and anxious. BP 88/72 mmHg (was 128/82 one hour ago), HR 118 bpm regular. JVP is 6 cm above the sternal angle (elevated). Heart sounds are muffled. Paradoxical pulse: BP drops 18 mmHg on inspiration. Bedside echo: large circumferential pericardial effusion with right atrial and RV diastolic collapse. IVC dilated with no respiratory variation.
Cardiac tamponade following ablation. Describe Beck's triad, the mechanism of pulsus paradoxus, and the pericardiocentesis technique.

## Beck's triad — the classic clinical presentation

Beck's triad (1935) describes the three signs of cardiac tamponade:

1. Hypotension: the pericardial fluid compresses the heart → reduced ventricular filling → reduced CO → ↓ BP
2. Elevated JVP: compressed ventricles cannot accept venous return → venous pressure backs up → elevated JVP
3. Muffled heart sounds: the fluid surrounding the heart dampens the transmission of valve closure sounds to the chest wall

Beck's triad is highly specific but has low sensitivity — not all three signs are present simultaneously, especially in subacute tamponade. More practically, the combination of hypotension + elevated JVP without pulmonary oedema (the JVP is elevated from obstructive physiology, not from LV failure) should always trigger tamponade consideration.

## Pulsus paradoxus — mechanism

Pulsus paradoxus: an exaggerated fall in systolic BP (>10 mmHg) during normal inspiration. Normal physiology: inspiration → chest expands → pulmonary venous return to LA falls slightly → SBP falls mildly (≤10 mmHg). In tamponade: the pericardial pressure is elevated. Inspiration → RV fills (venous return to RV increases with negative thoracic pressure) → RV expands → but the total pericardial space is fixed → RV expansion comes at the expense of LV filling (interventricular septum pushed left) → LV CO drops dramatically → SBP falls >10 mmHg. This ventricular interdependence — exaggerated by the fixed pericardial volume — produces the paradox. Measured: deflate sphygmomanometer slowly, note the systolic when sounds are heard only during expiration vs when heard in both phases — the difference is the pulsus paradoxus magnitude.

## Echo findings in tamponade

- Pericardial effusion: the fundamental finding — usually large (though the rate of accumulation matters more than absolute size)
- Right atrial diastolic collapse: first and most sensitive sign. The RA, being the lowest-pressure chamber, is the first to collapse under pericardial pressure during diastole. Seen in the subcostal view.
- RV diastolic collapse: more specific than RA collapse. The RV free wall invaginates inward during diastole.
- Dilated IVC with absent respiratory collapse: IVC >21 mm with <50% inspiratory collapse → elevated right-sided pressures from the tamponade
- Respiratory variation in transvalvular flows: >25% variation in mitral inflow velocity with respiration (Doppler echo equivalent of pulsus paradoxus)

## Pericardiocentesis — emergency drainage technique

Algorithm: Emergency Pericardiocentesis — Subxiphoid Approach
1. Position: patient semi-recumbent at 45° (gravity pools fluid inferiorly, making it more accessible). 12-lead ECG running. Defibrillator pads attached. IV access secured.
2. Echo guidance: ideally ultrasound-guided (dramatically reduces complications). Identify the largest fluid window — subxiphoid approach is most common (needle angled 30–45° above horizontal, aimed at left shoulder). Left parasternal approach if subxiphoid window is poor.
3. Anaesthesia: local anaesthesia (lidocaine 1–2% infiltrated at needle entry site). Conscious sedation (midazolam 1–2 mg IV) if time permits.
4. Needle insertion: 18G or spinal needle with 10 mL syringe (heparin-primed or with small amount of saline). Advance slowly with constant aspiration. Entry into the pericardium: sudden aspiration of fluid. If blood aspirates → check if it clots (blood = RV perforation; pericardial blood generally does NOT clot — it has been defibrinated by the beating heart). ECG needle-tip lead: ST elevation or new ventricular ectopy → touching the myocardium → withdraw slightly.
5. Drainage: aspirate as much fluid as possible. For ongoing drainage: Seldinger technique → exchange needle for guidewire → dilate → 6–8Fr pigtail catheter → drainage bag. Even 50–100 mL drained dramatically improves haemodynamics. Leave drain in situ for 24–48h and send fluid for analysis (cytology, cultures, protein, LDH, glucose).
6. Immediate haemodynamic response: BP should begin to rise within seconds to minutes of successful drainage. If no improvement → inadequate drainage OR surgical tamponade (clotted blood from perforation → cannot be aspirated with a needle → requires surgical drainage).

Exam tip: The fluid "bridge" before pericardiocentesis — a cautious strategy: In haemodynamically compromised tamponade awaiting pericardiocentesis, a small fluid bolus (250–500 mL IV normal saline) can temporarily increase RV filling pressure above the pericardial pressure → transiently restores CO. This buys minutes until drainage is performed. However: in very high pericardial pressures (e.g. massive effusion, surgical tamponade), fluids have limited or no benefit and waste time. Do not delay definitive drainage for IV fluids. Also: inotropes and vasopressors have limited efficacy in tamponade — they cannot overcome the mechanical constraint. The only definitive treatment is removing the fluid.
