Acute valvular emergencies — unlike chronic valvular disease — strike a heart that has not adapted. The unprepared LV in acute severe MR or AR decompensates rapidly, because the chambers have not had time to dilate and accommodate the new volume load. Time to surgery is measured in hours, not days.

Case: The Day-3 MI Patient Who Suddenly Deteriorated
A 64-year-old man is on day 3 of an inferior STEMI treated with primary PCI to the RCA. He was progressing well until this morning when he develops sudden severe dyspnoea and haemodynamic deterioration. BP drops from 118/72 to 78/52 mmHg in 20 minutes. New loud pansystolic murmur grade 4/6 at the apex radiating to the left axilla. SpO₂ 84% on high-flow O₂. Bilateral crepitations to apices. Bedside echo: hyperdynamic LV (EF 65%), severe MR with a flail posterior mitral leaflet, small non-dilated LV and LA (LA 3.8 cm).
Papillary muscle rupture — acute severe MR. Why does the LV look hyperdynamic and small when this patient is in severe cardiogenic shock? And what is the bridge to surgery?

## The paradox of acute severe MR — why the EF is misleadingly high

In acute severe MR from papillary muscle rupture, the LV suddenly ejects a large regurgitant fraction back into the low-resistance LA with each systole. The LA has not had time to dilate (it is acutely volume-overloaded by a previously normal LA), and it transmits this pressure directly to the pulmonary veins → acute pulmonary oedema. The LV appears hyperdynamic (EF 65–70%) because it is ejecting vigorously into both the aorta and the low-resistance LA — total SV is enormous, but forward SV (into the aorta) may be barely adequate. This is the same MR-EF inflation phenomenon covered in the VHD guide, but acutely and dramatically amplified.

The small, non-dilated LV and LA are the hallmarks of acute MR — contrasting sharply with chronic MR where both chambers are markedly dilated. In acute MR: the heart has not had time to remodel. The small, stiff LV cannot accommodate extra volume with a compliant diastole → LVEDP rises dramatically → pulmonary oedema.

## Causes of acute valvular emergencies

| Emergency | Cause | Echo clue | Bridge to surgery |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Acute severe MR — papillary muscle rupture | Posteromedial PM rupture (inferior MI, single blood supply) more common than anterolateral PM. Day 3–7 post-MI. | Flail mitral leaflet, hyperdynamic small LV, acute pulmonary oedema, very high regurgitant jet velocity | IABP (reduces LV afterload → less regurgitant fraction) + dobutamine + emergency surgery |
| Acute severe MR — chordal rupture (myxomatous) | Spontaneous chordal rupture in MVP/myxomatous degeneration. Can be sudden. | Flail posterior leaflet (most common), hyperdynamic LV | Vasodilators (nitroprusside) + urgent surgical repair |
| Acute severe AR — aortic dissection | Type A dissection strips the aortic root → AR. Acute, unprepared LV. | Large pericardial effusion, AR jet, dilated aortic root, new aortic root widening | Emergency surgery — simultaneous aortic repair + AVR if possible |
| Acute severe AR — infective endocarditis | Vegetations + leaflet perforation or destruction | Vegetation, leaflet perforation, early MV closure (high LVEDP closes MV before atrial kick — pathognomonic of severe acute AR) | IV antibiotics + emergency surgery if cardiogenic shock |
| Acute severe AS — rapid deterioration | Superimposed infection, dehydration, tachycardia in known severe AS → acute HF | Heavily calcified AV, high gradient, reduced EF | IV fluids cautiously, vasopressors if hypotensive, emergency TAVR or SAVR |
| Prosthetic valve thrombosis | Subtherapeutic INR → thrombus on mechanical valve → obstruction | Restricted prosthetic disc motion, elevated gradient, thrombus mass | IV thrombolytics (if obstructive + unstable) or emergency surgery |

## Management of acute severe MR from papillary muscle rupture

Algorithm: Acute Severe MR from PM Rupture — Emergency Management
1. Airway and oxygenation: CPAP/BiPAP immediately for pulmonary oedema. Intubate if SpO₂ not correcting.
2. IABP insertion immediately: the most critical bridge manoeuvre. IABP reduces LV afterload during diastole → proportionally more blood goes forward vs backward into the LA → reduces regurgitant fraction → reduces pulmonary oedema + improves forward CO. Insert via femoral artery, balloon positioned in the descending aorta, inflates in diastole.
3. IV sodium nitroprusside 0.5–5 mcg/kg/min: reduces SVR → reduces the pressure gradient driving regurgitation into the LA → more forward flow. Requires arterial line (BP monitoring). Contraindicated if SBP <90 mmHg — use noradrenaline to stabilise BP first, then add nitroprusside carefully. In cardiogenic shock with PM rupture: noradrenaline + dobutamine + IABP first.
4. Emergency cardiac surgery: the only definitive treatment. Mitral valve repair is preferred (if feasible — papillary muscle re-attachment + annuloplasty) or replacement (mechanical or bioprosthesis). The operative mortality for emergency surgery in PM rupture is 15–30% — but medical management alone has near-100% in-hospital mortality. Call the cardiac surgeon immediately on recognition of the diagnosis.

sections.body:
Acute RV failure is fundamentally different from LV failure — the thin-walled RV fails not from ischaemia alone but from acute pressure overload. Its management follows a logic diametrically opposite to LV failure in many ways: fluid that helps the RV fills the lungs; vasodilators that help the LV drop the coronary perfusion pressure of the failing RV. Understanding RV physiology is the key to managing it correctly.

Case: The Inferior STEMI with Hypotension and Elevated JVP — but Dry Lungs
A 57-year-old man arrives by ambulance with 2 hours of inferior chest pain. BP 80/58 mmHg, HR 48 bpm (3rd degree AV block on monitor). JVP elevated at 8 cm. Lungs: clear bilaterally — no crepitations. SpO₂ 92% on 4L O₂. Right-sided leads: V4R shows ST elevation 2 mm. Right ventricle on bedside echo: severely dilated, hypokinetic, with McConnell's sign pattern and leftward septal shift. LV is underfilled with a small cavity.
This is the RV infarction pattern of inferior STEMI. The management is the opposite of LV cardiogenic shock in one critical way — what is it?

## RV infarction — the pathophysiology

The RCA supplies the inferior LV, the posterior interventricular branch, and — in 90% of right-dominant circulations — the SA node and AV node AND the right ventricle (RV free wall). A proximal RCA occlusion can produce: inferior LV STEMI + AV block + RV infarction — all simultaneously. RV ischaemia causes acute RV failure:

- The RV dilates and hypokineses → inadequate RV output → LA receives less pulmonary venous flow → LV is underfilled (preload-dependent) → CO falls despite a normal or hyperkinetic LV (the LV hasn't been infarcted)
- The dilated RV pushes the interventricular septum leftward (D-sign) → further impairs LV filling by compressing the LV cavity
- JVP is elevated (RV failure backs up into the RA) but lungs are clear (LV output is reduced because it is preload-starved, not because LV is failing from volume overload — there is no pulmonary oedema)

Key concept: In RV infarction, the clinical pattern is hypotension + elevated JVP + CLEAR LUNGS — and the correct treatment is IV fluids, not diuretics
This is the critical reversal of the LV cardiogenic shock logic. In LV cardiogenic shock: elevated JVP + wet lungs → the patient is fluid-overloaded → diuretics. In RV infarction shock: elevated JVP + dry lungs → the LV is preload-starved because the RV is not pumping effectively through the pulmonary circulation. The treatment: IV normal saline 500 mL bolus rapidly, titrating carefully, to increase RV preload and push more blood through the pulmonary vasculature to fill the LV. Do NOT give diuretics — you will worsen the preload starvation and precipitate cardiac arrest. The target is to cautiously increase LV filling (CVP 10–15 mmHg) without overloading a non-compliant RV. Fluid responsiveness should be reassessed after each 500 mL bolus — if JVP rises dramatically and septal shift worsens → stop fluids and reassess with echo.

## RV infarction management protocol

Algorithm: Acute RV Infarction — Emergency Management
1. Reperfusion URGENTLY: primary PCI to the RCA is the most critical intervention. Restoring RCA flow reverses RV ischaemia and is the only definitive treatment. If in a non-PCI centre → thrombolytics immediately.
2. IV fluids: 500 mL normal saline bolus over 10–15 min. Repeat, assessing response (BP, JVP, lung auscultation). Target: MAP ≥65 mmHg. Stop if pulmonary oedema develops or JVP becomes massively elevated. Total fluid challenge can reach 1–2 L in volume-responsive RVI patients.
3. Temporary pacing for AV block: AV block in RVI is common (AV nodal ischaemia from RCA occlusion). As described in Chapter 7: transcutaneous then transvenous pacing. AV sequential pacing is preferred over VVI pacing in RVI — the atrial kick (which is preserved) contributes up to 40% of RV filling in an already-compromised RV. Loss of AV synchrony worsens haemodynamics significantly.
4. Avoid vasodilators and diuretics: GTN, morphine, diuretics — all reduce RV preload → worsen the output failure. In RVI: these drugs can cause sudden haemodynamic collapse. Even low-dose GTN for pain management must be given with extreme caution (small doses only if BP allows).
5. Vasopressors if fluid-refractory: noradrenaline 0.05–0.3 mcg/kg/min to maintain coronary perfusion pressure of the failing RV (RV coronary perfusion occurs in both systole and diastole, unlike the LV — but a minimum aortic pressure is still required). Dobutamine if RV contractility is the primary problem.
6. Pulmonary vasodilators for refractory RV failure: inhaled NO (20 ppm) or inhaled prostacyclin → reduce RV afterload (PVR) → improve RV output without systemic hypotension. Available in ICU settings. Sildenafil PO may be used for ongoing RV failure in stabilised patients.
sections.title: Study text

sections.body:
The cardiovascular emergency that kills is usually not the complex rare one — it is the common presentation with a misleading feature, or the correct diagnosis with the wrong drug. These patterns consolidate everything from this guide into the clinical recognition framework and the catastrophic error list.

## The 8 critical cardiovascular emergency recognition patterns

### Pattern 1 — Hypotension + elevated JVP + clear lungs

Three-way differential: RV infarction (inferior STEMI → V4R ST elevation), massive PE (D-sign on echo, McConnell's sign), cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad — add muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus). All are obstructive or RV-failure physiology. In all three: the LV is preload-starved, the RV is failing or compressed, and the lungs are clear (no pulmonary oedema) because the LV is underloaded. Management diverges: RVI → IV fluids + urgent reperfusion; PE → systemic thrombolysis; tamponade → pericardiocentesis. The differentiator: bedside echo within 5 minutes.

### Pattern 2 — Hypotension + elevated JVP + wet lungs

LV cardiogenic shock. The LV is failing → PCWP rises → pulmonary oedema → wet lungs. The JVP is elevated from fluid back-pressure or right heart involvement. Management: vasopressors (noradrenaline) + inotropes (dobutamine) + treat the cause (reperfusion for AMI). Do NOT give IV fluids (will worsen pulmonary oedema).

### Pattern 3 — Tearing chest pain + back pain + interarm BP difference

Aortic dissection until proven otherwise. Immediate IV beta-blocker (esmolol/labetalol) to reduce HR and dP/dt. Then CT aorta. Never thrombolyse until dissection is excluded. Never give vasodilator without beta-blocker first.

### Pattern 4 — New pansystolic murmur + haemodynamic deterioration on day 3–7 post-MI

Two surgical emergencies: (1) papillary muscle rupture → acute severe MR (echo: flail leaflet, hyperdynamic small LV); (2) ventricular septal rupture → new VSD (echo: LV-RV communication at the interventricular septum, step-up in O₂ saturation from RA to PA on right heart catheterisation). Both require emergency surgery. Bridge: IABP for PM rupture; IABP + vasopressors for VSR. These are often presented in MCQs as "inferior vs anterior MI complications" — inferoposterior MI → PM rupture (single blood supply); anterior MI → apical VSR (thin apical septum).

### Pattern 5 — Witnessed VF arrest + no ROSC after 3 shocks + 10 minutes of CPR

Consider: reversible causes (4H/4T) — is there a tension pneumothorax? (needle decompression). Is there a STEMI driving the VF? (immediate cath lab after ROSC). Is there a metabolic cause? (hyperkalaemia → calcium gluconate IV; hypothermia → active rewarming). Also: IV amiodarone 300 mg was given at shock 3 — if refractory VF after 3 more minutes → consider double sequential defibrillation (two defibrillators, simultaneous or nearly simultaneous dual shock). Extracorporeal CPR (ECMO during CPR) in selected patients with potentially reversible cause and young age.

### Pattern 6 — BP 240/140 + thunderclap headache + photophobia

Subarachnoid haemorrhage must be excluded first (CT head without contrast → if negative + high suspicion → LP for xanthochromia). If SAH confirmed: BP management is nuanced — reduce gradually (target SBP 140–160 mmHg) to prevent rebleeding but maintain cerebral perfusion. If hypertensive encephalopathy (papilloedema, confusion, no SAH on CT): labetalol or nicardipine IV, reduce MAP by 20–25% in first hour.

### Pattern 7 — Cyanosis + hypotension + AF + known mitral stenosis

AF with rapid ventricular rate in mitral stenosis → shortened diastolic filling time across the stenotic valve → acute pulmonary oedema → haemodynamic collapse. Immediate: rate control (IV metoprolol/diltiazem/digoxin) is the priority — the haemodynamics will improve dramatically when heart rate falls to 60–80 bpm. Cardioversion if medical rate control fails or patient is extremely unstable. Diuretics secondarily. This is not standard HF management — it is rate control as the primary haemodynamic intervention.

### Pattern 8 — New LBBB + chest pain in a 60-year-old

Until proven otherwise: STEMI equivalent. The new LBBB in the context of typical ischaemic symptoms should be managed as STEMI with the same urgency (primary PCI within 120 min if achievable, otherwise thrombolytics). The Sgarbossa criteria can help identify superimposed STEMI on LBBB (concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm, discordant ST elevation ≥5 mm, or concordant ST depression ≥1 mm in V1–V3) — but in haemodynamically unstable new LBBB + chest pain, treat as STEMI without waiting for Sgarbossa analysis.

## The 12 most dangerous errors in cardiovascular emergency management

| # | Dangerous action | What it causes / why it kills |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | IV verapamil for wide complex tachycardia (assuming SVT with aberrancy) | If WCT is VT (it almost always is in structural heart disease) → vasodilation + negative inotropy → haemodynamic collapse. Rule: WCT = VT until proven otherwise. If unstable → shock. If stable → amiodarone, not verapamil. |
| 2 | Thrombolysis for inferior STEMI with ST elevation — before checking for dissection | Type A dissection can occlude the RCA → inferior ST elevation. Thrombolytics in dissection → fatal haemorrhage into the aortic wall. Always assess: tearing pain? Back radiation? Interarm BP asymmetry? Widened mediastinum? |
| 3 | Aggressive fluid resuscitation in LV cardiogenic shock | The LV is failing from pump dysfunction, not volume deficit. IV fluids raise PCWP → worsen pulmonary oedema → worsening respiratory failure → arrest. Give vasopressors, not litre bags of saline. |
| 4 | Diuretics for hypotension + JVP elevation + clear lungs (RV infarction) | RVI shock is from LV preload starvation, not fluid overload. Diuretics worsen LV underfilling → CO falls further → cardiac arrest. Give IV fluids (500 mL boluses) instead. |
| 5 | IV GTN or morphine as the first drug in inferior STEMI with hypotension | Vasodilators reduce preload further in a heart that may already have RV infarction. Even small doses of GTN can cause sudden haemodynamic collapse in RVI. Check V4R leads before GTN in any inferior STEMI. |
| 6 | Vasodilator (nitroprusside) without beta-blocker first in aortic dissection | Vasodilator → ↓ BP → reflex tachycardia → ↑ dP/dt → propagates the dissection flap. Beta-blocker must be given first to control HR, then vasodilator added. |
| 7 | Normalising BP to 120/80 mmHg rapidly in hypertensive urgency (without ATOD) | Chronic hypertensive brains autoregulate at higher baseline MAP. Rapid normalisation → cerebral hypoperfusion → ischaemic stroke. In hypertensive urgency (no ATOD): oral therapy, gradual reduction over 24–48h. |
| 8 | Choosing adenosine for AF with WPW (irregular wide complex tachycardia) | Adenosine blocks the AV node → all AF conducted via the accessory pathway → ventricular rate 250–300 bpm → VF. In irregular WCT: never adenosine. Cardiovert (unstable) or IV procainamide (stable). |
| 9 | Continuing heparin infusion when ICH is found on CT during post-ROSC care | Post-cardiac arrest CT may reveal unsuspected ICH. Continuing anticoagulation → massive haemorrhage expansion → death. If ICH found: stop all anticoagulation, reversal agents if indicated, neurosurgical consultation. |
| 10 | Half-dose tenecteplase in a patient <75 years for weight-based dosing | Half-dose tenecteplase (TNK) is reserved for patients ≥75 years (to reduce bleeding). In patients <75 years, half-dose is subtherapeutic → inadequate fibrinolysis → failed reperfusion → ongoing myocardial death. |
| 11 | Overlooking the post-ROSC STEMI on ECG in a comatose patient | Comatose post-arrest patients with STEMI on ECG should have immediate angiography — regardless of neurological status. Waiting for awakening or GCS improvement before cath lab → ongoing myocardial ischaemia → worsened outcomes and higher mortality. |
| 12 | Fluid overload in acute massive PE with obstructive shock | The failing RV in massive PE is already volume-overloaded and pressure-overloaded. Fluid boluses further dilate the RV → more septum leftward deviation → LV compression worsens → CO falls further. Treat with vasopressors and thrombolytics, not fluids. |
sections.title: Study text

sections.body:
Emergency cardiology MCQs test time-critical decision-making, drug dosing precision, and the management of haemodynamic compromise. The same systematic approach — identify the emergency type, assess haemodynamic stability, select the correct intervention and sequence — solves every case.

## The CV emergency MCQ framework — 5 rapid questions

1. Is the patient haemodynamically stable or unstable? Unstable = shock/collapse/acute compromise → intervention is immediate regardless of diagnosis. Stable = time for diagnosis-first approaches.
2. What type of shock is this? Warm peripheral = distributive; cold clammy + wet lungs = LV cardiogenic; cold + dry lungs + elevated JVP = RV/obstructive. Management diverges completely.
3. What is the time to reversible cause treatment? Reperfusion for STEMI, drainage for tamponade, surgery for dissection, thrombolysis for PE — these are the definitive answers, not just bridges.
4. Is there a contraindication to the obvious treatment? Thrombolytics contraindications (recent surgery, ICH, dissection). Verapamil contraindication in WCT. Fluids contraindicated in LV cardiogenic shock.
5. What is the sequence? In dissection: β-blocker THEN vasodilator. In bradycardia: atropine → transcutaneous → transvenous. In VT: assess stability → shock or drug. Sequence errors kill.

## CV emergency trap library — 12 high-yield traps

| # | Scenario | Trap | Correct answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Inferior STEMI + BP 78/52 + JVP elevated + clear lungs | "Give IV furosemide 80 mg for the hypotension and elevated JVP" | RV infarction — give IV fluids 500 mL bolus, not diuretics. Check V4R leads. Furosemide will worsen haemodynamics. |
| 2 | WCT 195 bpm + known ischaemic CMP + BP 88/60 | "Give IV verapamil — could be SVT with aberrancy" | Unstable → synchronised DC cardioversion 150–200 J immediately. Never verapamil in unstable or in structural heart disease WCT. |
| 3 | Post-inferior STEMI day 3, new pansystolic murmur + step-up in O₂ saturation RA→PA | "Gives the clinical picture of papillary muscle rupture — start IABP" | The step-up in O₂ saturation (left-to-right shunt at ventricular level) = ventricular septal rupture. Different surgical approach. VSR is more common with anterior MI; PM rupture with inferior MI. Echo differentiates. |
| 4 | Cardiac arrest, non-shockable (PEA), bedside echo shows pericardial effusion | "Continue CPR and give adrenaline — PEA is managed medically" | Pericardial effusion in PEA = tamponade → pericardiocentesis during CPR. Pause compressions for <5 seconds at a rhythm check, confirm effusion, immediately drain. This is a reversible cause — treat it during the arrest. |
| 5 | Hypertensive encephalopathy, BP 250/145 mmHg — nurse gives IV sodium nitroprusside 5 mcg/kg/min immediately | "Nitroprusside reduces BP rapidly — correct" | At 5 mcg/kg/min nitroprusside immediately → too rapid BP reduction → risk of cerebral ischaemia. Start at 0.3 mcg/kg/min, titrate slowly. Also: labetalol or nicardipine is preferable first-line for encephalopathy. Nitroprusside at maximum dose requires arterial line. |
| 6 | Massive PE in a post-hip replacement patient day 5, BP 82/55 mmHg | "Systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated within 2 weeks of surgery" | Major surgery within 10 days is a RELATIVE contraindication to thrombolysis, not absolute. In massive PE with haemodynamic collapse (risk of death ~30–60%), the benefit of thrombolysis may outweigh the bleeding risk. Discuss with senior clinician — catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy are alternatives if the relative contraindication is felt to be prohibitive. |
| 7 | STEMI patient with tearing back pain + interarm BP differential 30 mmHg, GP refers for "immediate thrombolysis" | "STEMI = thrombolysis immediately" | Stop. This patient may have aortic dissection (Type A) with inferior STEMI from RCA compression by the dissection flap. Thrombolytics in dissection = death. Perform CT aorta URGENTLY before any thrombolysis decision. |
| 8 | Cardiac arrest, 15 min of CPR, coarse VF persists after 5 shocks + amiodarone 450 mg total. No ROSC. | "Nothing more to do — continue CPR and drugs" | Consider double sequential defibrillation. Consider reversible causes: is there a STEMI driving VF? Consider ECPR (ECMO during CPR) if the patient is young and arrest cause potentially reversible. Also check electrode placement, pad contact quality. |
| 9 | Post-ROSC patient, GCS 6, ECG: 2 mm ST elevation V1–V4. Intensivist says "wait until he wakes up before cath" | "Neurological assessment before any invasive procedure" | STEMI post-arrest → immediate coronary angiography regardless of neurological status. Comatose is not a contraindication to PCI. Most deaths in post-arrest STEMI are from continued ischaemia, not from the procedure. Class I recommendation. |
| 10 | Acute severe AR from Type A dissection. Bedside echo: severe AR jet, EF 35%. Cardiac surgeon says "stabilise haemodynamics first before surgery" | "IV dobutamine to improve EF first" | Acute severe AR from aortic dissection requires emergency surgery — there is no stabilisation adequate to defer it. Medical therapy (vasopressors, inotropes) cannot address the valve problem or the dissection. Every hour without surgery is another 1–2% mortality. Escalate immediately. |
| 11 | Hypertensive emergency with SBP 200 mmHg + acute ischaemic stroke (confirmed on CT, no thrombolysis given) | "Immediately reduce BP to 130/80 mmHg — target normal BP" | In acute ischaemic stroke NOT receiving thrombolysis: only treat if SBP >220 mmHg. The ischaemic penumbra depends on collateral perfusion driven by the elevated BP. Aggressive lowering → more infarction. Target SBP <220 mmHg cautiously. |
| 12 | Accelerated idioventricular rhythm (rate 70 bpm, wide complex) 45 min after thrombolytics for STEMI | "VT — give IV amiodarone immediately" | AIVR (accelerated idioventricular rhythm) at 60–100 bpm after thrombolytics is a benign reperfusion arrhythmia. No treatment required. Administering amiodarone or trying to suppress AIVR is incorrect and unnecessary. The patient is haemodynamically stable and this is a sign of successful reperfusion. |

## Final exam checklist — cardiovascular emergencies

Alert: Before every cardiovascular emergency answer:
✓ Haemodynamically unstable → electrical cardioversion (tachyarrhythmia) or pacing (bradyarrhythmia) FIRST
✓ WCT = VT until proven otherwise. Never verapamil/diltiazem in WCT.
✓ Inferior STEMI + clear lungs + elevated JVP → check V4R. RV infarction → IV fluids, NOT diuretics, NOT GTN
✓ STEMI + tearing pain + interarm asymmetry → CT aorta BEFORE thrombolytics
✓ Aortic dissection: β-blocker FIRST, then vasodilator. Never vasodilator alone.
✓ Hypertensive emergency target: MAP reduction 20–25% in first hour — NOT normalisation
✓ Ischaemic stroke without thrombolysis: treat BP only if SBP >220 mmHg
✓ Massive PE + haemodynamic collapse → systemic alteplase 100 mg/2h (check surgical contraindications)
✓ Tamponade: pericardiocentesis. Small fluid bolus as bridge only. Vasopressors have limited effect.
✓ Post-STEMI day 3 new murmur: PM rupture (inferior MI, flail leaflet on echo) vs VSR (step-up O₂ saturation RA→PA)
✓ Post-ROSC: avoid hyperoxia (FiO₂ titrated to SpO₂ 94–98%), normocapnia (PaCO₂ 35–45), temperature ≤37.7°C (TTM2)
✓ STEMI post-arrest + STEMI on ECG → immediate PCI regardless of GCS/neurological status
✓ ALS shockable (VF/pVT): shock → 2 min CPR → rhythm check (repeat). Adrenaline 1 mg + amiodarone 300 mg at cycle 3.
✓ AIVR (60–100 bpm) post-thrombolysis = benign reperfusion rhythm. No treatment needed.
✓ Thrombolytics in STEMI: half-dose TNK only if patient ≥75 years. Full weight-based dose for <75 years.
✓ RV infarction AV block: AV sequential pacing preferred — atrial kick contributes 40% of RV filling in RVI

sections.body:
Cardiogenic shock is the most lethal cardiovascular emergency — in-hospital mortality of 40–50% even in contemporary cath lab–capable hospitals. It demands simultaneous diagnostic precision and aggressive haemodynamic support, with the critical decision of when mechanical circulatory support is needed.

Case: Cold, Clammy, and Confused After a "Stomach Ache"
A 62-year-old diabetic man presents to a district hospital with 4 hours of epigastric discomfort, nausea, and vomiting. He is now confused. BP 82/58 mmHg, HR 116 bpm, RR 30 breaths/min, SpO₂ 90% on room air. He is cold, pale, and diaphoretic. Lung bases have fine crepitations bilaterally. JVP is elevated at 4 cm above the sternal angle. ECG: ST elevation 2–3 mm in leads II, III, aVF with reciprocal ST depression in aVL and V1–V3. Troponin result pending. Creatinine 178 µmol/L. The nearest catheterisation laboratory is 3 hours away.
He is in cardiogenic shock from an inferior STEMI. What are your immediate steps, and what is the decision regarding reperfusion strategy?

## Cardiogenic shock — definition and aetiology

Cardiogenic shock (CS) is defined by: (1) sustained hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg for ≥30 min, or requiring vasopressors to maintain SBP ≥90 mmHg) AND (2) signs of end-organ hypoperfusion (altered consciousness, cold clammy extremities, oliguria <30 mL/h, elevated lactate ≥2 mmol/L) AND (3) evidence of cardiac dysfunction (elevated LV filling pressures or reduced CO).

The most common causes in order of frequency:

- Acute MI with LV failure: ~80% of CS cases. Large anterior STEMI (LAD occlusion) is the classic scenario. RV infarction (inferior STEMI with RCA occlusion) causes a specific RV-dominant shock (see Chapter 14).
- Acute mechanical complications of MI: papillary muscle rupture → acute severe MR (Chapter 13); ventricular septal rupture; free wall rupture (haemopericardium → tamponade — immediate surgery).
- Acute decompensated HF: existing HFrEF with acute decompensation trigger.
- Myocarditis: particularly fulminant lymphocytic myocarditis — young patient, viral prodrome, biventricular failure.
- Severe valvular emergencies: acute severe AS, acute native valve endocarditis with valve destruction.
- Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy: usually haemodynamically well-tolerated but can cause CS in 5–10%.

## The "cold and wet" haemodynamic profile

The classic cardiogenic shock haemodynamic profile: the heart is failing → CO falls → compensatory ↑ SVR → cold, pale, clammy peripheries ("cold"). Simultaneously, backed-up LV filling pressure → pulmonary oedema → dyspnoea, crepitations, low SpO₂ ("wet"). This "cold and wet" pattern distinguishes cardiogenic from distributive shock (warm and wet or warm and dry).

## Acute management of cardiogenic shock — the simultaneous priorities

Algorithm: Cardiogenic Shock — Immediate Management Algorithm
1. Airway and breathing first: SpO₂ <90% or RR >30 → consider early non-invasive ventilation (CPAP/NIV — reduces work of breathing and improves oxygenation). If SpO₂ not improving with NIV or GCS ≤8 → intubation. Warning: intubation in cardiogenic shock → loss of sympathetic drive + vasodilation from propofol/benzodiazepines → BP can plummet further. Have vasopressor running before intubation.
2. Vasopressor if BP critically low (MAP <65 mmHg): Noradrenaline 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min IV via central line. First choice for CS with extreme hypotension — provides α-adrenergic vasoconstriction to maintain coronary perfusion pressure. Start while preparing for definitive management.
3. Inotrope for pump failure: Dobutamine 2–20 mcg/kg/min IV — β1-agonist improves contractility and reduces ventricular filling pressures. Use with noradrenaline if both low BP and low CO coexist. Monitor for tachycardia (dobutamine ↑ HR → ↑ O₂ demand) and arrhythmias.
4. Treat the underlying cause urgently: in AMI-CS → reperfusion (primary PCI or thrombolytics — Chapter 3). In tamponade → pericardiocentesis. In acute severe MR from papillary rupture → emergency surgery + IABP bridge. The vasopressor/inotrope is a bridge, not a treatment.
5. Fluid management: CS is not a fluid-deficient state. Do NOT give a large fluid bolus to a patient with "cold and wet" CS (the JVP is elevated, lungs are wet — more fluid worsens pulmonary oedema). Exception: RV-dominant CS (see Chapter 14) where RV requires adequate preload. Small cautious bolus (250 mL) only if JVP/CVP is low and lungs are clear.
6. Mechanical circulatory support (MCS) if haemodynamic targets not met with pharmacology: IABP (intra-aortic balloon pump) → reduces afterload + augments diastolic pressure. Impella CP/5.5 → directly unloads LV, provides superior haemodynamic support. VA-ECMO → for refractory CS or cardiac arrest, provides full cardiopulmonary support.

## Mechanical circulatory support — a practical comparison

| Device | Mechanism | CO support | Placement | Key indication |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| IABP | Counterpulsation — inflates in diastole (↑ coronary perfusion), deflates in systole (↓ afterload) | 0.5–1 L/min additional | Femoral artery → descending aorta | Bridge to PCI; CS awaiting definitive treatment. IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit over medical therapy alone in AMI-CS — but still widely used for stabilisation. |
| Impella CP/5.5 | Axial flow pump: draws blood from LV across the aortic valve → aorta. Directly unloads LV and increases forward CO. | 2.5–5.5 L/min | Femoral (CP) or axillary (5.5) → LV via AV | Severe CS with low CO not responding to medical therapy; high-risk PCI support; bridge to decision. DanGer-Shock (2024): Impella in AMI-CS → reduced 180-day mortality vs usual care. |
| VA-ECMO | Oxygenates and circulates blood externally — full cardiopulmonary bypass. Drains venous blood, oxygenates, returns via femoral artery. | 3–6 L/min (near-full support) | Femoral vein + femoral artery | Refractory CS, cardiac arrest, biventricular failure, bridge to transplant/LVAD. Note: VA-ECMO increases LV afterload → may worsen LV distension (add Impella or IABP to unload LV). |

## Returning to the case

This patient has inferior STEMI with cardiogenic shock. Immediate actions, all simultaneously:

1. Oxygen supplementation: 15 L/min non-rebreather mask → target SpO₂ ≥94%. Consider early CPAP (BiPAP) for pulmonary oedema component (crepitations + SpO₂ 90%).
2. Noradrenaline infusion: 0.1 mcg/kg/min, titrate to MAP ≥65 mmHg — peripheral venous line temporarily (central line to follow immediately).
3. Dobutamine 5 mcg/kg/min to support CO while perfusion pressure is being established.
4. STEMI management with shock = reperfusion is the definitive treatment: nearest cath lab is 3 hours away → thrombolysis NOW (tenecteplase weight-based IV bolus — Chapter 3 details the pharmacoinvasive strategy), then transfer for angiography within 3–24 hours. Do not delay thrombolysis for transfer in CS.
5. Avoid diuretics initially: the crepitations are from cardiogenic oedema but the kidneys are already hypoperfused (creatinine 178 µmol/L) — aggressive diuresis will worsen renal perfusion. Small dose furosemide (20–40 mg IV) after vasopressor stabilisation if SpO₂ remains low.
6. IABP: if available at the district hospital — insertion provides haemodynamic stabilisation and reduces afterload during the transfer. If not available, ensure the patient is on vasopressor/inotrope infusion throughout transfer with a nurse trained in monitoring them.

PERKI 2023 (national heart failure guideline) is the Indonesian anchor. Its section numbers were not available in the copy checked, so no section pointer is given: read the matching chapter. Full citations: topic Guideline sources, at the end of this domain.

The management of STEMI is one of the most time-critical workflows in all of medicine. Every minute from symptom onset to reperfusion represents irreplaceable myocardium. The decision between primary PCI and thrombolysis, and the execution of whichever strategy is chosen, must be flawless.

Case: The Chest Pain at the District Hospital
A 54-year-old male farmer presents to a district hospital (Puskesmas Rawat Inap) at 02:30 with severe central chest pain radiating to the left arm, onset 90 minutes ago. He is diaphoretic and distressed. BP 138/88 mmHg, HR 94 bpm, SpO₂ 96% on room air. ECG shows: ST elevation 3 mm in V1–V4, reciprocal ST depression in II, III, aVF. No prior cardiac history. The nearest catheterisation laboratory is at RSUD Provinsi, 3.5 hours away by ambulance.
The ECG confirms anterior STEMI. PCI will not be available within 120 minutes. What is the reperfusion strategy, what drug do you give, and what are the next steps after thrombolysis?

## STEMI diagnosis — time-sensitive ECG criteria

STEMI is defined by new ST elevation at the J-point in ≥2 contiguous leads:

- V1–V4 (anterior): ≥2 mm in men ≥40 years; ≥2.5 mm in men <40 years; ≥1.5 mm in women
- I, aVL (lateral): ≥1 mm
- II, III, aVF (inferior): ≥1 mm
- V7–V9 (posterior — apply leads posteriorly): ≥0.5 mm (posterior STEMI from LCx occlusion)
- New LBBB with typical ischaemic symptoms (Sgarbossa criteria if modified): treat as STEMI equivalent
- Right-sided leads V3R, V4R: ≥1 mm → right ventricular infarction (treat differently — Chapter 14)

## The reperfusion decision — primary PCI vs thrombolysis

Key concept: Primary PCI is always preferred — but only if it can be performed within 120 minutes of first medical contact. Beyond 120 minutes, thrombolysis is the standard of care.
The 120-minute threshold is the evidence-based boundary between primary PCI superiority and thrombolysis acceptability. Below 120 minutes: primary PCI achieves higher TIMI 3 flow rates (93% vs ~55% for thrombolytics), lower stroke risk, lower re-infarction, lower mortality. Beyond 120 minutes: the benefit of primary PCI over thrombolysis narrows significantly, and in many large trials the pharmaco-invasive strategy (thrombolysis → transfer for early angiography) achieves outcomes comparable to late primary PCI. The Indonesian reality: the majority of STEMI patients presenting to district hospitals and Puskesmas are beyond 120 minutes from a cath lab. Thrombolysis is the appropriate first-line reperfusion strategy for most Indonesian STEMI patients at non-PCI-capable facilities.

## Thrombolytic therapy — the pharmaco-invasive strategy

### Fibrinolytic agents and dosing

Drug: Tenecteplase (TNK-tPA) — preferred fibrinolytic
IV bolus over 5–10 seconds (weight-based — single dose, NO infusion):
<60 kg → 30 mg (6 mL)
60–69 kg → 35 mg (7 mL)
70–79 kg → 40 mg (8 mL)
80–89 kg → 45 mg (9 mL)
≥90 kg → 50 mg (10 mL) — maximum dose
Dilute in sterile water for injection (provided in kit). Flush with saline.
Half-dose tenecteplase in patients ≥75 years (major bleeding risk reduction).

Drug: Streptokinase — if tenecteplase unavailable
1.5 million units IV in 100 mL 0.9% NaCl over 60 minutes.
Lower cost, higher antigenicity (do NOT use if prior streptokinase in last 5 years or prior streptococcal infection).
Higher rate of hypotension during infusion — slow infusion if BP falls.

Drug: Alteplase (tPA) — for massive PE (Chapter 11) and STEMI
STEMI dose: 15 mg IV bolus, then 0.75 mg/kg over 30 min (max 50 mg), then 0.5 mg/kg over 60 min (max 35 mg). Total max dose 100 mg.
Also used for massive PE and ischaemic stroke (different dose — 0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg).

### Adjunctive antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy with thrombolytics

- Aspirin: 300 mg PO (or IV if unable to swallow) immediately. Then 75–100 mg OD lifelong.
- Clopidogrel: loading dose 300 mg PO (75 mg if ≥75 years). Then 75 mg OD. Continue for ≥1 year (DAPT with aspirin).
- Anticoagulation: enoxaparin SC (weight-based, age-adjusted dosing for ≥75 years — 0.75 mg/kg SC for elderly) OR UFH IV. Continue for minimum 48 hours or until angiography.

### Contraindications to thrombolysis — absolute

Alert: Absolute contraindications — never thrombolyse if any of these are present:
• Prior intracranial haemorrhage at any time
• Ischaemic stroke within 6 months
• CNS structural lesion (AVM, neoplasm, aneurysm)
• Recent major trauma/surgery/head injury within 3 weeks
• GI bleeding within 1 month
• Aortic dissection (CRITICAL — thrombolysis in dissection = fatal haemorrhage)
• Non-compressible vascular puncture in the last 24h (e.g. lumbar puncture, liver biopsy)
• Active bleeding (excluding menses)

## The pharmaco-invasive strategy — what to do after thrombolysis

After successful thrombolysis, the patient should be transferred to a PCI-capable hospital for coronary angiography ± PCI within 3–24 hours (not immediately, not >24 hours). This is the pharmaco-invasive strategy — the combination of thrombolysis for immediate reperfusion followed by systematic angiography to treat residual stenosis and prevent re-infarction.

### Signs of successful reperfusion after thrombolytics

- Chest pain relief: resolution of pain within 60–90 minutes of starting thrombolytics
- ST resolution ≥50% in the lead with maximum ST elevation at 60–90 minutes post-thrombolysis
- Reperfusion arrhythmia: accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR) — a regular wide complex rhythm at 60–100 bpm — is a benign sign of reperfusion (myocytes regaining automaticity as ischaemia resolves). Does NOT require treatment. Distinguish from VT (>100 bpm, symptoms, haemodynamic instability).
- Peak troponin earlier than expected ("washout" phenomenon — rapid enzyme rise from reperfused area)

### Failed thrombolysis — rescue PCI

If after 60–90 minutes: chest pain persists AND ST elevation has not fallen by ≥50% → thrombolysis has failed to reperfuse. Emergency rescue PCI is indicated — transfer urgently to the cath lab. Do NOT repeat thrombolytics (no evidence of benefit; increases bleeding risk). Rescue PCI achieves salvage of myocardium even after failed thrombolysis and is a Class I indication.

## Returning to the case

This patient: anterior STEMI, 90 minutes from symptom onset, 3.5 hours from PCI → thrombolysis is the correct choice. Immediate actions at the district hospital:

1. Aspirin 300 mg PO + clopidogrel 300 mg PO immediately
2. Tenecteplase: patient weighs approximately 65 kg → 35 mg IV bolus over 10 seconds
3. Enoxaparin: 1 mg/kg SC (age 54, <75 years — full dose) — first dose IV bolus 30 mg then 1 mg/kg SC
4. IV morphine 2–4 mg if pain not controlled (or fentanyl 25–50 mcg) + metoclopramide 10 mg IV
5. IV GTN (glyceryl trinitrate) 5–10 mcg/min if chest pain persists and BP allows (SBP >100 mmHg — he is 138/88 mmHg: GTN is safe)
6. Continuous cardiac monitoring and 12-lead ECG at 60 and 90 minutes post-thrombolysis to assess reperfusion
7. Arrange emergency transfer to RSUD Provinsi immediately with communication: "STEMI s/p thrombolysis, request angiography within 3–24h (pharmaco-invasive)"
8. If signs of failed reperfusion at 90 minutes: call the cath lab for urgent rescue PCI transfer

Indonesian context: STEMI management in Indonesia — the pharmaco-invasive strategy as the national standard: Indonesia's cardiovascular geography makes primary PCI inaccessible for the majority of STEMI patients presenting outside major cities. PERKI (Indonesian Heart Association) and MOH guidelines recognise the pharmaco-invasive strategy as the recommended approach for STEMI patients at non-PCI-capable facilities when PCI cannot be achieved within 120 minutes. Tenecteplase and streptokinase are available through BPJS Kesehatan formulary at hospitals with emergency capability. The national STEMI alert system (Kode Merah STEMI) is being implemented in several provinces to streamline transfer pathways. Key Indonesian challenges: (1) Door-to-needle time: should be <30 minutes at any capable facility — but ECG interpretation delays, consent processes, and drug availability issues often extend this; (2) Transfer quality: IV lines, monitoring, and vasopressors must be maintained during ambulance transfer; (3) Documentation of contraindications: a rapid, structured contraindication checklist at presentation prevents delays from over-cautiousness and prevents dangerous administration in true contraindicated patients.

NSTEMI is defined by myocardial necrosis (elevated troponin) without ST elevation — but its management is driven by risk stratification, not by a single threshold. Getting the timing of invasive strategy right — neither too fast nor too delayed — requires integrating clinical, biomarker, and ECG data into a coherent risk picture.

Case: Chest Pain Resolving in the Emergency Department
A 68-year-old woman with hypertension, DM, and prior PCI to the LAD 3 years ago presents with 2 hours of central chest tightness that partially improved during transport. Now largely pain-free. BP 154/92 mmHg, HR 82 bpm, SpO₂ 97%. ECG: dynamic ST depression 1.5–2 mm in V3–V5, T-wave inversion in V4–V6. hs-Troponin I at presentation: 180 ng/L (URL 52 ng/L — 3.5× elevated). Repeat troponin at 1 hour: 340 ng/L (significant rise = 89% increase). Creatinine 105 µmol/L. Bilateral clear lungs.
NSTEMI is confirmed by biomarker rise with dynamic ECG changes and symptoms. What is her risk score, what is the timing of invasive strategy, and what antiplatelet/anticoagulant do you prescribe?

## The hs-Troponin 0h/1h protocol

High-sensitivity troponin (hs-Tn) has transformed the diagnosis of NSTEMI — allowing a rapid rule-in/rule-out algorithm within 1 hour:

- Rule out: hs-Tn at 0h is very low (below the "rule-out" threshold — assay-specific) AND 1h delta is minimal → NSTEMI ruled out with >99% NPV. Patient can be discharged with outpatient follow-up.
- Rule in: hs-Tn at 0h is markedly elevated (>5× URL) OR 1h delta is significant (absolute rise meeting assay-specific threshold) → NSTEMI confirmed. Admit, anticoagulate, plan invasive strategy.
- Observe zone: intermediate 0h value and indeterminate delta → continue to 3h sample. This is where careful clinical assessment and risk scoring determines management.

## Risk stratification — GRACE score

The GRACE (Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events) score is the validated tool for in-hospital and 6-month mortality risk in NSTEMI. Variables: age, HR, SBP, creatinine, Killip class, cardiac arrest at admission, ST deviation, elevated cardiac biomarkers. Available as online calculators (GRACE 2.0):

- Low risk: GRACE score <109 (in-hospital mortality <1%) → early discharge may be appropriate after risk stratification
- Intermediate risk: GRACE 109–140 → early invasive strategy (within 24 hours)
- High risk: GRACE >140 (in-hospital mortality >3%) → urgent invasive strategy (within 24 hours, or earlier if haemodynamically unstable)

## Timing of invasive strategy in NSTEMI

| Timing | Indication | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Immediate (<2 hours) | GRACE >140 WITH any of: ongoing refractory ischaemia, haemodynamic instability, cardiogenic shock, life-threatening arrhythmia, acute HF | These features mean the patient is decompensating — stabilisation requires coronary anatomy knowledge and intervention. Same urgency as STEMI. |
| Early (<24 hours) | GRACE >140 without the above features; recurrent symptoms; dynamic ST or T-wave changes; elevated hs-Tn with significant rise/fall | High risk features predict large territory at jeopardy — early intervention reduces recurrent MI and revascularisation need. |
| Selective (<72 hours) | GRACE ≤140; no recurrent symptoms; stable ECG; troponin rise without significant delta or with plateau | Lower risk patients still benefit from invasive evaluation but the urgency is less. Non-invasive testing may guide selection. |
| Conservative (non-invasive) | Very low risk (GRACE <109); no recurrent symptoms; troponin within normal or minimally elevated; no dynamic ECG changes; patient preference or very high procedural risk | In well-selected low-risk patients, conservative management with stress testing is acceptable. |

## Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy in NSTEMI

### Antiplatelet

- Aspirin: 300 mg loading dose PO immediately. Then 75–100 mg OD indefinitely.
- P2Y12 inhibitor — add as soon as NSTEMI diagnosis confirmed:
  - Ticagrelor 180 mg loading, then 90 mg BD — preferred in most NSTEMI patients (PLATO trial superiority). Contraindicated: prior ICH, active bleeding, severe hepatic impairment. Side effects: dyspnoea (benign, adenosine-mediated).
  - Prasugrel 60 mg loading, then 10 mg OD — if coronary anatomy known and PCI planned. Contraindicated: prior stroke/TIA, age ≥75 (use 5 mg OD if unavoidable), weight <60 kg. Not before angiography (bleeding risk if CABG needed).
  - Clopidogrel 300–600 mg loading, then 75 mg OD — if ticagrelor/prasugrel unavailable or contraindicated. BPJS-covered first-line antiplatelet in Indonesian practice.

### Anticoagulation

Drug: Fondaparinux 2.5 mg SC OD — preferred in NSTEMI (OASIS-5 trial)
Least bleeding risk of anticoagulants in NSTEMI. Indirect Xa inhibitor. Give for duration of hospitalisation or until PCI (add UFH bolus at PCI if using fondaparinux, as it is not sufficient for catheter-related thrombosis prevention alone). Avoid if eGFR <20 mL/min.

Drug: Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC every 12h (0.75 mg/kg in ≥75 years)
Alternative. More widely available. Reduce to OD dosing if eGFR 15–30 mL/min. Avoid if eGFR <15 mL/min (use UFH instead, which is not renally cleared).

Drug: Unfractionated heparin (UFH) — if fondaparinux/enoxaparin unavailable or CKD
60 U/kg bolus IV (max 5,000 U), then 12 U/kg/h infusion (max 1,000 U/h). Titrate to aPTT 50–70 seconds (2–2.5× control). Stop 4–6h before angiography.

## Returning to the case

She has: dynamic ST depression V3–V5, rising hs-TnI (180 → 340 ng/L = 89% rise), prior PCI, DM, hypertension. GRACE score estimate: age 68 + elevated HR + elevated BP + elevated creatinine (105 normal range) + ST depression + elevated biomarkers → approximately GRACE 135–145 → high risk. Management:

1. Aspirin 300 mg PO + ticagrelor 180 mg PO immediately
2. Fondaparinux 2.5 mg SC (creatinine 105 µmol/L → eGFR ~50 mL/min — safe)
3. High-intensity statin: atorvastatin 80 mg PO now (regardless of prior statin use)
4. Beta-blocker: bisoprolol 2.5 mg OD if haemodynamically stable (HR 82, no acute HF)
5. GTN 5 mcg/min IV for recurrent chest pain (she is currently pain-free — have it ready)
6. Invasive coronary angiography within 24 hours (early strategy, GRACE >140 equivalent): arrange transfer to PCI-capable facility if not already there

Cardiac arrest survival is determined by three things: the time to the first shock, the quality of CPR in between, and the care given in the first 24 hours after return of spontaneous circulation. Every one of these is modifiable. This chapter covers the full ALS loop and the post-ROSC protocol.

Case: Collapse in the Hospital Corridor
A 58-year-old man who presented for elective angiography is walking to the ward when he collapses. A nurse finds him unresponsive. She calls for help and checks for a pulse — absent. The crash team arrives in 60 seconds. The defibrillator pads show: coarse ventricular fibrillation.
Coarse VF — a shockable rhythm in a witnessed arrest. Walk through the first 10 minutes of Advanced Life Support and what follows immediately after ROSC.

## The ALS algorithm — shockable rhythms (VF/pulseless VT)

Algorithm: ALS — Shockable Rhythm (VF / Pulseless VT)
1. Confirm unresponsive, absent breathing (or only gasping), absent carotid pulse. Immediately call resuscitation team. Start CPR: 30 compressions : 2 breaths ratio. Compression rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm, full chest recoil. Minimise interruptions (<5 seconds). Hard surface, locked elbows.
2. Attach defibrillator/AED as soon as available. If pads already on (as in this case) → assess rhythm without stopping CPR if possible. VF confirmed → prepare to shock.
3. Shock 1 (biphasic 150–200 J, or per manufacturer). Immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes — do NOT pause to check pulse after the shock. The heart needs 2 minutes to recover perfusion before checking rhythm.
4. After 2 minutes CPR: rhythm check. If still shockable → shock 2 (same energy). Resume CPR 2 minutes. Obtain IV/IO access and secure airway (intubate without interrupting CPR — use a supraglottic airway if intubation is slow).
5. After shock 3 (3rd rhythm check still VF): give Adrenaline 1 mg IV and Amiodarone 300 mg IV. Adrenaline: repeat every 3–5 min (every other 2-min cycle). Amiodarone: second dose 150 mg IV if VF persists after shock 5.
6. Continue 2-min CPR cycles with rhythm checks and defibrillation. Search for reversible causes — the 4H + 4T: Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo/Hyperkalaemia + metabolic, Hypothermia (4H); Tension PTX, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis (PE/coronary) (4T).
7. ROSC (Return of Spontaneous Circulation): organised rhythm with pulse. Do NOT celebrate — start the post-ROSC protocol immediately.

## ALS for non-shockable rhythms (PEA / asystole)

PEA (pulseless electrical activity) and asystole have a worse prognosis than VF — they rarely respond to defibrillation. The key is identifying and treating the reversible cause:

- Adrenaline 1 mg IV every 3–5 min — the only drug with any evidence in PEA/asystole. Maintain CPR cycles.
- No defibrillation in PEA/asystole (unless rhythm converts to VF).
- Actively search for the 4H + 4T: PEA is almost always caused by a reversible cause. The most common in a cardiac patient: hypovolaemia (bleeding), tension pneumothorax (after procedures), tamponade (post-cardiac surgery or procedure), massive PE, severe metabolic disturbance.
- Bedside echo during CPR (without interrupting compressions): operator holds the probe, pauses compressions for <5 seconds at rhythm check → if pericardial effusion → tamponade → immediate pericardiocentesis during resuscitation.

## CPR quality — what makes the difference

CPR quality is the most modifiable determinant of survival once a defibrillator is attached. Evidence from large registries shows that even 10% variation in CPR quality significantly alters survival:

- Rate: 100–120 compressions/min — a metronome or feedback device improves this
- Depth: 5–6 cm for adults — too shallow is ineffective, too deep causes rib fractures
- Full chest recoil: leaning on the chest prevents cardiac refilling — devastating for CO generation
- Interruptions: pre-shock pauses <5 seconds, post-shock: immediately back to compressions — no pause to check pulse
- Rescuer change: every 2 minutes — rescuer fatigue causes CPR quality to degrade rapidly; rotate with minimal pause

## Post-ROSC protocol — the golden hour after resuscitation

Post-cardiac arrest syndrome affects all organ systems. The post-ROSC protocol addresses each simultaneously:

Algorithm: Post-ROSC Protocol (First 60 Minutes)
A. Airway: If not already intubated → intubate for airway protection (comatose patients post-arrest cannot protect their airway). Target: PaO₂ 75–100 mmHg (SpO₂ 94–98%); PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg (normocapnia — hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction → worse neurological outcome).
B. Avoid hyperoxia: 100% O₂ post-ROSC causes reperfusion injury (free radical generation). Titrate FiO₂ to SpO₂ 94–98% once ROSC achieved. Do not continue 100% O₂ if SpO₂ is already at target.
C. Haemodynamic targets: MAP ≥65 mmHg (consider ≥75 mmHg if known hypertensive — higher BP target for cerebral perfusion). If MAP <65 mmHg → noradrenaline ± dobutamine. 12-lead ECG immediately post-ROSC → if STEMI or new LBBB → immediate coronary angiography regardless of neurological status.
D. Temperature management (TTM): TTM2 trial (2021): strict hypothermia 33°C vs normothermia (target ≤37.5°C) — no significant difference in outcome at 6 months. Current practice: prevent fever (>37.7°C) actively. Controlled normothermia for at least 24 hours. Treat shivering (sedation, magnesium, buspirone, meperidine). Targeted temperature management = fever avoidance in most patients.
E. Glucose control: target glucose 7.8–10 mmol/L. Avoid hypoglycaemia (devastating for the post-arrest brain). Avoid hyperglycaemia (worsens neurological injury). Insulin infusion if needed.
F. Neuroprognostication: defer neurological assessment for at least 72h post-arrest and 72h after normothermia (sedation and temperature affect neurological exam). Use multimodal approach: clinical exam (pupillary reflexes, corneal reflex, motor response), EEG, SSEP (N20 bilaterally absent = poor prognosis), CT/MRI brain, NSE. No single test is definitive — combine.

## STEMI after cardiac arrest — the immediate angiography decision

In post-arrest patients with ST elevation on the post-ROSC ECG: immediate angiography and PCI is a Class I recommendation — regardless of neurological status. Comatose post-arrest patients with STEMI can still achieve TIMI 3 flow and myocardial salvage; survival is better with revascularisation than without. Do NOT wait for neurological recovery before PCI in STEMI post-arrest.

In post-arrest patients WITHOUT ST elevation (NSTEMI or normal ECG post-arrest): COACT trial (2019) and TOMAHAWK trial (2021) showed immediate vs delayed angiography were similar in 90-day outcomes. Current approach: immediate angiography for clinical shock or haemodynamic instability; early but not emergency angiography for stable post-arrest patients without ST elevation (within 24 hours).

The acutely decompensating patient with ventricular tachycardia demands an immediate binary decision: is this patient haemodynamically stable enough for pharmacological cardioversion, or do they need immediate electrical cardioversion right now? The wrong answer to this question can be fatal.

Case: The Wide Complex Tachycardia in the CCU
A 61-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (EF 28%, ICD implanted 2 years ago) is in the CCU on day 2 post-NSTEMI. He suddenly becomes pale and diaphoretic. Monitor shows: regular broad complex tachycardia at 188 bpm with left bundle branch block morphology. BP 84/60 mmHg (was 118/76 just 10 minutes ago). He is conscious but extremely distressed and cannot speak in full sentences.
He is haemodynamically unstable. What is your immediate action, and how do you manage VT storm if it recurs?

## The haemodynamic stability decision — the most critical branch point

Key concept: Haemodynamically UNSTABLE tachycardia (any type, any mechanism) → immediate synchronised DC cardioversion. This rule has no exceptions.
Haemodynamically unstable = any of: BP <90 mmHg, altered consciousness, acute pulmonary oedema, chest pain from the tachycardia, signs of shock. In an unstable tachycardia: DO NOT try to diagnose the exact mechanism first. DO NOT trial drugs first. DO NOT wait for a specialist to arrive. Immediate synchronised cardioversion. Every second of an unstable VT is potentially the last second before the patient loses consciousness and needs an unsynchronised shock (defibrillation). The 200 joules biphasic shock takes seconds to deliver — it takes longer to draw up amiodarone. The haemodynamic state — not the rhythm diagnosis — determines the intervention.

## Immediate management of haemodynamically unstable VT

Drug: Synchronised DC Cardioversion — immediate (conscious sedation if possible)
1. Call for help + attach pads (already on if CCU patient).
2. Administer brief sedation if patient is conscious: IV midazolam 1–2 mg + IV fentanyl 25 mcg (or ketamine 0.5 mg/kg IV if BP very low — ketamine maintains sympathetic tone). Do NOT use propofol alone in haemodynamically compromised patients.
3. Select SYNCHRONISED mode (ensures shock delivers on R wave, not on T wave which could trigger VF).
4. Energy: 150–200 J biphasic for monomorphic VT. Start at 150 J; escalate to 200 J if unsuccessful.
5. Stand clear. Shock delivered.
6. Immediately reassess rhythm and haemodynamics. If sinus rhythm restored → IV amiodarone infusion to prevent recurrence. If VT persists → repeat shock at maximum energy.

## Haemodynamically stable VT — pharmacological approach

If the patient is haemodynamically stable (BP maintained, conscious, no shock signs): a pharmacological attempt to terminate VT is appropriate while preparing for cardioversion:

Drug: Amiodarone IV — first-line for sustained monomorphic VT
Loading: 150 mg IV over 10 minutes (slow bolus — faster → hypotension).
Infusion: 1 mg/min for 6 hours, then 0.5 mg/min for 18 hours.
Additional 150 mg bolus for breakthrough VT. Maximum 2.2 g in 24 hours.
Always via central line for infusions — causes peripheral phlebitis. For the initial bolus in emergency: large peripheral line + diluted in 100 mL D5W acceptable.

Drug: Procainamide IV — alternative (not available in many Indonesian centres)
10–15 mg/kg IV at 25–50 mg/min until VT terminates or hypotension/QRS widens >50%. Maintenance: 1–4 mg/min infusion. Superior to amiodarone for short-term VT termination in some studies.

Drug: Lidocaine IV — for VT in the context of acute ischaemia
Bolus: 1–1.5 mg/kg IV. Additional 0.5–0.75 mg/kg if needed (max 3 mg/kg in 1 hour).
Infusion: 1–4 mg/min.
Preferred in peri-ischaemic VT (acute MI setting) where amiodarone may not be immediately available.

## VT storm — definition and management

VT storm: ≥3 sustained VT episodes in 24 hours requiring intervention (cardioversion or ICD shocks). It is a life-threatening emergency with very high short-term mortality. This patient has had one episode — management must prevent storm:

1. IV amiodarone infusion: maintain at 1 mg/min (from loading bolus); escalate if VT recurs.
2. Deep sedation: reduces sympathetic tone (the primary trigger for VT storm). Propofol infusion in intubated patients; IV benzodiazepine in conscious patients. Reducing catecholamine drive breaks the VT storm cycle.
3. IV beta-blockade: IV esmolol 0.5 mg/kg bolus then 0.05–0.2 mg/kg/min infusion — rapid-onset, short-acting beta-blocker ideal for VT storm management. Reduces sympathoadrenal-triggered VT. Contraindicated: severe cardiogenic shock or severe bronchospasm.
4. Correct electrolytes: hypokalaemia (target K⁺ ≥4.5 mmol/L) and hypomagnesaemia (Mg²⁺ ≥0.8 mmol/L) are pro-arrhythmic substrates.
5. Urgent VT ablation: if VT storm continues despite pharmacological suppression → emergency catheter ablation of VT substrate. VT ablation in storm can be lifesaving; procedural risk is high but the alternative (untreated storm) has near-100% mortality.
6. ICD reprogramming: if patient has ICD — adjust ATP (antitachycardia pacing) settings with electrophysiology input. Inappropriate shock settings can worsen storm.

Warning: NEVER give IV verapamil or diltiazem for a wide complex tachycardia — even if you think it might be SVT with aberrancy. If the tachycardia is VT (and it almost certainly is, especially in a patient with known cardiomyopathy), verapamil causes vasodilation and negative inotropy → haemodynamic collapse → pulseless VT/VF → cardiac arrest. The rule: wide complex tachycardia = treat as VT until definitively proven otherwise. The proof requires AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, or an EP study — not just a ECG pattern that "looks like aberrancy."

Symptomatic bradycardia with haemodynamic compromise requires a response that progresses from pharmacological (atropine) to electrical (transcutaneous then transvenous pacing) within minutes. The key is identifying the level of block and predicting whether the escape rhythm is reliable or not.

Case: Syncope on the Ward — the Inferior MI Patient
A 60-year-old man was admitted 18 hours ago with inferior STEMI (successfully treated with primary PCI to the dominant RCA). He suddenly loses consciousness on the ward. The nurse calls for help. ECG monitor shows: complete heart block with a ventricular rate of 28 bpm, broad QRS escape complexes. BP 68/40 mmHg, unresponsive.
Complete heart block with haemodynamic collapse in the context of inferior STEMI. What is the management sequence?

## Bradyarrhythmia causes in the acute cardiac setting

- Inferior STEMI (RCA occlusion): the AV node is supplied by the RCA in 90% of patients. Inferior STEMI → AV nodal ischaemia → AV block (progresses from 1° → Mobitz I → complete heart block). The escape rhythm is usually junctional (narrow complex, rate 40–60 bpm) and relatively reliable. Often transient and reversible with reperfusion.
- Anterior STEMI (LAD occlusion): the bundle of His and bundle branches are supplied by the LAD. Anterior STEMI → infranodal block. Complete heart block from anterior MI carries a ventricular escape rate of 20–40 bpm (unreliable, may not sustain). This is the most dangerous AV block — it implies a very large area of myocardial damage.
- Drug-induced bradycardia: beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, amiodarone, anti-cholinesterase inhibitors (organophosphate poisoning).
- Hyperkalemia: sinoventricular conduction → progressively widening QRS + bradycardia → sine-wave pattern. Check K⁺ in any bradycardia of unclear aetiology.
- Sick sinus syndrome: profound sinus pauses post-tachycardia (tachy-brady syndrome).
- Hypothyroidism: sinus bradycardia, slow rate, flat T waves.

## Emergency management algorithm — symptomatic bradycardia

Algorithm: Symptomatic Bradycardia — Emergency Management
1. Is the patient haemodynamically compromised? (BP <90 mmHg, syncope/presyncope, acute HF, chest pain). If YES → proceed immediately to steps 2+. If NO and HR >40 bpm → monitor, prepare for pacing, seek reversible cause.
2. IV Atropine 0.5 mg — give immediately. Repeat every 3–5 min up to 3 mg total. Atropine blocks vagal tone → increases SA node rate → speeds AV conduction. Effective for: sinus bradycardia, 1° AV block, Mobitz I. Less effective for: Mobitz II, complete heart block with infranodal escape (the block is below the vagal input → atropine cannot overcome it). May worsen infranodal block paradoxically (increases sinus rate → more P waves hitting a blocked AV node → increases metabolic demand without improving ventricular rate).
3. Transcutaneous pacing — if atropine inadequate or no response. Apply pads (anterior-posterior if possible — better capture than anterior-lateral). Set rate 70–80 bpm, start at minimum mA and increase until electrical capture (QRS after pacing spike, 1:1 capture). Confirm mechanical capture: feel femoral pulse for each QRS or check SpO₂ waveform. This is painful — IV analgesia/sedation (morphine 2–4 mg IV or fentanyl 25–50 mcg) is mandatory for conscious patients.
4. Isoprenaline (isoproterenol) infusion — 0.02–0.1 mcg/kg/min IV. Pure β1/β2 agonist → ↑ HR and improves AV conduction. Used as a bridge when transcutaneous pacing is inadequate or not available. Increases myocardial O₂ demand — use with caution in ischaemia.
5. Transvenous pacemaker (TVP) — the definitive temporary intervention. A pacing lead is inserted via the femoral or internal jugular vein → into the right ventricle → delivers reliable RV pacing. Requires fluoroscopy or echo guidance. This is the correct management for any high-degree AV block with haemodynamic compromise in a cardiac patient. Should be arranged within minutes to an hour of presentation.
6. Permanent pacemaker — if the cause of bradycardia is irreversible or structural (not expected to recover). In inferior STEMI with AV block: usually resolves within 3–7 days — temporary pacing, PPM rarely needed. In anterior STEMI: AV block may be permanent → PPM at 5–7 days if not resolved. Criteria for PPM post-MI: see Chapter 7 in the Arrhythmia Deep Dive guide.

## Returning to the case — and the inferior MI specifics

Complete heart block post-inferior STEMI is usually an AV nodal block (not infranodal) — the escape rhythm is junctional at 40–60 bpm. In this patient the escape is 28 bpm and broad complex — suggesting either the AV nodal ischaemia is profound or there is concurrent right bundle branch involvement. The RCA-territory block:

- Atropine 0.5 mg IV → repeat to 1.5 mg if response occurs (look for acceleration of junctional escape to 40–60 bpm)
- Transcutaneous pacing immediately (he is haemodynamically collapsed — atropine can be given during pad application)
- Transvenous pacemaker urgently — in a patient who has already had primary PCI, the catheterisation lab team is likely still available; transvenous pacing can be inserted from the femoral venous approach under fluoroscopy
- AV block post-inferior STEMI: usually resolves within 48–72 hours as the AV nodal ischaemia resolves with reperfusion — bridge with TVP, reassess at 48–72h. If block persists >5–7 days → permanent pacemaker discussion.

Flash pulmonary oedema — the patient sitting bolt upright, gasping, SpO₂ 80%, soaking wet — is one of the most immediately threatening presentations in cardiology. The treatment is fast, layered, and highly effective when correctly applied. The goal is to reduce preload, reduce afterload, and support ventilation without drowning the patient in the process.

Case: The Man Who Couldn't Lie Down
A 72-year-old man with known HFrEF (EF 30%) is brought in by his daughter at midnight. She found him sitting up in bed, unable to lie down, gasping for breath. He has been on furosemide 40 mg OD and carvedilol 12.5 mg BD but admits he "stopped his water tablet 3 days ago." BP 195/110 mmHg, HR 110 bpm irregular (AF), RR 36 breaths/min, SpO₂ 79% on room air. He is in a cold sweat, using all accessory muscles. Bilateral fine to coarse crepitations to the apices. JVP elevated at 5 cm. CXR shows bilateral perihilar haziness ("bat wings"), upper lobe blood diversion, and cardiomegaly.
Flash pulmonary oedema in decompensated HFrEF triggered by medication non-adherence. What are the simultaneous treatment priorities in the first 30 minutes?

## Pathophysiology of acute pulmonary oedema

Acute pulmonary oedema develops when pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) rises above the oncotic pressure of plasma (~25 mmHg) → fluid transudation into the alveolar and interstitial spaces → impaired gas exchange. In HFrEF: the failing LV cannot eject adequately → LV end-diastolic pressure rises → LA pressure rises → pulmonary venous pressure rises → pulmonary oedema. The increased work of breathing (stiff, fluid-filled lungs) further increases oxygen demand → a vicious cycle of increasing hypoxia, tachycardia, and more LV failure.

## Immediate management — the LMNOP framework

All actions in the first 15 minutes are simultaneous — not sequential:

Drug: L — Upright position (Legs down)
Sit the patient upright (90°), legs dangling over the bed edge. This transfers approximately 500 mL of blood from the lungs to the dependent lower extremities by gravity → reduces venous return → reduces pulmonary venous pressure. Simple. Free. Effective within 2 minutes. Never lay a pulmonary oedema patient flat — it dramatically worsens their respiratory distress and can precipitate arrest.

Drug: M — Morphine (with caution)
2–4 mg IV slowly. Reduces anxiety (sympathetic activation worsens vasoconstriction), reduces respiratory distress, mild venodilatory effect → reduces preload. Caution: morphine in acute HF was associated with worse outcomes in observational data (ADHERE registry) — possibly from respiratory depression masking deterioration or reducing the drive to seek ventilatory support. Use with caution, in small doses, only if patient is very distressed and not at risk of respiratory arrest. Not routinely recommended by ESC 2021 — consider non-opioid sedation or early NIV instead.

Drug: N — Non-invasive ventilation (CPAP or BiPAP)
CPAP 5–10 cmH₂O → continuous positive airway pressure → recruits collapsed alveoli, reduces work of breathing, reduces preload by increasing intrathoracic pressure, improves oxygenation dramatically. Start within 5–10 minutes of presentation if SpO₂ <90% or RR >25 despite oxygen. BiPAP (two-level positive pressure) → provides inspiratory pressure support + PEEP → better for hypercapnic patients or those too weak to breathe against CPAP alone. Target: SpO₂ ≥94%, RR <25/min, improvement in distress within 15–20 min. If no improvement → consider intubation.

Drug: O — Oxygen supplementation
High-flow O₂ via non-rebreather mask 15 L/min while CPAP is being set up. Do NOT use low-flow nasal cannula alone in SpO₂ <85% — insufficient flow. If SpO₂ doesn't improve → CPAP is more effective than increasing O₂ flow.

Drug: P — IV Furosemide (diuretic)
Start with IV furosemide 40–80 mg bolus (40 mg if not on oral furosemide; 80 mg or 1.5× the oral dose if already on diuretics). IV furosemide has two mechanisms: (1) within 15 minutes → venodilatory effect (reduces preload before diuresis begins); (2) over 1–2 hours → diuresis → removes excess fluid. Monitor urine output. If insufficient response at 1–2h → double the dose or add furosemide infusion (5–10 mg/h). Target: ≥0.5 mL/kg/h urine output. Monitor K⁺ and creatinine (diuresis → hypokalaemia and renal impairment risk).

Drug: P — IV Vasodilators (for hypertensive pulmonary oedema)
This patient has BP 195/110 mmHg — hypertensive pulmonary oedema is primarily a pressure problem. Vasodilators dramatically reduce afterload → relieve the LV, reduce pulmonary venous pressure, improve forward CO: IV GTN (glyceryl trinitrate): 5–20 mcg/min infusion (start 5, titrate to symptom relief while maintaining SBP ≥100 mmHg). At low doses → venodilator (↓ preload). At higher doses → arteriolar vasodilator (↓ afterload). Most effective drug for hypertensive pulmonary oedema. IV sodium nitroprusside: 0.3–5 mcg/kg/min — more powerful arteriolar vasodilator than GTN. More rapid BP control but requires arterial line monitoring. Reserved for refractory hypertensive oedema. Contraindication: Do NOT use vasodilators if SBP <90 mmHg — in cardiogenic shock, vasodilators cause haemodynamic collapse.

## Precipitants of acute HF decompensation — the "CHAMPIONS" mnemonic

Every patient with acute HF should have their precipitant identified and treated — medical therapy alone treats the consequence, not the cause:

- C — Coronary event (ACS triggering acute HF)
- H — Hypertension (uncontrolled — flash oedema)
- A — Arrhythmia (AF with rapid rate → HF decompensation)
- M — Medications stopped or non-adherence (this patient!)
- P — Pulmonary embolism
- I — Infection/Inflammation (sepsis, myocarditis, endocarditis)
- O — Overload (fluid, sodium, iatrogenic IV fluids)
- N — Non-compliance with diet (high salt intake)
- S — Surgery / Stress

## Returning to the case — integrated management

Simultaneous first 15 minutes: (1) Sit upright, legs over the side; (2) High-flow O₂ → start CPAP 7.5 cmH₂O immediately (SpO₂ 79% — no time to wait); (3) IV access × 2, 12-lead ECG (AF confirmed — rate control: IV metoprolol 2.5–5 mg or digoxin 0.5 mg IV if EF <40%); (4) IV furosemide 80 mg IV bolus; (5) IV GTN 5 mcg/min → titrate up to 20 mcg/min (BP 195/110 → target SBP 150–160 mmHg in the first 60 minutes, not aggressive normalisation). At 30 minutes: reassess SpO₂, RR, BP, and comfort. Most patients respond to this combination within 30–60 minutes. If not improving → consider intubation and mechanical ventilation (protect the airway before the patient arrests, not after).
